SEA DREAMING& To day a bird, on wings as white as foam That crests the blue gray wave, With the vesper light upon its breast, flew homer Seaward. The God who gave To the birds the virgin-wings of snow Somehow telleth them the way they go. Unto the Evening went the white-winged bird— Gray clouds hung round the west— And far away the tempest's tramp was heard The bird flew for a rest Away from the grove, out to the sea— ls it only a bird's mystery? Nay! nay! lone bird ! I watched thy wings of white That cleft thy waveward way— Past the Evening and swift into the Night Out of the calm, bright Day— And thou didst teach me, bird of the sea, More than one human heart's history. Only men's hearts—tho' God shows each its way That leadeth hence to home— Unlike the wild sea birds, somehow go astray, Seeking in the far foam Of this strange world's tempest-trampled main A resting-place—but they seek in vain. Only the bird can rest upon the deep And sleep upon the wave; And dream its peaceful dreams where wild winds sweep And sweet the God who gave - -.it-place on the restless sea— The bird a • r,ot Ills way with thee. But this, my heart, Ls _.. Over the world, ah! passiou's tem,.-,est3 roll— And every fleck of foam Whitens the place where sank some sin-wrecks foul That never shall reach home. Ah the tranquil shore of God's sweet, cairn grace, My heart 1 is thy only safe resting-place. —Leeds Mercury. FATHER n.y.LN.

THINGS ern WOULD RATHER HAVE LETT UNSAID.— Nervous Person (speaking at late to his neighbour): " Do you know who that remarkably ugly person is just opposite —talking tc the black-haired lady, you know—um—eh ?" Neighbour: That, Sir, is my brother !"—Nervous Person: " Yes ? I—l—l beg your pardon—l—l—Stupid of me not to have seen the family likeness—A—A—A— -" [Collapses and disappears].—Punch. A Com 'erre THE EVE.—ThIS is a very common affection, and consists of an inflamed condition of the membrane covering the eye-ball and lining the eye-lids, and is often due, as the name impliee, to exposure to a draught. The patient feels as if some dust had got into the eye, and can sometime be hardly persuaded to the contrary; the white of the eye itself is seen to be reddened, and there is a Con- stant flow of blinding scalding tears. The best treatment is to foment the eyes with pure warm water, or better, with water in which two or three crashed pappy-heeds have been boiled for half an hour, to extract their sedative qualities A shade should be worn over the evea daring the intervals of fomenting, and a dose of rhubarb and magnesia should be administered. If the infl inn:Wien dues not sneside in a day or two, a doctor should be consulted, if possible; but. it this is not possible, good will probably be done by drop- ping into the eyes, two or three times a day, some solution of sulphate of zinc or white vitriol, in the proportion of one grain to two tablespoonfuls of water.—The Family Physi- cian. A BEIrD BOYS' ADVENTURES.—" I was very fond of hunting and flailing, in company with my brothers. I could ascend ths most inaccessible mountain cliffs; I became an expert clinaher. Once far from home we decided to quit the path, and descend the steep face of the mountain, swinging oarselvesefrom tree to tree. I could climb any tree that I could clasp with my arcs. In my boy-life among the mountains my chief enemies were the snakes, rattle-snakes, copper-heads, cotton-mouths, and vipers. Often I stepped unconsciously over them, sometimes on them. Once, work- ing in the corn-fields, I took up a Large snake in an armful of corn. it struggled to free itself; I felt it. and threw it violently from me, which probably saved my life; the snake was killed,-and I resumed work. I wonder if I have the moral courage to face equal dangers and difficultiee still ! To all our farm animals I was devoted, especially the farm horses. My father kept one especially for me. She was a fiery, wide-a-wake little cob, but if else had been a human being she could not have understood my blindness better. She would acme to me anywhere—wait patiently for me to mount, which I could do without saddle or bridle—and though on her metal with others, with me she always picked her way. Even in the mountains I could trust her impli- citly. giving her the rein in difficult places, sure that she would carry me safely over."—Good Words. Tree RrGeer SORT OF Max.—You will 'End, as a rule, that the men who ara favourites with men are the best and truest in their relations to women Yee, the men who turn their 'backs on all women and go off "with the other fellows," e.nd have a good boyish time on the water, 'or on the mountain, or in -come other man's "den." Women never need be afraid to trust their happiness to those whom other gocd men esteem good fellows ; but if a man is avoided by men, however mue-la women admire him, shun him. It is he who has flirtations that come to nothing, and has "not been very nice" to the girls who have broken their eg a • ments with him; who, when he marries, wrings hispg wife's heart, If she has one, and spoils her temper if she le naturally an angel. Manly men are the beet lovers, the beet husbands the best •companions for women, just as womanly women are the best sweethearts and wives.. What do we think of women who shun their own sex, however charming men may find them? It is seldom, if ever, that your men's favourite ill-uses his wife. perhaps it may be explained in this way—friendship of a sublimated sort is what love be- comes after a year or so of marriage, and he who is friendly to the very depths of his soul enters into this state happily, and is ready for all the delights that follow But a man who Is capable of nothing but that fleeting affection which ever pursues a new object, and cares for no woman when she is won, hates the domestic ties, and becomes detestable in con- sequence. It is the man who would die for his friend, and for whom his friend would die, who makes a miraculously happy wife of the woman to whom he scarcely knew how to make love when he courted her. Mr. Sutton, of Ballarat, has improved his electr:cal storage battery, by a newly-constructed cell, which ha describes as a flat copper case shaped as a Grove's cell. - a view to make aix the spring brings a new pressure of work. vv „ some sharp weather yet, so be not lulled into imaginary se- curity by the growing of the grass and the evident inclina- tion of the trees to push their leaves before their time. All lands needed for summer cropping should be broken up with- out delay, for good winter work goes a long way towards a golden harvest. • Grass lands will soon require attention now, more especially such as require a top-dressing prepara- tory to the hay crop.—The Gardener's Magazine. FIELD EXPEEIMENT.—Professor Scott, in his report at the close of the College term, says that the following conclu- sions are to be deduced from the field experiments which have been carried on this year at the Royal Agricultural College, Cirencester :—I. Unmixed Manures on draSg ry, F. (a) The effects of nitrate of soda and of sulphate of am- monia were equal, and surpassed all other manures used. THE CONSUMPTION OF FOREIGN CHEESES IN ENGLAND. —Year by year, and rapidly during the past year, the con- sanption of foreign fancy cheeses has increased in this country, and there must have been a corresponding decline in the consumption of home-made produce. The Lancet has recently noticed this circumstance and has made the following cemments on it :—" Everyone must have noticed the great increase which has taken place of late years in the censumption of foreign cheese in England. Gruyere, Cemembert, Roquefort, and Gorgonzola, not to speak of Bondon, Brie, and Parmesan, which a few years ago were hardly known in this country, are now to be found in thou- sands of houses and in almost all hotels. We are inclined to think that this apparent alteration in public taste is due in put to a deterioration in the quality of English cheese. American cheese of goed thotegh ordinary quality has come over in enormous quantities, and can be sold at a low price. The English makers seem to have been discouraged by this competition, and instead of endeavouring to raise the quality of their goods, they have fallen beck on the never-failing demand for milk, and have stopped or diminished the manu- facture of cheese; and, what is worse, have become careless in its manufacture. Chee,e imported from abroad is almost invariably good, and offers a great variety of delicate fiavours. The makers of some of the best kinds are able to produce that much-prizid green mould formerly so often and now so seldom seen in English cheese. Even Stilton seems to us to be harder and drier than it used to be. Surely careful study would Vetch English makers to keep up with their Continental rivals, and So preserve to this country a manufacture which was formerly so important and lucra- tive. They probably could not compete with the Americana aad Duteh in the commoner makes, but they might surely ' rival other countries in the production of the finer kinds." The facts are undoubtedly as the Lancet has staled them, . but we do not endorse all the deductions made from them. The fancy foreign cheeses come into competition with Eng- lish stilton and the finest makes of Cheddar and Cheshire, and it is the few, not the many, who consume these luxu- ries. It is quite possible that fancy cheeses could be made here which would find equal favour with consumers; we can see nothing to prevent it but the want of enterprise which characterises British farmers. Nevertheless, the cheese-making industry of this country has been depressed by the competition from the United States in what may be termed household cheeses rather than by the consumption of fancy foreign cheeses in hotels and restaurants. It is the whole-milk factory cheese of the United States which has beaten the English producer out of the field, and we can see no other means of meeting this competition successfully than that of adopting the factory system at horde. Cheese for the million must form the staple of the home producers' industry, and to hold their own with regard to this article British farmers will have to fight the United States farmers with their own weapone.—Mark Lane Express. THE CONVEYANCg OP STEAM.—The convevande to long —..ncea of ir.teata for power or heating purposes has long been a problem with engineers, and its use has in many in- stances been discarded for compressed air. In fact, the measure of the distance to which steam may be carried with economy is not yet determined. A suggestion is now made by which owners of establishments in which steam is largely used might effect a large saving by concentrating their boilers in one place adjacent to a railway station or to the shore, or even constructing a large central boiler, where their coal may all be landed and used without cartage, and thence distributing the stet i to their several works. The difficulty has al7;:ays been to find a coating for steam-pipes Absohrtely preventing the radiation of heat, and, according to the Boston Journal of Comnerce, such a cmrering may now be prepared. It is made of four parts coal ashes sifted through a riddle of four meshes to the inch, one part cal- cined plaster, one part flour, and one part fireclay. Mix the ashes and fireclay together to the thickness of thin mortar, in a mortar trough; mix the calcined plaster and flour together, dry, and add it to the ashes and clay as you want to use it; put it on the pipes in two coats, according to the size of the pipes, For A 6-inch pipe put on the first coat ainui 1.4- inch tuck; the sect)lid coat wants to be about inch thick. Afterwards finish the outside with hard fiaish, same as is applied to plastering on a wall, We think it would not be unprofitable to make experiments here as above suggested.—lron. THE EFFECTS OF COLD ON STEEL.—From observations made on Rassian railways it appears that the frequency of fractures of steel rails rises as the temperature falls, the Pentage of breakages having been found highest in March (18 per cent.) and lowest in June and August (3 per cent.). The same condition has been observed to prevail on German railways in the case of tires. From figures pub- lished we learn that from October 1, 1879, to March 31, 1880, 480 fractures of tires, or 18.9 per cent., Occurred while the temperature was above zero; 105 fractures, or 4.1 per cent., at zero, and 1,952 fractures, or 77 per cent., at tem- peratures below zero. The greatest number of fractures happened on December 9, 10, 17, and 23, 1879. The above interesting data prove, what has been advanced before, that the frequency of fractures during the period stated must be attributed to its abnormal atmospheric conditions. Of the fractures recorded, 3,269 occurred in ingot steel tires (cru- cible, Bessemer, Martin, and manganese steel) and 1,045 in tires of puddled steel or wrought iron. Although the num- ber of tires which were under observation is not classified as to description, the figures given enable us to draw the inference that paddled steel and wrought iron compare favourably with steel. Tires of fine-grained iron and paddled steel appear to be safer, while ingot steel offers greater advantages as to wearing. The thickness of tires also plays an important part in their resistance to the effects of told, the greater number of fractures occurring in Close of smaller thicknesses.—lron.

THE TELERADIOPHONE. M. Merca.dier, the eminent French electrician, has ingeniously adapted the photophone of Professor Bell to telegraphy. In the photophene a ray of light is reflected by a mirror, so as to fall upon the sensi- tive surface of a "selenium cell" joined up in the circuit of a voltaic battery and a speaking telephone. When the light strikes the cell its electric resistance is diminished, and a wave or. pulse of current flows through the telephone, causing it to sound. By eclipsing the ray of light a great many times per second, this sound can be exalted into a continuous hum, like that of a tuning fork, and by again occulting the intermittent ray for long and short intervals, corresponding to the fla.shas of a signalling lantern, this hum or drone can be broken up into audible signals. Thus, if the Morse telegraphic code is used a short occultation, producing a short pause in the note of the telephone, will stand for a "dot" and along occnitation, producing a long pause, will stand for a "dash." This photo-electric tele- graph is realised by M. Mercadier with the help of a gas flame forming the source of light, a mirror and lenses to direct its rays upon the selenium cell in circuit with a bat- tery and the line wire. The beam is regularly eclipsed by means of a rapidly rotating disc, perforated with a circle of holes, tied the telegraphic occultations of the intermittent beam are effected by means of a signalling key, which in- terposes a dead screen in the track of the light whenever the key is pressed. These apparatus form the transmitter, and the receiver at the other end of the line is of course the telephone, which is fitted with a resonator to reinforce the sound. There is no gain in such an arrangement over the ordinary telegraph now in use; but it has the merit of lending itself to multiple telegraphy. Thus by multiplying the number of transmitters at one end of the line and thel number of telephones at the other, several different mes- sages can be sent along the same wire at once. In order to do this it is only necessary to rotate the eclipsing wheels at different speeds, so as to produce notes of different pitch in tbe receiving telephones, and to fit each resonator PO as to enhance a particular note. Then, although the complex current flows through all the telephones in turn, each tele- phone will only render to the ear of the clerk the particular note for which he listens, and the makes and breaks of tlat note will be interpreted as the message. Not bnly can several messages be sent in one direction along the same wire together, but from opposite ends simultaneously with- out confusion, and M. Mercadier reckons that with 10 trans- mitters and 10 receivers at each end of a line he can send 200 despatches ol 30 words each per hour, or 100 words per minute, in either direction. The effects of induction, so troublesome in speaking by telephone, are not experienced in this process owing to the employment of musical notes and resonators.

Humoun AT HomE.—A good thing to have in the house is a sense of humour, or the capacity to see a little fun lurking under the humdrum cares and work of life. We all know how it brightens up things generally to have a lively, witty companion, who sees the ridiculous points of things, and who can turn an annoyance into an occaston for laugh- ter. It is a great deal better to laugh over some domestic mishaps than to cry or scold over them. Many homes are dull because they are allowed to become too deeply im- pressed with the cares and responsibilities of life to recog- nise its bright and especially its mirthful side. Into such a household, good but dull, the advent of a witty, humorous friend is like sunshine an a cloudy day. While it is always oppressive to hear persons constantly striving to say witty and fanny things, it is comfortable to see what a brightener a little fun is—to melee an effort to see some at home. It is well to turn off an impatient question sometimes and to regard it from a humorous point of view, instead of becom• lug irritated about it. " Wife, what is the reason I can never find a clean shirt?" exclaimed a good but rather im- patient husband, pfter rumaging all through the wrong drawers. His wife looked at him steadily for a moment, half inclined to be provoked, then, with a comical look, she said, "I never could guess conundrums ; I give it up." Then he laughed, and they both laughed, and she went and got his shirt, and he felt ashamed of himself and kissed her; and then he felt happy; so what might have been an occa- sion for hard words and unkind feeling became just the contrary, all through the little vein of humour that cropped out to the surface. Some children have a peculiar faculty for a humorous turn of things when they are reproved. T does just as well to laugh things off as to scold them r-t Laughter is better than tears. Let us have a little - „ 4,1,1 it at home.

IL LUSi'PLIOITS IRISH 'JEN. No.IV.—HENRY GRA TTAN. Ever glorious Grattan! the best of the good ! So simple in heart, so sublime in the rest! With all which Demosthenes wanted endued, And his rival or victor in all he possess'd. Ere Tully arose in the zenith of-Rome. Though unequall'd, preceded, the task was began But Grattan sprung up like a god from the tomb Of ages, the first, last, and saviour, the one! With the skill of an Orpheus to soften the brute, the fire of Prometheus to kindle mankind, Even tyranny listening, sat melted or mute, And corruption shrunk, shamed from the glance of his mind, Byron. The first Octennial Parliament will ever be memorable in the annals of Ireland because in it one of the greatest patriots who ever arose for the salvation of any people took his seat as a member for Lord Charlemont's Borough. This new member was Henry Grattan, son of the Recorder for Dublin, and a descendant of the po.werful and influential family of whom Jonathan Swift had said,-.-" The Grattane can raise 10,000 men." He appeared in Parliatnent at a very °pi:T.oPa time for himself. There was in the Irish House of Commons a lamentable dearth of genuine eloquence. Flood had deserted his party and the 'band of patriots' was without a leader. There was no one who with commanding eloquence could assert the principles of Molyneux and Swift; When, therefore, the greatest orator of the day appeared upon the scene as the champion of Ireland's rights, and the denunciator of Ireland's wrongs, the disheartened band of patriots rallied round him, and with one consent acknow- ledged him as their leader. It was not, however, during this Parliament, which only lasted four years, that Grattan gained for himself the position which his eminent .t:,!lvits entitled him to occupy. During this ^ P.:,:iianaent he made it his study to acquaint Wapiti with the detsils of public business. Z.7the torr.:l's of the House. It was not until the Meeting Of the new Parliament under the Administration of Lord Buckinghamshire that Grattan's lofty character and splendid genius became known to his countrymen and to the world.

In 1775, last as hostilities commenced between England and her American Colonies, Lord Harcourt demanded the services of 4,000 men out of the 12,000 which then consti- tuted the effective force of regular troops in Ireland, to be despatched to America for duty there. At the same time the Lord-Lieutenant said it was His Majesty's intention to supply the place of the 4,000 with Protestant soldiers, in short, with Hessians. Tee Parliament agreed to send these 4,000 "armed negotiators," as Flood called them; "to cut the throat e of the Americans," as another expressed it; but refused to accept the Hessians. Indeed, the Irish Parlia- ment refused to accept the servicee of any foreign soldiers by 106 votes to 68. The House accordingly voted an ad- dress to his Excellency expressive of their sense and resolu- tion upon this subject, stating that "with the assistance of the Grovernment His Majesty's loyal p Ireland mayeeplee 12e able so to exeri therneelVe4 a io inak6 such ail at this juncture unnecessary." No sooner had the troops left for America than Ireland was threatened with a French inva- sion. Then arose one of those national movements of en- thusiasm that occur now and then in a nation's history. So alarmed was the Government that in 1788 the Irish Parlia- ment passed a Militia Bill authorising the formation of Volunteer forces for the defence of the country. The cry to arms passed through the land, and was speedily responded to by all classes and creeds. Up sprang as if by magic, or like Rhoderick Dhu's men, a host of Irish Volunteers, From TloA•th Connemara, from the Giant'i! Causeway to Cape Olear, the spirit of enthnsiasne pae.eed, and the ranks of Patriot Band swelled till it became more than 75,000 strong, determined to defend their country, not only from the foreign invader, but from the encroachments of alien legis- lation. Faithful to the connection between the two islands, they determined that the connection should rest upon mutual respect; In Vac words of one of their reeolations, "They knew their duty to their Sovereign, and they were loyal; they knew their duty to themselves, and they were resolved to be free." And these professions were justified by the men whom the Volunteers selected as their officers. "Whom," asks Mac Nevin, "did this Democratic army se- lect to rule their councils and direct their powers? Not the low ambitious, not the village vulgar brawlers, but the men who by large possessions, lofty character, and better still, by virtue and by genius, had given to their names a larger patent than nobility. Flood, and Grattan, and Cherie- relent, and Leinster, the chosen men in the Liberal profes- sions—the orators who led the Patriot Party in the House of Commons—the good, the high, the noble—these were the officers who held unpurchased honours in the Volunteers. We may well look back with mournful pride through the horrid chaos where rebellion and national ruin rule the murky night to this one hour of glory, of power uncorrup- ted, and of opportunities unabused." The Volunteers soon spoke in no uncertain tones on Irish politics. They formed themselves into a regular Conven- tion to consider the condition of the country, for they held " that citizens by learning the use of arms did not forfeit their civil rights." They first of all condemned the com- mercial restrictions of the country, and the first measure they adopted to convince England that Ireland NM entitled to an unrestricted trade was "the nonimportation agree- ment," which many of the Volunteer Corps, as well as town Corporations, solemnly adopted by resolution daring the year 1779. In consequence of these resolutions the manu- factures of Ireland began to thrive, and the demand for British goods in a great at tied/vase& a circumstance which tended to produce a disposition in England to attend to the complaints of the country different indeed from that which Ireland had hitherto experienced. It cannot be denied that this agreement also produced a feeling of irritation, and the Government partisans did, not hesitate to cleneunce the Volunteers and the commercill movement. Lord Shelhourne designated the Irish army an "enraged mob"—a desigfia- tion which was partly true and partly false. They were enraged, but they were not a mob. They had no one quality of a mob. They had discipline, arms, and a mili- tary system. Their ranks were filled with gentlemen, and officered by notice. • The voice of the enraged and louder in its denun. mob, however, waxed stronger 'e-sation of the commercial restrictions of the country, an. the Hoe 44 when the question of supplies came be- forese on the 25th Nov., 1779; the Patriots, backed -Volunteers, determined to withhold the grant or to by til mlt the duration of the Money Bill until Free Trade was yielded by England. The Attorney-General moved that the supplies be granted for two years. An amendment was moved that it be granted forsix months. A brilliant debate I followed, in which Hussey Burgh distinguished himself by the splendour of his oration. In concluding his speech he said :—" The usurped authority of a foreign Parliament has kept up the most wicked laws that a zealous, monopolising, ungrateful spirit could devise, to restrain the bounty of Providence and enslave a nation whose inhabitants are re- corded to be a brave, loyal, and generous people; by the English code of laws to answer the most sordid views.. e'„ey have been treated with a savage cruelty; the w.'erus penalty, punishment, and Ireland are synalymous, they are marked in blood on the margin of their statutes and though time may have softened the calamities of the nation, the baneful and destructive influences of those laws has borne her down to a state of Egyptian bondage. The English have sowed their laws like serpent's teeth, and they have sprung up in armed men." The amendment was carried by 138 to 100, and the triumph of the principles of Free Trade was insured. Vrnen Parliament met again in Oct., 1779 Burgh moved fte an amendment to the address from the I throne a 15ti'.7ron for "an extension of trade." Flood suggested that the expression "Free Trade" should be adopted , The amendment was carried, and the House went 'oody to present their petition to the Lord-Lieutenant, "while the Volunteers lined the road and presented arms to theer as they passed. Free Trade could no longer be with- held, and Lord North soon after brought forward a series of measures in the English Parliament which removed the chief grievances that were complained of. The Acts pro- hibiting the Irfish from exporting their woollen and glass manufactures were repealed, and the Colonial trade was thrown open to Ireland; And so for the first time since William 111. destroyed the woollen manufacture of Ireland, and his English Parliament laid restrictions on her produc- tive industry, her people were tree to use the resources a liberal nature offered:them, and which had been sealed from their anxious hands. - -

CHAMBERLAIN." A WORKHOUSE SCANDAL.—The Sheffield guardians were on Wednesday engaged in investigating a grave workhouse scandal. A man named John Wood, formerly a draper in Sheffield, but now in reduced circumstanees, became seri- ously ill at his lodgings, and was removed to the workhouse, where he died last Tuesday. The funeral was about to take place, but upon the coffin being opened that the relatives might see the deceased, it was found to contain the body of another man. Upon enquiry it was ascertained that Wood's body had been removed to the medical school, three miles away. It Was subsequently brought back, and the widow persisted tleat it bears the marks of tile lancet. This, how- ever, is denied, and it is affirmed that the body was removed by mistake. The guardians adjourned the inquiry, in order that the case might be thoroughly sifted. At a meeting of the Zetetical Society, held in London on Wednesday, Mr. Henry Richard, M.P., lectured on "The gradual triumph of law over brute force." Mr. Richard commenced by decrying the evils of war, and asked whether there could not be found any remedy by which great organised communities might be brought to recognise the jurisdiction of a common law, and to seek adjustment of *their disputes by a system of judicial reference in lieu of their present appeal to the arbitration of brute force. The history of the past pointed to that consummation as not only possible but certain, and those who fully believed this were only moving in a line with the inevitable laws of Pro- vidence. Some attempts had been made to bring communi- ties of men under the anthem ity and protection of general law, though in a very timid, hesitating, and tentative manner. Nations had agreed to appeal to certain usages that had been established by common consent as constitut- ing what was called international law. He urged that by degrees a code of international law should be formed to clear up the points which remained unsettled, and thus be the means, in the words of the late President Garfield, of "returning to productive industry millions of men now maintained to settle the disputes of nations by the bayonet and the broadsword."

The commercial tyranny of England being now broken down, and the country obviously ripe for a farther advance, Henry Grattan fixed the 19th of April, 1780, as the day on which he would make his celebrated Declaration of Rights. Accordingly on the date named he arose in his place in the Irish House of Commons and moved the three following resolutions :

Ist. That His Most Excellent Majesty, by and with the consent of the Lords and Commons of Ireland, are the only power competent to enact laws to bind Ireland. 2nd. That the Crown of Ireland is and ought to be in- separably annexed to the Crown of Great Britain. 3rd. That Great Britain and Ireland are inseparably united under one sovereign by the common and indissoluble ties of interest, loyalty, and freedom. Grattan moved these resolutions in a speech of splendid eloquence, in which he imparted to the doctrines of freedom .a more spiritual cast than they had ever before assumed in Ireland, and these resolutions were seconded by Mr. Stewart, father of the man who of all others was most active in destroying the great fabric of freedom which Henry Grattan commenced upon that day to rear. Flood, however, perceived that these resolutions were somewhat premature, and would have been defeated, and so had them withdrawn. Bat although the Declaration of Rights was not on this oc- casion pressed to a division, vet virtually its object was achieved. The eloquence of Grattan fired the Volunteers with redoubled enthusiasm in the cause of Irish Indepen- dence, and even the Government was forced to admit that the newly-born national spirit of Ireland was both strong and deeply rooted. Writing the day after to Lord Hills- borough Lord Buckinghamshire said :—" It is with the ut- most concern I must acquaint your Lordship that although so many gentlemen expressed their concern that the subject had been introduced, the sense of the House against any obligation of any statutes of the Parliament of Great Britain within this kingdom is represented to me to have been al- most unanimous."

But the cause of the country was soon removed to a higher court than that of 'a corrupt Parliament. The year 1781 had been a time of active organisation of the Volun- teers, and at length it was resolved to hold a Convention at Dungannon. This was Grattan's idea. He had failed in his endeavours to join issue with England by his Declara- tion of Rights in Parliament, and he resolved now to throw himself upon the country. Both friends and enemies of the Irish National cause were almost bewildered by the bold- ness of the conception. "Will nobody stop that madman Grattan ?" cried Edmund Burke. How A JEWELLER. GOT FLEECED.—" Of all the tricks, devices, subterfuges, sharp dodges, or deceptions I ever saw," said a jeweller to a reporter, "was one by which a sharp fellow stole from me three pairs of diamond ear-rings. He evidently knew when I was not in the store. He came in one day and said to one of my clerks: Mr. Johnson in?" Nu,' was the reply. lam sorry for that,' he said, 'I wish to bay a pair of diamond ear-rings for my wife.' This was repeated on four or five successive days. The last time he said he would not wait to sea me, but would look at some ear-rings. The clerk showed him an assortment, and he finally selected three pairs, valued at 450-dols., and said, I guess I will let my wife select from these. She will be at my store in an hour, and I want you to tell Mr. Johnson to bring these around himself, as he is acquainted with my wife." All right, sir, I will,' replied the clerk. 'By the way,' s tid the fellow, if you will permit me, I will write a note to Mr. Johnson." Certainly,' said the clerk, as he showed him to a desk, and painted out where he could get paper and envelopes. He sat down, wrote a short note, folded it, and pat it an an envelope and directed it to me. Then he went back to the counter and said to the clerk, "I think you had ' batter put three pairs of ear-rings in here, so that Mr. Johnson will be sure to bring the right ones." Very well,' said the clerk, who handed out three pairs of earrings. The fellow dropped them la the envelope before the Clerk's eyes, and was apparently about to seal tip the envelope when he til seddenly, 'Oh, I guess you may put in that other pair,' plintin,s to a pair which the clerk had laid on the shelf be- hind Win. The clerk turned and got the other pair and handed them to the fellow, who dropped them apparently into the same envelope, sealed them up, handed them over, and said, 'Let Mr. Johnson bring the four pairs to my store as soon as he cornea back,' giving the address of a well- known store in the vicinity. Then he left, and the clerk laid the envelope on one side until I returned. Of course we found but one pair of diamond ear-rings in-the envelope; which was the last pair dropped in. The other three pairs were paste, about the same size. The fellow had taken two of my envelopes, and into one he had placed the three bogus pairs. When the clerk turned to get the fourth pair the fellow had put the genuine into his pocket and substituted the others. Dungannon large enough to hold the assembled delegates, land so the church was used for that purpose. Every county in Ulster sent delegates, and the delegates who assembled represented 30,000 armed men. But though the Convention was composed of only Ulster representatives, the delegates felt that they had full power and credentials to deliberate and decide for a great army—not only for the Ulster Volun- teers, but for those in all Ireland. Grattan, in co-operation with Flood and Charlemont, drew up a series of resolutions, which were adopted unanimously, asserting the Irish Inde- pendence, and Grattan alone drew up another resolution expressing the gratification with which the Volunteers had witnessed the relaxation of the penal code. This was a reso- lution, the importance of which it is scarcely possible to exaggerate, "It marked," says Lecky, "the solemn union between the two sections of Irishmen for the purpose of ob- taining the recognition of the country's rights. It showed that the old policy of governing Ireland by the division of her sects had failed, and that if the independence of Parlia- ment was to be withheld it niaqt be withheld in opposition to a nation united and in arms." It was not long after this Convention when Lord North fell from power. and Charles Fox assumed the reigns of OVernment. On more than one occasion the new Premier 6ad exjre3sell viewi !..11 the British acmse of Commons in favour of granting Ireland her independende. )3ut now in office he seemed to think that the bite hld lordll ari4,7ed for granting it. He therefore endeavoured to persuade the Irish Leaders to relax their efforts. Grattan was breaking down in health. If Fox could influence Charlemont and others he might frustrate the hopes of Ireland for a time. He therefore wrote a flattering letter full of graceful com- pliments to his old and esteemed friend Lord Charlemont. These blandishments were almost too much for the Earl. Grattan perceived the danger, and from his slck bed wrote to Obarletnont vehemently exclaiming "No time! No Utile r, ai Chatiemont, fired once more into patriotic ardor, wrote to the English Prennier "that they" (the Irish Leaders) "could not delay, that they were pledged to the people, that they could not postpone the question tor that it was public property." Fox yielded. He would rather have seen Ire- land wholly separated from the Crown of England than kept in subjection by force. " Unwilling subjects," said he once, "are little better than enemies." The Duke of Portland accordingly was sent over as Lord Lieutenant with permis- sion to grant the required boon. On the 16th of April, 1782, the Declaratory Act of George I was repealed amid an out- burst of almost unparalleled enthusiasm. It was a never- to-be-forgotten day in history. Grattan had risen from his sick bed, and to the surprise of everyone was at his post "as the herald and oracle of his armed countrymen." It was a grand occasion, and the orator was equal to it. Emaciated and careworn as his slender fratzt appeared, his noble spirit shone brighter than ever as he rose to proclaim that the strife of six Oenturies had terminated—that the cause for which so mach blood had been shed and so much genius expenr'eed apparently in vain, was at last triumphant, and tl'.;;t a new era had dawned upon Ireland. In a few glowing sentences he painted the dreary struggle that had passed—the magnitude of the victory that had been achieved and the prospects that were unfolding concluding in the memorable words :—" I am now, he exclaimed, to address a free people. Ages have passed away, and this is the first moment in which you could be distinguished by that appel- lation. I have spoken on the subject of your liberty so often that I have nothing, to add, and have only to.admire by what heaven-directed steps you have proceeded until the whole faculty of the nation is braced up to the act of her own deliverance. I found Ireland on her knees. I have watched over her with a paternal solicitude. I have traced her progress from injuries to arms, and from arms to liberty. Spirit of Swift! spirit of Molyneux ! your genius has pre- vailed ! Ireland is now a nation. In that character I hail her, and, hewing in her august presence,l Say esto perpetual' The whole epAecla was worthy of the orator and of the occasion. An English critic says that his speech on this great day was distinguished for "its fire, sublimity, and immense reach of thought." Charlemont used often to say, "It ever spirit could be said tO act indvendent of body it was on that occasion." The whole House indeed was elec- trified and lost in admiration. Shortly after £100,009 was voted by Parliament to Grattan in recognition pf hiS Revices. Grattan reftsed so large a sum, and would only accept half. This grant enabled him to devote himself exclusively to the service of the country, without practising at the Bar, to which he had been called.

So the evidence might be multiplied ad infinitum, but we cannot refrain from giving one quotation from a speech by the late Bishop of Lichfield, as it relates to one of our own colonies, and "much-abused Pat." Bishop Selwyn said In New Zealand the English, Scotch, and Irish people live together on the best terms. The qualities of each class blend together for the improve-nent of all. No dispute as to tenant right can arise, because every tenant has the right of purchasing the land he holds at a fixed price. Under these circumstances the tenants, instead of being lazy and drunken, strain every nerve to become owners of the land they occupy. In this way it happens that the most irregular people of the Irish become steady and indus• trious, acquiring property, and losing all their wandering habits, and it becomes implssible to distinguish between the comparative value of the Irish and Scotch elements." It will appear conclusively, therefore, that wherever the Land Laws have been reformed in such a way as to multiply the number of ownerships, the capital and labour employed in agriculture, and the produce of the scil, are all very largely increased, the habits, social position, and character of the people much improved, and the greatest encourage- ment given to the home commerce and m anufactures, as the profit of the land is spent in the district, instead of being abstracted in the form of rent to be spent by the landlords in the metropolis, or in any country but their own, as is too often the case now. A further illustration of the great ad- vantages resulting from free land will be given in the next article respecting a portion of the United Kingdom, viz., the Channel Islands.

div.head: STATE OF IRELAND.
div.p: THE STATE OF IRELAND.

Mr. Dillon is said to be extremely ill. A car driver, returning to Mullingar, was brutally beaten, and his life is despaired of. No arrests have been made. • Thos. Kerley, shopkeeper, Frankford, King's County, and Wm. Hefferman, farmer, were arrested en Tuesday under the Cordon Act.

Lord Bandon has fixed the rent of his tenants, whose leases had expired, at about Griffith's valuation. They ex- pressed their satisfaction. The Sub-Commissioners at Armagh made some large reductions in rents on Thursday. A rent of .0 was dropped to £2, and one of £7 to £2 10e. Mr. Clifford Lloyd, R M., with a large detachment of police and military, made over forty arrests in counties Clare and Limerick on Saturday. The Lord Lieutenant has refused to permit representatives of the Dublin Corporation to visit Kilmainham Gaol to con- fer the city freedom upon Messrs. Parnell and Dillon. Lord Kenniare on Saturday refused a request from a large number of his tenants that he would accept their rents at the figures they paid before the present agent was appointed. A Limerick correspondent states that the dynamite magazine of Messrs. Cleeve and Co. was on Sunday night broken into, and 6201b5. of that explosive, with caps, taken away. A Tullamore telegram reports that on Monday night Mr. George Stephenson, manager of Messrs Goodbody's factory at Clara, where a strike recently took place, was fired at and dangerously wounded. A number of tenants on the estate of Count de Boissey have refused to pay any rent as long as " Mr. Gladstone and Mr. Forster rule Ireland." In a letter the Count says he will send the "British army " to evict them. On Monday night, at Kilcrohane, a dwelling-house and forge.of a smith named Sullivan, who shod the horses of some boycotted farmers, was burnt to the ground. The police are making every effort to arrest the incendiaries. The officers of Athlone garrison, having purchased a pack of harriers, attempted to hunt at Knockdowney, on Tues- day, but were attacked by men with farming implements. One officer received a severe blow from a coulter, and another had his clothes torn with a fork. Three dogs are missing. A Castlerea correspondent states that Thomas Abeam, process officer, was shot in his own house at Granlogan on Sundae., night, at about ten o'clock, and died from his wound. rt is added that the deceased some time since lost one of his eyes from the effects of a beating which he received in the course of an attenipt to serve ejectment processes. A Dublin telegram states that there are now nearly 70,000 claims for the fixing of fair rents listed in the Land Court. There is a rumour of the appointment of six mo-e sub-com- missioners, as the rate of business with the 12 is very slow. The 12 sub-commissioners are dealing on an average with at most 30 claims each in a week, making a total per week of about M. On an average not more than 40 cases are settle" during a week out of court. At the Munster assizes, on Saturday, Timothy Byan and James Driscoll were sentenced each to seven years' penal servitude for having grievously wounded, at Skibbereen, a farmer named Sullivan, who subsequently died. Cornelius M'Auliffe was sentenced to seven years' penal servitude fur having formed one of an armed disguised party who attacked the dwelling of Eugene Mahony, at Newmarket. James Cahill and John Cusson pleaded guilty to a similar offence in County Limerick; sentence deferred. A Washington telegram states that at Monday's sitting of the House of Representatives Mr. Outh repo-ted back from the Foreign Relations Committee a resolution that Presi- dent Arthur be requested to obtain a list of American citizens now imprisoned by the British Government, especially in Ireland. Mr. Robinson, one of the members for New York, discussed the resolution, declaring that there were five Americans now confined in English prisons, and that the United States Government should demand their release. On Saturday the police succeeded in seizing no lees than 10,000 copies of United Ineland at the North Wall, Dublin. The papers were enclosed in strong timber cases, such as those in which bacon is usually packed, and purported to come from " Kearney Station, Liverpool," and addressed "Kavanagh and Co., wholesale paper merchants, Merchant's quay," but no such person is known. Inside the papers were made up in packages as if they were loaves of sugar, and they were addressed to different newsagents throughout the country to be forwarded by rail. The case containing papers came by a City of Dublin Steam Packet Company's steamer, which arrived from Liverpool on Saturday after- noon at North Wall. At Munster Assizes, on Tuesday, three members of the Gladworth Land League, Staunton and Hannon, farmers, and Connell. newspaper correspondent, were charged with having intimidated John Fleming, under agent of the Earl of Donoughmore, to quit his employment. Fleming was hooted by a crowd, of which the prisoners formed part, and took refuge in a house until the police arrived. The jury acquitted Staunton and Hannon, but disagreed with respect to Connell, who was allowed out until next Assizes. Maurice Wallace, Doctor Wales, James and John Leahy pleaded guilty to wounding Michael O'Brien, near Kilmallock. Maurice Wallace, who stabbed O'Brien, was sentenced to three months imprisonment; the others were discharged on giving bail. Archbishop Croke, speaking at Waterford on Sunday afternoon, said the land agitation had done an immense amount of good for the people. It might be said to have re- duced the rental of Ireland by one quarter, so that, taking the entire rental at twenty millions, it placed five millions a year in the pockets of the tenant farmers of Ireland. The effect of this would be to prevent the Irishman planting his foot upon the emigrant ship to seek a living in foreign lands. He was against emigration. They, as Irishmen, had as much right to live in Ireland as Frenchmen had to live in France. But what was the fact? While only 300,000 Frenchmen were living away from France, for they loved their country, there was no country in the world from which more people ' had gone than from Ireland. The Cork Assizes, which, excepting the Christmas holi- days, had lasted from the 6th December, were brought to a close on Wednesday. Sentences of imprisonment for terms ranging from twelve months to two years were pissed on a number of men convicted of " Whiteboy " offences. The indictments against the informer Connell were withdrawn. Mr. Justice Fitzgerald said the jurors had discharged their duties with wonderful discrimination' impartiality, and fear- lessness, and be was not without hope that good might I result from this protracted assize. He hinted that when , peace was restored to the country the Government might be willing to reconsider some of the sentences which had been I passed, and he advised the people to lend their aid to the law in putting down outrage. In conclusion the learned Judge said it appeared to him there had been too much I cowardice among the people—cowardice created by too much protection. He was amazed at the extent to which the con- I stabulary had been employed in the work of protection ; if people were not prepared to defend themselves they were not worth defending. In the Queen's Bench, on Saturday, the Lord Chief Justice . delivered judgement on the legality of imprisoning the" Lady Land Leaguer," Miss Reynolds, who was on Friday released at the expiration of her sentence. The Chief Justice said the case came before the Court upon motion showing cause against making absolute the conditional order obtained for ' a certiorari to bring up and quash an order of the 23rd De- cember last, made by Mr. E. B. Warburton, magistrate of , the county of Cork. By that order, which recited a complaint ! that Hannah Reynolds had unlawfully incited Catherine Murphy, a tenant of the Earl of Bantry, to refuse to pay rent ! to her landlord, Miss Reynolds was bound to be of good be- ! haviour for six months, herself in £5O and two sureties in £25 each, or in default to be imprisoned for one month. I After calling to mind the circumstances of the case, and ex- ! pounding the law having reference to it, the Chief Justice came to the conclusion that Miss Reynolds was engaged in an illegal course of conduct, and that he was well warranted in restraining or endeavouriag to restrain a continuance or ; recurrence of such acts on her part. It was scarcely neces- ! sary to say that if it clearly appeared that any subject under such an order as the one in question had been deprived of liberty without sufficient ground, the Court would interfere; thoug'ln considering the very wide discretion given to jus- tices in the exercise of this salutary jurisdicti .n, the Cella would interfere only in a strong and clear case of mistake of the magisterial authority. In this case it was, on the contrary, clear that abundant grounds were shown to have existed for the order made, that it was a perfectly proper order, and made in the due exercise of the jurisdiction of the justices, and that the cause shown must be allowed, with costs.

div.head: PUBLIC MEN ON PUBLIC AFFAIUS.
div.p: PUBLIC MEN ON PUBLIC AFFAIUS.

Speaking at a Liberal meeting at Portmadoc on Tuesday, Mr. Rathb7-me, M.P., said there were two parties in the House of Commons who were determined, if possible, to stop every beneficial measure introduced by the Govern- ment, and the country must declare emphatically against this procedure.

Mr. It. Davies, the.member for Anglesey, and Mr. W. S. l Caine, M.P., addressed Liberal meeting- at Llangefni and Menai Bridge on Monday. Mr. Caine advocated the reform of the English land laws and local taxation, a redistribution of seats, and licensing reform; but said that before any of these matters could be touched, the procedure of Parliament would have to he. reformed with a view to rendering the House of Commons capable of performing its functions. In a second address to his codstituents, Mr. S. William- son, member for the St. Andrews' Burgs, speaking at Cupar on Monday, said he should support AL.. Peddie's resolution in favour of disestablishment on the principle of religious equality. He favours security of tenure, compensation for unexhausted improvements, and low rents, and maintains that so far the Irish Laud Bill has failed only because dis- affected Irish desired disintegration. He hoped the Oaths Bill would pass. Mr. W. E. Briggs, 'M.P., delivered his annual address to his constituents on Monday in the Blackburn Exchange, which was crowded to excess. The proceedings were some- what disorderly, there being an element of opposition present. Unabated confidence in the hon. gentletnan and in the Government was voted by an overwhelming majority, an amendment condemning Mr. Briggs' support of the Govern- ment in regard to coercion in Ireland receiving the support of but a small number of persons. Lord E. Cavendish, M.P., speaking at a dinner given to his father's tenantry at Furness Abbey, on Wednesday, inti- mated that the Duke of Devonshire had agreed to remit 10 per cent. from the rcnts of his Furness and Cartmel tenants. His Lordship said there was a disposition in certain quarters to alter the tenure of land, but anything reasonable asked by the farmers it was the interests of the landlords to grant, and for improvements made in the land they ought to be re- imbursed.

MR. CHAMBERLAIN AND M. ASHMEAD BARTLETr.-Mr. Chamberlain's secretary, acknowledging the receipt of a letter which was sent to him by an Accrington correspon- dent, together with a report of a lecture delivered recently at Accrington by Mr. Ashmead Bartlett, says :—" Mr. Chamberlain desires to acknowledge receipt of your letter of the 21st inst., with thanks. He has not received the copy of the paper mentioned therein, but he can easily imagine the kind of statements which Mr. Ashmead Bartlett would be likely to make. He does not think that even the Tories are silly enough to attach the slightest importance to what this gentleman may say." Sir William Harcourt presided on Monday at the meeting of the Derby Charity Organisation Society. In the course of his remarks he spoke of the advantages of an organisa- tion this character in preventing the abuse of one of the greatest of human graces. It was not always the most deserving subjects of charity who were the most pertinacious in their applications for relief. Very often those who should most properly be the subjects of our benevolence were those least disposed to thrust their claims forward, but who re- quired to be sought out in order that their suffering and want ' might be relieved. The object of institutions like that was, on the one hand, to detect itnpostures, and, on the other, to discover those who were deserving objects of chaiity. Lord Richard Grosvenor, M.P. for Flintshire, and -Mr. John Roberts, M.P. for the Flint Boroughs, on Monday addressed-a crowded meeting of their constituents at St. Asaph. Lord Richard Grosvenor spoke at considerable length, and referred to the probable work of the coming session, and the necessity for an alteration of the rules of the House of Commons before any attempt at other legisla- tion was made. Some Conservatives' he said, were object- ing enrirely to the introduction of the cloture, though they had not the faintest idea in what way that would be brought forward by the Government. That there would be difficulty in passing a remedial measure against obstruction he had no doubt whatever, but the Government, supporte,',l ag it s efforts to -,-x itvpuld be 1--; 42,10 c9lllltry, would rpl4 ,11 t I tual(e the House of Commons in the future, as it had been hitherto, a true representation of the people of this country. Votes of confidence in both members were afterwards passed. Mr. R. N. Philips, the member for Bury, gave his annual addres to his constituents on Monday, the hon. gentleman !Icing accompanied by Mr. G. 0. Trevelyan, M.P., Secrekary of the AdmirAltY• Mr. Philips expressed his complete ap- proval of the polity of the Government both at home. and abroad, and contended that the Tory party had no rational remedies to offer for the dilculties of the country at the Present time. The Tories, he ga, were now led in the House of Lords by a statesman more reMa:lcable for courage than for prudence, and in the House of Commons a states- man more remarkable for prudence than for courage. A ;-pte of confidence in the hon, gentleman was unanimously passed, as was a resolution expressing unabated confidence in the Government, and urging them to advance generally in the path of progress and reform. Speaking in acknowledgment of the latter resolution, Mr. Trevelyan repEed to tbe mmarks on the strength of the navy recently made by Lord Henry Lennox, showing not merely that the noble lord's figures with regard to the French and English navies were altogether wrong, but that he had inaccurately estimated the strength of the guns with which the ships were armed.

div.head: IRON AND COAL TRADES.
div.p: IRON AND COAL TRADES.

LANCA SHIRE, Wednesday.—ln both the coal and iron trades of this district business during the -week has been quiet. For all classes of house-fire coal the demand con- tinues extremely dull, and notwithstanding that many of the collieries are working little more than half time, con- siderable stocks are accumulating. For ironmaking and other trade purposes the demand is good, but the supplies of common round coal for steam and forge purposes are plenti- fu, owing to the large quantpy of common coal thrown upon the market, which, with severer weather, would have gone into consumption for kitchen purposes. Prices for all descriptions of round coal show a tendency towards weak- ness, and although list rates as a rule are nominally unal- tered, there is a good deal of underselling in the market, and both Yorkshire and Derbyshire coals are coming in at very low figures. With the continuance of the present mild weather it is not improbable that some revision of the list rates may be carried out with the close of the month, but in the actual selling prices this has already been pretty largely discounted. At the pit mouth best coal at present averages about 9s. to 9s. 6d., seconds 7s. to 7s. 6d., and common round coal ss. to 6s. per ton, according to quality. Engine classes of fuel move off well, but with the exception of the better qualities of slack, which are scarce at some collieries, there is no deficiency of supplies, and customers have no difficulty in covering their requirements. Burg,y at the pit mouth averages 4s. 6d. to 65., and slack 3s. 6d. to 4s. 3d. per ton. In the shipping trade there is still only a limited busi- ness doing, owing to the scarcity of vessels, and there are a good many orders on hand which sellers are unable to execute in consequence. In the iron trade the amount of business doing has been only limited. The weak tone reported from Middlesborough and Glasgow naturally causes buyers, who are for the most part well covered so far as their present requirements are concerned, to hold back further orders in anticipation of the market turning in their favour. Makers in this district, however, are quite as indifferent as buyers with respect to further orders at present, and, being well sold as a rule ov3r the next two or three months, there is no disposition to press sales. Lancashire makers of pig iron are holding firmly for their full rates of 525. 6d., less 21-, for forge and foundry qualities delivered equal to Man- chester, but at this figure outside brands are coming into competition with the local irons, and Lancashire makers have during the week only been able to secure a few small orders. For Lincolnshire and Derbyshire iron makers' prices remain at about 425. 6d. to 435. 6d. up to 445. 61 and 455. 6d., less ; but Middlesborough iron, which is easier, has been offered at about 51s. to 51s. 4d., net cash, delivered equal to Manchester. In the finished-iron trade no great weight of new business is at present being given put, but mikers as a rule have sufficient work already in had to carry them well over the quarter; and pric3s for delivery into the Manchester district are firm, at an average figure of .£7 2s. 6d. for local bars.

div.head: ELECTION INTELLIGENCE.
div.p: ELECTION INTELLIGENCE.
MALMESBURY.

Colonel Miles, the Conservative candidate, has issued a circular to the electors accepting the honour conferred upon him by his selection as a candidate, and intimating that as it is at preSent uncertain when the election will take place, he will content himself for the present with asking for their support when the proper time shall arrive.

div.head: NORTH RIDING.
div.p: NORTH RIDING.

The result of the poll in the North Riding was declared on Wednesday as follows :—The Hon. G. C. Dawnay (C), 8,135; Mr. Rowlandson (L), 7,749; majority for Mr. Dawnay, 386. The late Viscount Helmsley was also a Con- servative. A London correspondent says: The result of the North Riding election has been received at the London Clubs with much disappointment upon one side and with great exultation on the other. Everybody has his explana- tion of the event, which has been accepted by the Liberals with surprise. Some say that the farmers of the North Riding are for the most part grazing farmers, and that no reforms which the Liberals have proposed or which they are supposed to advocate touch their interests, while they . are attached to the Opposition candidate as repre- sentative of the party upon whom they may rely most surely in no way to relax and if possible to increase the restrictions upon the import of sheep and cattle. Others place the responsibility of the Liberal failure entirely upon the fact that all the present forms of electioneering are new to the electors of the North Riding, who have no experience of a contest with the ballot, and whom no teaching has convinced of the secrecy of the present mode of voting. The lessons of the contest are however, said to be two—that the polling of only four-fifths of the I electors in a contest which excited interest throughout the ; whole country indicates not indifference so much as defects ; and want of simplicity in the law of registration, and that the extension of the franchise in counties receives some impetus from the defeat and disappointment of Wednesday.
