div.head: FREE TRADE V. FAIR TRADE.
div.p: FREE TRADE V. FAIR TRADE.

Under this title the Coblen Club have published a handbook of 200 pages, written by Mr. T. H. Farrar, the per- manent secretary to the Board of Trade. In the preface the author says he has written the work with the encouragement of the President of the B)ard of Trade, without which he should scarcely have felt justified in undertaking a duty trenching so closely on the politics of the day. Mr. Farrer says that when he was asked by the President of the Cobden Club to write something in defence of Free• Trade it seemed to him very much as if he had been asked to prove Euclid or to give a reason for the rules of grammar; and adds 'That governments can by protective or prohibitory duties prevent and diminish, but cannot create or increase trade; that every tax on trade is a diminution of the produce of industry, felt most certainly and probably most severely by the country which imposes it; that it is just as unwise and unrighteous to nrevent the number of men who make up a nation from buying their food and their clothes where they can get them bestand cheapest, as it would be to compel me to buy my bread from the nearest farmer or my coat from the nearest tailor ; that a law which prevents the people' of England from buying in France or America is in no essential respect different from a law which prevents the people of Middlesex from buying in Surrey or Lancashire; that every innocent operation of trade is necessarily an advantage to both parties concerned in it, and that to stop it by law is necessarily an evil to both ;—all these, with the numerous consequences derived from them, abeam' to me to be such elementary truths that I did not know where to begin." Eventually he found out from the Quarterly Review and other sources what the Protectionists propose, and then lie proceeds to discuss and refute all the specious arguments adduced in a manner which we think must succeed in con- vincing the warmest Fair Trader that his views are entirely wrong. The final conclusions at which Mr. Farrer arrives are as follow :—" The proposals.of the Fair Trade League, worthless as they may be in themselves, have afforded an opportunity for discussing points of some real interest, and for answering some questions which desetve an answer. On the Colonial question it is impossible not to feel sympathy with the desire to draw closer the commercial bonds between ourselves and those growing communities of our own lineage and habits which it is England's greatest pride to hare brought into existence. It has been the object of the first part of this paper to'show that all the proposals which have been made for effecting this object by legislative means involve either restrictions on our trade with other coantaies, or restrictions on colonial self-government; and that any such restrictions would tend to disruption, and not to closer union. The great fact is that Governments cannot create trade; they can only impede and injure it. They cannot divert it without diminishing it. When people talk of its being the duty of the Government to find markets for their people, what they mean is that the Government shall deprive their people of the markets which they find for themselves. On the second great question which I have treated, namely, Retaliation, there can be no such sympathy. Retaliation appears tome to be the natural offspring of a state or mind which regards our gain as others loss—a state of mind which is the hot-bed of Chauvinism, Imperialism, and Protection. A wave of feeling springing out of this state of mind has lately swept over U 3 and over the world ; and it is not surprising that it should bring with it a mode- rate revival of Protection in countries where protected • interests rule the State, and a feeble attempt to revive it in our own. But the great tide sweeps on its course, and this is but an eddy in the stream. The Alabama Treaty, and its present success; the courage which has dared to give back the Transvaal to the victorious but powerless Boers ; the power of a minority, for the first time in our history, to offer a stout resistance to an impending war; the rapid reversal of an aggressive policy by the constituencies— these are the real landmarks by which to judge of a progrees in international morality Cobden could scarcely have dreamed of. In the Sallie, way the great stream of commer- cial fEr.:•;:lom sVe•ps on ; here are temporary eddies, but time and circumstances are in its favour, aid its main course t is in one direction. Steam and telegraph have brought the nations of the world together; Prohibition has bten suc- ceeded by Protection, and Protection in many cases by Freedom; the limits of petty States have been enlarged into Customs Unions and Federations, which embrace whole continents; and England leads the van in a way which excites the jealousy of those who do not understand the secret of her real progress. It is the misfortune of the state of mind to which I have referred that it fails to apprehend and appreciate that moral element in trSde which gives to it its greatest value and significance—that element, namely, by virtue of which each act of trade is a good to both the parties to it, and each removal of a national restriction on trade is a good to all the nations concerned. It is twice blessed. It blesseth him that gives and him that takes. It reconciles self-interest with morality— duty to ourselves with our duty to our neighbour; and it thus ;;;•ings the nations a little nearer to the distant ideal of the Christian raljst. I cannot end this paper better than with Cobden's own fords: 41 do not think the nations of the earth will have a chsnoe oi Advancing morally in their domestic concerns to the degree of excellence which we sigh for until the international relations of the world are put upon a different footing, 'rho present system corrupts society, exhausts its wealth, raises up false gods for hero- worship, and fixes before the eyes of the rising generation a spurious if a glittering standard of glory. It is because I believe that the principle of Free Trade is calculated to alter the relations of the world for the better, in a moral point of view, that I bless God I have been allowed to take a prominent part in its advoc icy.'"

div.head: TRADE NOTES;
div.p: TRADE NOTES;

The Bolton spinners resolved on Wednesday to send in applications for an advance of 5 per cent. "as promised conditionally about twelve months ago." Twelve or four- teen thousand operatives are affected. The accountants' averages in the selling prices of iron in Cleveland, give the net average selling price at £5 18s. 11d. This will not alter wages for the current quarter. Total production exceeded 170,000 tons, of which plates repre- sented over 65 per cent.

A meeting of miners was held at Jarrow-on-Tyne, on Tuesday, when it was resolved to have nothing to do with the sliding scale of the Northern Board of Arbitration and Conciliation, and the workmen connected with the Arbitra- tion Board join the Ironworkers' National Association. Eight hundred ironmoulders in the Marybill district, Glasgow, have struck owing to the refusal of their em- ployers to give them back 71 per cent. as part of the per- centage which had been taken off their earnings during the last three years. The ironmoulders in Kirkintilloch have made a similar demand.

WAGES IN THE CO—T-TON TRADE.—The subject of weavers' wages in North and North• East Lancashire was under the consideration of a conference of representatives of the masters and operatives, at the Mitre Hotel, Manchester, on Tuesday. At a meeting of weavers' delegates from all the districts concerned, held on the Bth instant, it was resolved that an immediate application for an advance be made, and it was in consequence of this resolution that the conference took place. The resolution did not result in the adoption of any definite resolution, and the meeting was adjourned.— On Tuesday a conference between employers and operative spinners, strippers, and grinders, on the subject of a 5 per cent. advance on wages, was held at Oldham. The position and prospects of the cotton trade were discussed at some length by representatives of both bodies, and finally the em- ployers stated that trade at present would not allow of the advance, and, therefore, they declined to grant it.

div.head: NEWTON AND EARLESTOWN.
div.p: NEWTON AND EARLESTOWN.

BILLIARD HANDICAP AT THE LIBERAL CLPB, EARLES• TOWN.—OH Monday night a billiard match was commenced at the above club between the members for a silver lever watch of the value of £1 10s., given by Mr. J. W. Thorpe and Mr. J. F. Peace. There. were 90 entries, and the game was pretty evenly contested in the presence of a large num- ber of spectators.

WESLEYA.N CHAPEL, EARLESTOWN.—TWO sermons in aid of the Wesleyan schools were preached in the above chapel on Sunday, by ;he Rev. E. Moulton, of Preston. The con- gregations were large, and the collections amounted to £5 109. Mr. Moulton read a statement showing that the num- ber of scholars on the books was 600, and the average II attendance 450. He also made mention of the last examin- ation of pupil teachers at the Wesleyan Training College in Manchester, when five frem Earlestown passed "excellent," and out of 13 prizes (there being 200 examined) two were gained by Earlestown pupil teachers. RAILWAY FACILITIES FOR TRAVELLING. A correspon- dent writes as follows :—Since Monday, the 16th inst., and every Monday during the continuance of the pantomime, trains run to Liverpool in the afternoon, returning a few minutes to twelve; and what is as good or better, cheap trains began for the first time to run on Saturday morning from Newton and Earlestown to Liverpool. This may be considered a boon by the inhabitants at large, and no in- justice to the work people of the railway company, who for many years have had the privilege of going anywhere on this system at much reduced rates. And a reduccion of a a shilling on the return fares is something appreciable. And whether it is to be considered as pure generosity or as a. counter attraction to the tramway now approaching com- pletion in Haydock it will be equally acceptable to the in- habitants of Newton and Earlestown. With a practical mono- poly of the traffic, the railway company have steadily kept to their penny a mile for half a century till now rhen there are rutnoura rife about making the whole of the companies reconsider their fares and charges. Now that they have done so well we sincerely wish they would make an under- ground passage to the booking office in Earlestown as they have done in Newton, with a polite request that passengers would only cross the rails by this means, as the Company by so doing make out by some quibble of the law that a Person thus crossing is really a trespasser. At Earlestown, however, there are no notices of this kind, and for the best reason imaginable, because there is no alternative but to cross the lines, and that twice in the direction where one would suppose it easiest to go without crossing, namely, td New- ' ton. Perhaps they will fulfil their promise soon made to the writer seven years ago. A Fact, WORT/I KNOWING.—The recently published re- ports of medics! officers of hellth show that tha mild autumn weather and excessive rainfall h•ve produced an unusual amount of scarlet and typhoid fevers throughot4 the United Kingdom. There is also in many districts excessive mortality from measles and smallpox. Every cautious householder should nee rel:able preventive measures, and none are bAter than washin2 with Wright's Coal Tar Soap, recommended alike by the entire mPclicsl profession and the public. Let the soap be in every bed-room, bath-room, and nursery. and when you purchsse, insist unon being supplied with Wright's. Refuse all imitations.—Adet.
ST. HELENS TOWN COUNCIL.
SPECIAL MEETING.

A special meeting of the St. Helens Town Council was held on Wednesday, the Mayor (Councillor H. Pilkington) presiding. There were also present Aldermen Harrison, Johnson, Cook, Gamble, Mcßryde, Councillors J. C. Gamble, Fisher, T. Cook, Baxter, McKechnie, Walker,_Hanson, Belsher, aud Wilcock. The meeting was convened "to consider the petition of the Town Council to the Local Government Board praying that the Council may, with reference to certain land and premises situate at or near to the junction of Arthur-street and Liverpool-road, under lease to William Fletcher, put in force the powers of the Lands Clauses Consolidation Acts, 1845, 1800, and 1839, with respect to the purchase and taking of lands otherwise than by agreement; and to pass resolutions thereon."

The Tows CLEnic said he had prepared a petition for their sanction. It must be presented before the let Feb. ruary, and that was the reason of the meeting being called together. Mr. CRACK then read the petition, which stated that "It is expedient that Arthur-street, a public highway within the borough, and vested in your petitioners, should be widened and improved, particularly at and near its junction with Liverpool-road; and in order that your petitioners may effect this improvement they desire to purchase and take the land following, that is to say: all that piece or parcel of land, containing 1,80 square yards or thereabouts situate in Arthur-street and Liverpool-road, in the said borough, bounded on the northerly side thereof in part by Arthur-street and in other part by a passage four feet wide, on the easterly side thereof by Arthur-street, on the southerly side thereof by Liverpool-roed, and on the westerly side thereof by land and premises belonging or reputed to belong to William Fletcher and Henry Flint, together with the buildings erected thereon, and which piece or parcel of land is more particularly described in the plan accompanying the petition. To enable your petitioners to purchase and take the said land for the purpose aferesaid, they are desirous of putting in force, with reference to such lands, the powers of the Lands Clauses Consolidation Acts, 1845, 1860, and 1869, with respect to the purchase and taking of lands otherwise than by agreement; and your petitioners have accordingly made due publication in the newspaper and served the several notices as required .by the Public Health Act, 1875. The following table contains the names of the owners, lessees, and occupiers of lands proposed to ba taken, who have consented, dissented, orareneuterin respect of the taking of such lands. Owner. IN'uter
Lessee. Occupier. As 't Diss'tt G reenal I, Whit- ley & Co 1 Win. Fletcher Wm. Tickle 1 'Pima Barker 1 Thos. Naylor 1 Th. Johnson 1 •

Your petitioners therefore humbly pray that they may, with reference to the lands herein-before referred to, put in force the powers of the Lands Clauses Consolidation Acts of 1845, 1860, and 1869 with respect to the purchase and taking of lands otherwise than by agreement. And your petitioners will ever pray. Passed under the common seal of the said mayor, aldermen, and burgesses this 25th day of January, 1882, in the presence of Richard Pilkington, mayor." Alderman Cool( I beg to move that the petition be ap- proved, that the Corporate seal be affixed, and that the Town Clerk be instructed to forward it to the Local Government Board.

Mr. IflNsox : I beg to second that. Mr. WALKER: Has there been any communication with Fletcher about this; any offer or proposal made to him? Alderman GAMBLE: It is questionable whether such a question as that should be asked. It any communication has been made it is part of the negociation, and we have always considered those things should not be made Trablic. Mr. WALKER: We offered £l,OOO, which has been made known, lnd if he has made an offer I cannot see what objec- tion there is to our knowing. The Towat CLERK: There has been no counter offer made. It is just possible an arrangement may be made; but there has no counter offer ever been made. The resolution was carried.

div.head: FRANCE.
div.p: FRANCE.

Some of the accounts of M. Ga.mbetta's conversation with the Committee of Thirty-three on Saturday, on the revision question, attach very serious importance to his remarks as to the powers of the Congress. The Premier is reported to have said that "if the Congress transcends the limits fixed for discussion it would not be treated as an illegal assembly, and the Government would use the rights it had against' revolutionists." M. Gambetta's friends deny that he used the menacing words attributed to him. A despatch from Paris says it was agreed on Monday by the Parli tmentary Committee on Treaties of Commerce that no prolongation of any existing treaty should be granted to countries which had not signed new treaties on Feb. 1. A Paris correspondent says the Bill empowering the French Government to renew its adhesion to the mixed tribunals in Egypt states that five years' experience has shown the expediency of certain improvements, which are being studied by an international commission; but as its deliberations may be somewhat long, a temporary renewal has already been agreed to, and parliamentary ratification of an indefinate renewal is desirable. _

The telegram from Paris and Vienna with respect to the financial crisis are somewhat reassuring. In Paris it is stated that the Bank of France has placed 100;000,000 of francs at the disposal of the commeicial community of Lyon's, against Adequate securities, and that a great com- bination has been arranged in PariAto tide over the approach- ing settlement.

div.head: UNITED STATES.
div.p: THE UNITED STATES.

tnat strong feeling,' . A telegram from Tyashinigton is being manifested througnout the United States against the continuance of polygamy in Utah. A Kentucky Court of Justice a few days ago offerCa to the lovers of sensational reading attractions superior even to those which the Gniteau trial presents. The Circuit Court at Mount Vernon was engaged in a trial for murder, and Mr. John Mullins entered the room in a state of intoxi- cation. For disrespect to the tribunal he was fined ten dollars, and the penalty was twice repeated on repetitions of the offence. Mr. Mullins was finally threatened with imprisonment, but with the assistance of his father, a venerable gentleman who is sAid to be one of the strongest men in the State. he defied the Judge, the Marshal, and the whole posse. The Judge ordered him to be arrested, but the decree could not be executed. A correspondent of the New York World thus described the thrilling scene which followed :—" The large crowd in the court-room broke into the wildest disorder. Men were knocked down and pistols drawn. The guards rushed in with shot guns, and the rush for the doors and windows was tremendous. The Mullinses and officers fought their way out of the court-room and ' down stairs into the street, where John was handed a pistol, with which he fired two shots. Both men were finally placed in gaol. The excitement was at fever heat for a while. When the disorder began Judge Bradly left the bench and shouted, I call on every man in this house to help arrest these men, and I will assist myself,' and he did lend such assistance as he could." It is pleasing but astonishing to learn that nobody was hurt, but at the ter- mination of the shooting the jury in the murder case could not be found. They bad dispersed, and the trial was per- force adjourned to the next term of Court. CLOSE OF GUITEAU'S TRIAL. VERDICT OF THE JURY.

Guiteau, Mr. Porter, and Mr. Scoville were "all shouting together" at one stage of the " trial " on Monday. Mr. Porter spoke for three hours, and was then so much ex- hausted that an adjournment was agreed to. Washington telegrams say that the reason Mr. Scoville spoke for five days was to postpone the final sentence by delaying the con- clusion of the trial past Monday, when the new term of the Court began. Guiteau cannot now be sentenced, if con- victed, till next term, which begins in April. He cannot then be hanged till 30 days after that ends, thus postponing the execution probably till July. WASHINGTON, JAN. 25.—Mr. Porter, the counsel for the prosecution, resumed his speech to-day. Guiteau began to interrupt as usual, and frequently called the counsel a liar. As Mr. Porter proceeded with his damning arraignment the prisoner winced and nervously twisted in his seat, finally making such an uproar that he drowned the voice of the counsel, who was obliged to cease speaking. Guiteau then shouted, "A saint from heaven could not stand Porter's abuse." Mr. Porter then went on to contend that the ques- tion for the jury was whether the prisoner was sane or in- sane on a given date. Guiteau was roused almost to fury by Mr. Porter's scathing remarks, and absolutely bellowed, completely drowning the speaker's voice. Mr. Porter finished his address at three o'clock, when Judge Cox began summing up his charge, which occupied an hour and a half, and was generally regarded as a most careful, clear, and con- scientious review of the law and the evidence. The jury retired at 4 40, and as they had not returned at fly e o'clock the court adjourned until 5-30. At 5-36 the jury came into court, and in reply to the usual questions, gave a verdict of guilty. PRINCE BISMARCK ON THE RESCRIPT.—SCENE

IN THE GERMAN PARLIAMENT. BERLIN, Tuesday.—ln to-day's sitting of the German Parliament Prince Bismarck, replying to the discussion upon the recent Royal Rescript, declared that the Rescript was perfectly justifiable and remained unshaken by attacks made upon it. In conclusion, the German Chancellor asked whether anyone could reproach him with cowardice, a re- mark which caused great uproar on the left. The Prince then reiterated his challenge, and great tumult followed. A Central News telegram thus describes the scene :—A most exciting scene occurred in the Reichstag to-day on the occasion of the debate on the Royal Rescript. Professor Haenel, who brought on the discussion, staled in the course of his speech that the 'Government had attempted to cover its policy with an Imperial mantle. Then, while the House was almost breathless with excitement, Prince Bismarck strode from his seat into the centre of the House, and, in a stentorian voice, with impassioned action, said "You accuse the Government of cowardice, and you on the Left appear to applaud this statement." Then turning to the members of the Left, the Prince in a still angrier voice cried out, "Let him who applauds come forward." A scene of inde- scribable confusion followed, loud and continued shouts of "Nobody, nobody," from the members of the Left being heard above the din. The Chancellor appeared to regard this disclaimer from the Left as being to a certain degree satisfectory, for he returned to his seat, and then, still ad- dressing the members of the Left, said in a greatly modified, still significant tone, "Well, if that is the case, you can thank God." The episode thus ended, and the Chancellor went on to explain that the Royal message was not a serious intrusion on the rights of the official voter. He upheld its provisions, and declared himself perfectly willing to accept all the responsibility. The German Parliament resumed on Wednesday the dis- cussion, nominally of the Budget, but really of the Royal Rescript. Herr von Putkamer, who is styled Prussian Minister of the Interior, assured the House that it was a delusion to suppose that the Government had been foiled at the elections. The Hamburg question had been settled favourably, the Chancellor's policy had succeeded in other respects, and the Budget would be voted. The Minister used words which may be either a repetit;on of an old device of his chiefs, or may mean that we are on the eve of grave events. He predicted that "in the European crisis Which threatens, the Imperial Royal monarchy will again prove itself to be the bulwark of the rights of freedom " of the country. The great Chancellor appears from all the accounts of the scene in the Reichstag on Tuesday to have been in a " towering " passion. After saying that he had (wee been threatened with imprisonment by the party in opposition, he advanced from his usual place and marched up directly to the ranks of the Extreme Left, and said in a loud vice, "The untruthfulness of your statements that I am a coward should make you blush to the roots of your hair." Then followed amidst the greatest excitement cries from the Left denying the truth of the assertion. The President called them to order, but fresh cries were beard. The Chancqlor ' said, "You gentlemen on the left appear to reiterate your statements." Loud cries were heard of "No, no." Prince Bismarck turned reund and said in great excitement, "You inav then thank God." Tremendous noise followed.
The death is announced of Sir Daniel Macnee, president of the Royal Scottish Academy.

div.head: SCHOOL ATTENDANCE: COMMITTEE,
div.p: SCHOOL ATTENDANCE: COMMITTEE,
The moilthly meeting of this committee was held on Wed- nesday, Mr. W. W. Pilkington presiding. There were also present Alderman Cook; Councillors T. Cook, Wilcock, Hanson, Fisher, and Johnson.

div.head: ANNUAL REPORTS.
div.p: THE ANNUAL REPORTS.

The officers submitted their annual reports. Mr. DUTTON reported: I have the honour of submitting to you a report for the past year, 1881, accompanied by statistics, showing the numbers on th 3 registers and the average attendance in each department of the eleven public elementary schools in my district, from information supplied by the teachers. Number on registers 5,557, against 5,526 last year. The average attendance is 3,990, against 3,812 the previous year, showing an increase of 177-2 or 3 p, r cent. in the average :attendance. The number presented for examination by the Government Inspector at the last ex- amination was 3,607, against 3,555 in the previous year, showing an increase of 52 in the number presented. The number of absent and irregular scholars reported by the teachers is 9.516, against 10.213 reported in the previous yaar, showing a decrease of 697 in the year. During the year 553 parents, representing 1,035 absent and irregular scholars, were served with notices to appear before your Investigation Committee, and in the previous year 546 notices were served on parents for that purpose, representing 879 irregular, showing an increase of 7 and 206 respectively. The number of prosecutions in my district ordered by your Investigation Committee after they had thoroughly investi- gated the cases were 223, and they have been carried out with the following results :-186 fined under the bye laws, 16 attendance orders granted under the 11th section of the Act of 1876, 7 fined for non compliance with the orders under the 12th section of the said Act, 7 dismissed or with- drawn, 4 committed to industrial schools under the 14th section of the Industrial Schools Act, 1 to a truant school, and 2 cases now stand adjourned. In 28 of the above-named cases the defendants not paying the fines, 25 commitments and 3 distress warrants had to be taken out to recover them; 21 paid on commitment or distress warrant, and 7 not paying were sent to prison. The number of prosecutions in the previous year were 171. I have signed 989 children's school books during the year, against 1,374 in the previous year. A return from the Education Department is herewith laid before you.—Mr. BAMFORD reported: I beg to submit to you the following report for the past year. The total number of children on the registers of the 14 public elementary schools, December, 1881, was 6,824, and the average attendance for the same quarter 4,741, showing an average attendance of 691- per cent. The numbers for the corresponding period last year were on registers 6,682, aver- age attendance 4,669, or 64 per cent. The number pre- sented for examination by the Government Inspector during the year 1881 was 4,323, the number presented during the previous year was 4,337, showing a decrease of 14 children presented for examination during the past year, which fall- ing off is due, I believe, to sickness in Windle district in October, in which month most of the schools in that district are inspected. Daring the year 10,116 absent and irregular scholars have been reported by the teachers in No. 1 district. 608 notices have been served upon the parents of 1,015 of the most irregular of the above children to appear before your sub-committee to explain the cause for such absence and irregularity ; 262 not being able to give reasonable excuses for their children's absence from school, were ordered to be summoned before the magis- trates with the following results, viz.: 243 under the bye- laws, 218 of whom were fined Oct. and costs; 5 dismissed, 3 , withdrawn after adjournment, the children in the meantime having attended school regularly; and 17 boys committed to industrial schools under the 14th section of the Industrial Schools Act. Nineteen summonses were issued under the Elementary Education Act, 1876, 14 under section 11, and attendance orders granted in each case; and 5 under section 12 for non-compliance of attendance orders previously granted. The boys were committed to the Liverpool School Board Industrial School, Hightown. Four of these boys are now out on license and attending school regularly, and one boy is waiting for a vacancy at the school. During the year we have had to ask the magistrates to grant 43 com- initments to recover fines and costs from defaulters, 35 de- fendants paid on commitment, and 8 have been committed to prison for seven days. The number of prosecutions during the previous year was 212. I have signed during the year 939 children's school books. from evidence of age submitted therewith taken from baptismal registers, family bibles, and parents' declarations. The boy John Campbell, committed on the 23rd of August, 1880, at a cost of 2s. 6d. per week to your committee, was discharged from that in- stitution on the 24th December last, with a good character ; and John Skelly, committed on the same date, under the In- dustrial Schools Act, was discharged, on the 19th of the present month, with a good character. The cases you , authorised me at your last meeting to summon before .the magistrates were . heard on the 16th instant, when Walter Abbott was committed to the Liverpool Certified Industrial School, Everton-terrace ; the other defendant was fined Gd. and costs. I have prepared statistics for my district asked for by the Education Department, and submit them for your inspection to-day. The reports were approved. It was de- cided to get the following results at an early magistrates court :—Hugh Carr, and Margaret and William Rigby to the Industrial School; Thomas Leaby and John William Thorp to the Truant School. Thomas Rigby and Thomas Dixon to be summoned on account of their children's neglect of attendance. It was stated that Rigby had been fined 10 times and had paid £3 6s. 6d. in fines. In Mr. Dutton's district, Alfred Murphy was ordered to be placed before the magistrates as a candidate for the Industrial School, and William Hall and Thomas Roscoe for the Truant School.

div.head: SE HELENS COUNTY COURT,
div.p: SE HELENS COUNTY COURT,

WEDNESDAY.—BeCore Mr. T. P. Thompson, Judge. A WIDNES POCTOR AND HIS PATIENTS.—Mary Shaw was sued by John Edward Booth, physician. Farnworth„ near Widnes, for £2 9,. 6d.—Plaintiff stated the claim was for attendance on the defendant's sister, and defendant main. • tamed the money had been paid, but was unable to prove it as her father was dead.—His Honour said the defendant could not be liable for her sister's debt.—Defendant's solicitor said defendant had paid £2 2s. 6d. on account.— His Honour : But that does not make her liable.—Mr. Husband : She is her father's admin strator.—Defendant_. said her father only left £lO, which was received from a club.—The case was adjourned for a month.—Dr. Booth obtained orders for the payment of debts for medical attend- ance from Thomas Smith £1 35., William Clare £2 7s. 6d , 6 eorge Esmond £1 7s. Gd. CLAIM FOR DAMAGE BY FOWLS.—Mr. James H. Brether- ton, of Whiston Hall, claimed £2 from Mr. Fowler, of the same neighbourhood, for damage done to his land by the defendant's fowls.—Plaintiff said he had a garden and two fields of two statute acres each upon which the defendant's fowls were continually trespassing, doing much damage, especially when wheat was growing. He wished to put a stop to the annoyance.—Defendant said one field was only divided from the surrounding land by a ditch, and thought the plaintiff should fence it.—His Honour: He is not bound to fence against fowls. You must keep them off the land in future.—Judgment for the plaintiff.

PLEDGING A TEICSDA.ND'S CREDIT .—Thomas Mannion, a labourer, of Widnes, was sued by James Porteous for £l6, balance of an account for goods supplied.—Mr. Riley ap- peared for the plaintiff, and Mr. Massey for the defendant. —Mr. Riley said sometime after be was married defendant thought his wife's wedding dress had been charged to him by the plaintiff, and he asked for a bill of all his transac- tions. This was given, and he expressed his pleasure that ' the wedding dress had not been charged to him, but did not dispute her right to purchase goods on credit. He also re- commended his mother to trade with the plaintiff. The wife subsequently traded with him. Plaintiff had also measured the defendant for a suit of clothes.—Cross- examined, plaintiff said he had never told defendant he had bought the debt from Mr. Ray. Mr. Ray was his agent, and had delivered the goods to the defendant. He bad received payments on account for the goods, which, he thought, proved that they had been received. Defendant had never told him not to trust his wife.--Mr. Massey, in defence, said that plaintiff on one occasion told defendant he had bought his debt from Mr. Ray. Defendant denied that he owed Ray ' anything., and gave plaintiff instructions not to trust his wife. If he did so, unknown to the husband, there could be no sympathy felt for him. Some of the goods were such as a man in the defendant's position could not afford to supply his wife.—Defendant stated that all the articles supplied by Ray were paid for, and cornburated his advocate's state- ment that ha ordered plaintiff not to supply any goods to his wife. Neither he, nor his wife in his presence, had paid the plaintiff any money. One day lie entered the house aid demanded money, and defendant ordered him away telling him that "he had not half an ounce of tobacco." Plaintiff gave him 2d, and if he had change for is. he would pay him back. (i.aughter.)—His Honour said he was satisfied de- fendant's wife had his authority to pledge his credit, and made an order for the payment of the amount at 10s. per month.

EXTRAORDINARY PIANO TRANSACTION.—Mr. J. 0. Swift on behalf of Thoinas Houghton Chadwick, glassblower, of 45, Cropper's Hill, sought to recover from James Singleton, of Sr. Helens, the sum of £l5, money paid on account of a piano purchased by the plaintiff from the defendant.—Mr. Riley defended.—ln his opening statement Mr. Swift said the claim was made, firstly, bacause there was an express agreement that if the piano was not suitable it could be re- turned, and secondly, because of a number of rt presentations by the defendant which proved untrue ; also for breach of warranty. Plaintiff was in want of a piano on the 20th Sep- tember, and on that day defendant told him he had one on sale for £2O, stating it was a very good one, that he had a short time previously purchased it from Mr. Ilenty, music dealer, for £3O; and that Mr. Gabriel, who had much expe- rience in musical instruments, bad pronounced it a "splendid one." These were representations upon which the claim was based, and they undoubtedly had a considesable effect on the plaintiff's mind, and the following day he saw the piano. Defendant said his reason for disposing of the piano was be cause he thought he should not 112 to learn music. On a subsequent oCeaSierl, plaintiff ll!k'?d if some person might examine the instrument, but to this defendant answered that the piano, having been in a (lamp room, would be "sticky," and that he had better take it home and have it inspected there. If it was stated not to be worth £3O; or did not stilt, he would return the m n ey, nd take the instrument back-. Plaintiff agreed to purchase the piano for £2O, to be paid in monthly instalments of .£5. Tie instrument was removed to the plaintiff's house without accident, but he allowed nearly two months to elapse before having it examised. Mr. Woodward then found that the pin block and the sounding board were cracked in several places, and, in fact, the instru- ment was coming to pieces, and not worth above a sover- eign. Mr. Ilenty would state the instrnment was not purchased from him within the last six years, and Mr. Gabriel was prepared to contradict that he had touched the piano. Defendant had tried to get rid of the piano in May by a raffle, it being then described as a "walnut piano, value £35." Mr. Swift maintained that if he proved these facts, the plaintiff was entitled to recover.— Plaintiff was called and confirmed his advocate's statement. —Mr. It. B. Woodward, organist at the Parisi Church, said he had dealt in pianofortes for over thirty years. On the 14th November, he examined the piano, in regard to which this action was brought. It professed to be made by Robinson dr Son, of London, but there was no such firm. He considered it a "garret" instrument,—that was, made by a joiner or a cabinet maker, who had worked in a piano manu- factory. Dealers were always opeh to buy such things. It was the worst instrument he had ever seen, and horribly out of tune. Green or damp timber had been used in its construction; the wood had consequently contracted when dry; the pin block was cracked, as was also the sounding board; and it was impossible to tune it. As a musical instrument it was worthless.—Mr. Massey cross-examined the witness to show that the instrument might have become in that condition durirg the time that the plaintiff had had it in his possession, but this he said was impossible.—There being other 12 witnesses to examine, the case was adjourned . to the next Court day.

div.head: DISTRESSING SUICIDE AT ST. HELENS.
div.p: DISTRESSING SUICIDE AT ST. HELENS.

An inquest was held on Friday at the Star Inn, Merton Bank-road, on the body of Henry Thomason, 16 years of age, who committed suicide on Thursday afternoon, and which was reported in these columns last week.—Eli7.abetk Thomason, wife of Frederick Thomason, brlcksetter, 5, Back Cottages, in Merton Ban F-road, said deceased was her son and was 16 years of age last August. He lived with her- He was a dataler at Laffak-Garswood Colliery, and had always enjoyed goal health. On Thursday morning, over- sleeping herself, she did not call him up as usual at fire o'clock, but at half-past. He started to go to work, but came back at six o'clock and " sauced " her, saying she might have wakened him at five o'clock. He went to bed again, and got up at ten and ate his breakfast. He see 'Led all right, and stayed in the house until between one and two o'clock. Ho was in the habit of going to the theatre every night. He met with an accident, four years ago, to his arm, and had since become passionate. He was trying to catch sparrows with a riddle between one and two o'clock, and she laughed at him, remarking that he had a nice game on. He returned the laugh. At ten minutes to three he went upstairs, she being then sat by the fire sewing. He did not say what he was going upstairs for, and witness did not hear any noise after he had gone up. Ten minutes after- wards she went upstairs for a handkerchief, and found him hanging by the neck to a strap which was fastened to one of the posts of a camp bedstead. An apron was over his face, and his feat were drawn up, the legs being tied together by a scarf. She lifted him up and cried for help. A neighbour came in and helped her to take deceased down. He was then quite dead. A doctor was sent for. There was nothing to trouble him, except they were very poor and the father was out of work. Deceased had never threatened to do anything to himself. O.R. further examination, wit- ness said that she "sauced" him during the day for throw- ing a hammer on the floor. Deceased's little brother took it up and threw it at another child, hitting it on an abscess. She then told him he was a lazy fellow for not putting it out of the way, and he replied, "If I am lazy I'll be hanged." He was greatly excited when he said that. After saying that he sat a few minutes by the fire, then went upstairs. No member of their family had been deranged, but deceased's cousin drowned himself two years ago.— Ellen Havler, a neighbour, said she was called into the house. She found the last witness holding deceased up. Deceased was a cheerful youth, and steady.—Frederick Thomason, father of deceased, saw his son on Thursday, and he was then in his usual health and spirits. He had always been a good lad. Witness had been out of work for some time.—The verdict was that the deceased had com- mitted suicide, but that there was no evidence to show the state of his mind.

div.head: MR. BRIGHT AND THE WELSH
div.p: MR. BRIGHT AND THE WELSH
FARMERS.

Replying to a communication detailing certain grievances from which the farmers in Wales are represented to suffer, Mr. Bright writes I dare not undertake now to discuss with you the subject of Welsh agriculture, and the position and demands of Welsh farmers. I must leave your people to consider their own question, and to come to something like a conclusion upon it. That there are changes which require to be made which will come, I do not doubt, bat I am not sure that, after being so long asleep, the farmers will, on suddenly awaking, be able to measure accurately what they seem- to see, or judge wisely of remedies for grievances under which they believe themselves to suffer. As this moment, too, I am so burdened with correspondence and engagements that I must shun all invitations to enter upon new questions. I may, however, conclude by saying that lam glad to see that the farmers in all parts of the kingdom are stirring themselves, and I hope this unrest may be useful to themselves and to their landlords."
Liverpool cartowners are suffering serious losses from an epidemic among horses similar to that which has prevailed at Newcastle and other places.

THE LIABILITY FOR RATES OF OUTGOING TENANTS. —The overseers of the poor for the township of Moss Side have drawn up a petition to the Local Government Board on the subject of outgoing tenants. Copies of the petition have been sent to all Lancashire townships asking them to adopt a petition similar to that drawn up, and it is arranged that a meeting of overseers shall be held to consider the sub- ject on the 15th February, at Exeter Hall, London, prepara- tory to the appointment of a deputation to wait upon the Local Government Board. The petitioners state that they have been notified by the district auditor of his intention in the future "to insist upon the overseers carrying out the pro- visions of the 16th section of the Poor-rate Assessment and Collection Act, 1869, in the manner laid down by the judges in their decisions in the recent cases of St. Werburgh's v. Hutchinson' and Hare v. Overseers of Putney." The petitioners, on the other hand, "have hitherto understood and carried out the provisions of the section as limiting, and as being intended to limit, an outgoing occupiers liability to the payment only of a portion of the rate pro- portionate to the time of his occupation within the period for which the rate was made; whereas, in the cases quoted, it is held that the outgoing occupier (if in occupation at the making of the rate) is liable for the whole rate, should the premises remain empty, and obtains no relief, unless he is succeeded by an occupier, who is liable to pay a proportion- ate part of the rate, and then only to the extent to which his successor is liable." It is pointed out, moreover, that "the carrying out of the provisions of the section as now required by the district auditor will inflict very serious hardship upon outgoing occupiers, who, under the same section, will be liable to be rated as well from the premises from which he has removed (unless and until he is succeeded there by an occupier), as also for the premises into which he removes after the making of a rate." It is, therefore, asked that in the forthcoming session of Parliament a bill may be intro- duced into the House of Commons for the amendment of the section, in order to bring the provisions of the Act referred to more into harmony with sub-section 3 of the 211th sec- tion of the Public Health Act, 1875.
THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, JANUARY 28, 1882.

HALTON PARISH CHURCH SUNDAY SCHOOLS. - The annual distribution of prizes to the children of this school took place on Sunday afternoon in the girls' school, where a large number of children and teachers had assembled. Lady Brooke presented the prizes to the number of 40.

PRIMITIVE METHODIST SABBATH SCHOOL, RUNCORN.— The annual tea and public meeting in connection with this school was held on Wednesday. The chair was occupied by the Rev. J. Pickwell, resident minister. The committee's report stated that there were 22 male teachers and nine female teachers on the roll, and 231 scholars, being a slight increase over last year. The financial statement was also satisfactory. The distribution of prizes to the scholars for early attendance was then made. WESTON READING ROOMS.—The reading rooms opened at Weston about twelve months ago have been carried on with great spirit, the result being much benefit to the inhabitants. With the object of bringing thess benefits more clearly before the public, an entertainment was held at the Church of England School, Weston, the other night. The chair was occupied by the Rev. J. J. Bryant. A very interesting pro- gramrne was gone through by several local amateurs. The total proceeds of the meeting amounted to £3 13s. 41. HALTON PARISH CHURCH MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY• —On Tuesday evening a meeting was held in connection with the above society, Mr. T. Miller reading a paper entitled "Food," in which he showed the best things for people t^ eat in order to be healthy. Mr. Bosworth occupied the chair At the close of the paper a discussion was opened, in which the following members took part :—The Rev. J. Lockwood Messrs. J. Bosworth, T. Wright, J. W. Haddock, and J. Han- cock. A vote of thanks to the essayist and chairman closed the meeting.

MESSLOIR FROM THE SEA.—Our correspondent at Frod- sham has received a piece ot paper which purports to be a message from the sea, and was found in a bottle by the river side on Mr. Andrew's marsh, on Tuesday last, by a man named Richard Oakes, of Seven Houses, Frodsham Bridge. The bottle was covered with mud, but the paper is in a good state of preservation. and is to the following effect, viz.:— "November 30th, 1881.—Expect sinking every minute ; sprung a leak; nothing to eat ; good bye; vessel's name, Pretty Jane,' Runcorn, England." The above may be the result of a stupid and silly hoax on the part of someone, but we give the information for what it is worth. The mes- sage is written on a piece of paper which has evidently formed half of a counterfoil in a book.

PRESBYTERY OF WELSH PRESBYTERIANS AT RUNCORN.— A quarterly meeting of the Lancashire and Cheshire Pres'Jy- tery was held at St. John's Presbyterian Chapel, Runcorn, on Wednesday. There were 42 delegates present, the Moderator being the Rev. Wm. Evans. of Bootle. Deputa- tions were appointed to visit the following churches for the election of officers:—Bangor, Salem, St. John's Runcorn, and Summer Hill. 'Attention was called to the Sustenance Fund newly formed. and churches were urged to be faithful in its support as well as in other matters. Delegates were appointed to attend the quarterly synods of the connexion and the General Assembly for 1882. A young candidate, Mr. John Rogers, of Summer Hill, was received as a member of the Presbytery. An animated discussion on the subject of "Preaching:" took place. The general feeling seemed to be that there was more warmth and sympathy between audience and minister wanted. The report of the Presby- tery Sunday School Examination was reed by the secretary, the Rev. J. TI. Jones. of Ton. near Mold. The next ex- amination is fixed to be eld in April, in the various schools of the Presbytery.. The Rey. Edward Parry, 8.A., of Newton, and the Rev. Edward Jores, B A., of Liverpool, were appointed examiners The next Presbytery will be held at Wrexham, on the 20th March.--in the evening the annual congregational tea meeting was held, when there was a large number present. At the public meeting held after- wards the Rev. E. Williains presided. The meeting was a purely congregational one, when the finances are considered, and the general arrangements fully discussed. The annual report, read by Mr. Humphreys. stated that there had been an increased attendance in the Sabbath school, in the sanctuary, and at all the means of grace; and they were enabled to rejoice in accessions to their number. The total income had been £272 15s. Bd., and the expenditure £275 is. 3d , leaving a balance due to the treasurer of £2 7s. sd. Addresses were made by Mr. Leach. the Rev. W. Evans, Bootle, the Rev. Jones, and Mr. J. H. Humphreys. Mr. Thomas Pritchard, senior steward, stated that he had been connected with St. John's Chapel for 00 years, and be had never seen their affairs in a more flourishing condition than they were at the present time. THE LATE MR. W. H. OCKLESTON, OF RUNCORN. —We regret to haTe to announce the death of Mr. William Henry Ockleston, of Runcorn, after a protracted illness. For two years Mr. Ockleston had suffered from a wasting dis- ease, which, despite the resources of medical science and the assiduous attention of his medical advisers, Drs. Fitzpatrick and Waters, has ended in death. In Runcorn and the neicr,h- bourhood the deceased was well known, and his loss will be much felt. He came to Runcorn 25 years ago, when opera- tions were commenced by him at the tannery now owned by Mr. Robert Pierpoint. He subsequently built an extensive tannery, which he, in conjunceion with his son, carried on up to the time of his death. He was a gentleman of thoroughly business habits great integrity, and large liberality, and was enabled in early life to found a business on a very firm basis. He was very popular among his workmen. At one time be closely identified himself with public matters, and was elected a member of the Runcorn Board of Commissioners. He was a member at one of the most important periods of the history of the Board, and took an active part in the dis- cussion of the water question. Besides living in Runcorn for several years, he also resided at Halewood, and subse- quently at Halton, and afterwards at Alder Hey, West Derby. He died at his residence on Thursday, Januiry 10th, at the comparatively early age of 50 years. The funeral took place on Tuesday at Halewood Church. The hearse and mourning coaches left West Derby at 10-30, ar- riving at the church at 12-15. The body was here met by the late employes of the deceased and a large number of friends many of whom had come from Manchester and Lon- don, the express having been stopped at Halewood to allow them to alight. The hearse was drawn by four horses, and was followed by the private carriage of the family with drawn blinds. The second carriage was that of Mr. James Ockleston, containing the two sons of the deceased, Mr. William and Mr. John Ockleston. The carriage of Mr. Mc- Kibbin contained Mr. James Ockleston and Dr. Robert Ockleston. The carriage of Mr. Tyrer held Dr. Bromfield and Mr. Briscoe. In the carriage of Mr. Cropper there were the Rev. Robert Salthouse, Dr. Fitzpatrick, and Dr. John- son. In Mr. Dennis' carriage there were Mr. Tom Ockles- ton and Mr. G. J. Knight. The body was borne to the grave by several of the employes, who attended the funeral in very large numbers. On the coffin were placed several very beau- tiful wreaths. The burial service was read by the Rev. Robert Salthouse, of St. James's, Liverpool. RUNCORN YOUNG MEN'S CHRISTIAN ASSOCIATION. An adjourned meeting of the members of this body was held on Wednesday evening, Mr. Robert Shaw, the president, in , the chair, for the purpose of considering the financial position lof the association. At the previous meeting a proposal in favour of closing the rooms bad been lost, and anamendment passed in favour of a deputy being appointed to wait upon , various gentlemen in the town to see what contributions could be obtained towards the payment of the sum of about £5O, which is owing. Mr. Coventry, Mr. Shaw, missionary, and the Rev. E. Williams made rather encouraging reports as to their canvass. The last named gentleman said he thought the feeling that there was a want .of sympathy with the association in the town was a mistake, for he had found during his canvass a very large amount of sympathy with them, which, if utilised, might assume a very practical shape, and a readiness to come forward and assist. He and the others appointed for the object, had seen at least 20 gentle- men who were each willing to contribute one guinea per year towards the association, and many of these would also give something towards the deficit. He believed it was highly probable that they would be able to get 20 young men out of the number connected with the association, who would be willing to raise their subscription to half a guinea for the privileges which the institution offered.—Mr. S. C. Beckett moved that the work of the association be continued, and a deputation appointed to wait upon the directors of the Runcorn Coffee and Cocoa Rooms Conapany for the purpose of seeing whether the rooms formerly occupied in their building by Mr. Linaker could net be obtained for the use of the members, at a payment of £2O per year, including gas.— Mr. Shaw, seamen's missionary, seconded the proposition, and said he thought he should be able to get no fewer than 20 members to join.—ln reply to Mr. Johnson, the Chairman said he was of opinion that Mr. Hazlehurst, the owner of the present building in which the association meet, would not press his rights as to the time when they should vacate the tenancy.—Mr. Smith, the secretary, reported that Mr. Philip Speakman had been seen as to the sum he would let the rooms for which were formerly occupied by the Literary and Mechanics' Institute. He first asked £3O a year, and ultimately agreed to accept £25. (Laughter.)—Mr. J. W. Clough asked if the benevolent offer of Mr. Speakman was to be considered.—lt was stated, amidst laughter, that it would not be, aril that there were several things in connec- tion with the rooms referred to which would render them scarcely fit for the purposes of the association. The resolu- tion was carried; and a number of gentlemen were appointed the deputation, on the motion of Mr. Clough, seconded by Mr. W. Massey.—Mr. Beckett moved, and the Chairman seconded a motion in favour of Mr. Meadowcroft, agent to the Bridgewater Navigation Company, being asked to.take 'the position of president.—The Chairman spoke very strongly in favour of a change being made in the presidency, and the resolution was carried unanimously. After some other formal business the meeting was again adjourned. We may state that the deputation met the directors of the Coffee and Cocoa Rooms Company yesterday, and they consented to let the associalion the rooms in question at a rent of £25 a year, including gas, coal, and rates. LORD DERI3Y ON THE LAND LAWS.—Writing to a Welsh correspondent, the Earl of Derby says :—" I am not aware that the laws of Wales as regards farming matters are different from those of England, and I shall be surprised if Parliament thinks it right to legislate specially and separ- ately for the Welsh tenant farmers. Nor do I think it , likely that fixity of tenure and rents settled by law will be accepted as a principle for legislation for England and Scotland."

RUNCORN RITRAL SANITARY AUTITORITY.—The fort- nightly meeting of this authority was held at Dutton work- house, on Tuesday, under the presidency of Mr. John Ashton (vice-chairman). There were also present the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Messrs. J. cllalloner, R. Ashton, T. Andrews, W. Jackson, C. Rigby, James Darbyshire, J. Weir and H. Linaker (clerk). The Frodsham Sewerage Scheme : A letter was read from Mr. Bancroft, stating that he had received the resignation of Mr. Defty, the Clerk of Frodsham sewerage works, who had obtained a permanent situation. It was decided on the proposition of Mr. Challoner, seconded by the Rev J. W. N. Tanner, that Mr. Samuel Davies of Frodsham, be appointed clerk of works at a salary of £2 2s. per week. DIE ABRAM COLLIERY ExmostoN.—On Wednesday, Mr. Rowbotton, coroner, met the jury empanelled on the in- quest on the bodies of the two men who died at the Wigan nfirmary, from the effect of the injuries received in the ex- plosion at the Abram Colliery, for the purpose of arranging as to a further adjournment. After a short consultation, it was decided to adjourn the inquiry until March 1, when it is expected that the principal investigation by the county coroner at Abram will have been closed. COLLIERY ACCIDENTS.—The Miners' National Asso- ciation have drawn up a circular-letter to all colliery owners, pointing out that a large percentage of non-fatal accidents prove fatal through the want of speedy attention, efficient appliances, and suitable conveyances. They request the masters to provide a small house, with needful appliances, such as bath, splints, straps, bandages, and an ambulance conVevaiii3c in which to carry the injured home or to the hospital. The circu:ar adds that the appeal is made on the j the ground of common humaZl.ty, and that they would j rather see it a voluntary act than to have. these provisions made by the operation of law. FOOT AND MOITTII DISEASE.—On Monday, two new cases and two re-appearances of this disease were reported to the Clerk of the Peace. The former are on the premises of Mr. Thomas Foster, New Stead Farm, Little Woolton, near Liverpool, where the disease has broken out among 15 cattle, two of which are affected; and on the premises of Mr. William Howarth, Critchley Farm, Althani, where three in a herd of eleven are suffering. The re-appearances are on the 'premises of Mr. William Kaye, Great Stone Farm, Stretford, where three cows are affected in a herd of 14- and the premises of Mr. George Ashburner, Low Hall, Kirby Ireleth, who has 56 cows suffering in a herd of 71. The returns for the week ending, the 22nd inst., show that dur- in, the week seven animals had been affected, making a total of 80 in the county. The disease existed in the hundreds of Lonsclale, Blackburn, and Salford.

THE LAND SUBSIDENCE IN CHESHIRE.—The subsidence .)f land in the Cheshire salt districts continues to excite increasing interest and considerable alarm. The Dunkirk district, the scene of the great subsidence in December, 1880, has shown it-elf to be thoroughly shaken, and the subsidences going on there are visible from day to day, whilst at intervals sudden sinkings of great depth appear and let in fresh water to the brine pits. The amount of damage done to Ashton's works alone (which are situated close to the sinking centre) is estimated at £2,000. In Marston the sinking called "Neumann's Flash " extends and deepens continuously. The subsidence, which, how- ever, has caused most consternation to the inhabitants of the town is the one in Leftwich, which for the last three months has developed itself and every few days taken in a portion of the main highway. Since September last the local board have filled in a number of holes forming in the same spot, which in the aggregate have amounted to 50 feet in depth. At Winford and up the Weaver the sinlang con- tinues, as also it does at Billinge Green and Whatcroft. The subsidence is of course ascribed to the brine pumping going on in all directions. During the past year there has been a scarcity of brine, particularly at Winsford. The make of salt seems to require more brine than is producel from the percolating rainfall. Even at Northwich the top brine has been scarce. -

SERIOUS EXPLOSION OF GAS NEAR, WIGAN.—Early on Wednesday morning an extraordinary explosion of gas took place at the works of the Haigh Brewery Company, near Wigan. The brewery is an extensive one, and the cellaring extends underneath the Haigh Schools, which are close to the main building. The men started work at six o'clock on Wednesday morning as usual, and lighted the gas through- out the whole of the cellaring. Shortly before seven o'clock a terrific explosion occurred in the cellars below the schools, smashing beer barrels and vats, blowing down the props sup- porting the school floor, and tearing up the flag flooring of the cellar. There were several men there at the tiuie, but these escaped with slight injuries. The windows and doors of the echool and the master's house were blown out, the drain running round the building was torn up, and much damage done to the brickwork. An examination subse- quently made disclosed a leakage in the gas main which runs along the highway a short distance away from the brewery, and close to a sewer drain and water-pipe com- municating with the school cellar, it is supposed that the escaping gas has by this drain made its way to the brewery. Fortunately, the workmen engaged in the cellar had, owing to the mildness of the season, opened the win- dows on commencing work. Had not this been done it is most probable, judging fron the force of the explosion, that the school would have been almost wrecked, and the brewery itself materially damaged.

9TH LANCASHIRE' RIFLE VOLUNTEERS SHOOTING CLUB.—The fourth and fifth competitions of the above club took place at the Lymm range on Saturdays, January 7th and January 21st. On the day of the fourth competition the wind blew very strong and variable from the left front, which was the means of many a ball hitting the turf instead of the targets, thereby reducing the scores very consider- ably. The weather during the fifth competition was more favourable, and allowed some of the members to retrieve their position. The distances fired at were 200 and 500 yards, seven shots at each distance, Wimbledon targets and regulations. FATAL FALL AT WAURINGTOTT. —The county coroner, Mr. C. E. Driffield, held an inquest at the Bowling Green Inn, Warrington, on Tuesday, to inquire into the cause of death of Ann Ray, a widow, 74 years of age.. From the evidence of the deceased's daughttr Sarah, it appeared that the family bad on Thursday removed into the house 1, Thewlis-street, Liverpool-read. On Friday morning, about four o'clock, the deceased arose from bed in the dark to call her sons. Her daughter told her it was too early, and also to remember that they were in a strange house. Deceased, however, wertt out of the room, and she was almost im- mediately heard to fall down the stairs. The sons Wallace and Robert, went and assisted her back to bed, and in answer to an inquiry as to where she was injured, she placed her band to her forehead'and said "there." She then became in- sensible, and Dr. Lees was called in. He said deceased was suffering from concussion of the brain, and that there was no hope of her.recovery. She remained in an unconscious state until Saturday evening at six o'clock, when she ex- pired. The jury returned a verdict of accidental death.
The monthly meeting was held on Thursday afternoon. Mr. Bradshaw presided, and there were also present, the Rev. Thomas Finegan, and Messrs. O'Keeffe, Hartland, Shaw, Deacon, and Brock.

DISTRICT EDUCATION COMMITTEE. Mr. Deacon read the report of this committee, which was approved, and showed that during the month of December (three weeks), the number of cases summoned before the committee had been 243, of which 51 were applications for payment of fees, and 192 for controvention of the Act. Fees were recommended to be paid in 42 cases, and eleven applications had been refused. SCITOOL MANAGEMENT COMMITTEE. The various recommendations of the managers of the various scbools, which were approved, were as follows:— That the resignation of Miss A. S. Hunter, assistant mistress in the junior girls' at West Bank School, be increased from £45 to £5O per annum; and that the resignation of Miss Alice L. Hunter be accepted. The committee also reported that Mr. Thomas Balmer had been appointed chairman, and Mr. W. Crabtree correspondent of the West Bank managers, for the year ending December 31st; also that Mr. and Mrs. Joseph Robinson, Mrs. Hough, and Mr. T.
