A ST. JOHN'S AMBULANCE ASSOCIA- TION FOR ST. HELENS.

On Tuesday evening a meeting was held in the Brook- street schools, to hear explained, by Colonel Paris, of Liver- pool, the objects of this association. There was a good at- tendance, among those present being His Worship the Mayor (Mr. R. Pilkington), who occupied the chair; the Mayoress, Mr. and Mrs. J. C. Gamble, Mr. and Mrs. William Gamble, Mrs. and Miss Bishop; Revs. R. J. Ward, J. Brown, W. G Pascoe, S. Topham, Major Windus, Major Ogle, Sergt. Major Tyson, Capt. White, Dr. McNicoll, Dr. Hay, Dr. Garton, Dr. Reid: Messrs. A. Sinclair, J. H. Martin, F. France, W. Waterworth, Coop, Jesse Boydell, J. H. Craik, Wenham, B. Leach, S. Wolfenden, H. L. Riley and Mrs. Riley, W. B. File, Steel, the Misses Sharpies. The MAYOR said there were more present that night than he expected to see, and that pointed out to him that more interest was taken in the movement than he was aware of. He understood that the objects of the society were to dis- seminate such knowledge as would enable persons like them- selves in case of accident during their occupations in life to render sufficient help to wounded persons between the time of the accident and the time it was possible to get medical aid on the scene; so that life might be saved, when in many cases where there was- not the knowledge that such all association desired to see prevalent, loss of life wou'cl i.e the result. The Mayor then called upon Col. PARIS, who said it gave him great pleasure to come there. If people were fully impressed with the value of the objects of the Society; if they had a fixed determina- tion to acquire the knowledge of the doctor they did credit and honour to the doctors themselves. They had generally very large classes at the commencement, and very small ones at the end. id not know that it was due to the raO 1-e.:t_ i non-appreciation of the teachings, t was a lamentable fact. He did not, and he dared say those present s'i:d not like to commence things unless they went right through to the end. The knowledge imputed by the lecturers at those classes was of the simplest deccription. The great bugbear to most of the members of the classes was perhaps what they considered a very great ordeal, that is, the examination at the end. But it was the simplest thing in the world. As to the necessity or the advisability of the society, let him take them for a moment to the scene of an accid, et. Those were occurring every day, and especially in a town like St. Helens. Take an accident in the street. The most sympathetic sex got round the man, perhaps threw up their arms and screamed, and called for somebody ; then they tried to suffocate the poor wretch by taking away all the air from him. Everybody was good hearted enough to wish to be able to do something, but nobody knew what to do, except to give him brandy. Some with more wit about them would think of getting the doctor, but in many c ises the doctot could not be got immediately. And there were many cases in which the doctor should be got immediately, otherwise the man might die. The main object of that seciety was to disseminate amongst the people and eletneutary knowledge to enable them to deal with cases of accident before the doctor could be brought upon the sccne. He did not morn to say that everybody even with a theoretical knowledge would be able to render aid. He knew people who had had as much knowledge or more than the society attempted to impart to them, who were perfectly powerless to render any aid at all in an emergency. That subject would be dealt with by the lecturer at the classes in all probability. In Liverpool they had been doing, as far as their time permitted, a great work. As usual, ladies were even more prominent in the work than men. They had volunteers from Lyme-street station, lectures had been given to the Birkenhead police force, and only recently he (Col. Paris) had distributed prizes to 100 of the Birkenhead police force. The sailors they had not been able to tackle yet, but they were very ambitious to do so, because what they taught would be of great value to the sailors, who were sometimes unable to see a doctor for several weeks. If they had more workers they could do more ; if they had more spare time, if they could infuse into the members of the classes more pertinacity and a stronger nerve, they might do more. He did not know that it was a criterion of the good of the society to have amongst them the highest in the land, but if it were they had Lord Derby and the Prince as presidents of some branches, and a lot of big swells in other places. (Laughter.) There was no greater satisfaction than to be able to render aid in case of injury. The society was unsectarian and non-political. They knew no creed but the highest, and knew no politics. If they had any creed it had its foundation in brotherly- love and charity. He gave all humanity credit for that. The class lecturers would probably give examples of handling people who were injured in a proper way ; and hove handling them in an improper way might cause death or further injury. He could give them instances where death had resulted from careless handling. Colonel Paris pointed out that tile lecturers to the classes proposed to be started would teach them the elementary structure of the human body, and in case of hemorrhage the vital difference between arterial and venous bleeding ; how in the case of arterial bleeding a patient might bleed to death. The speaker went on to say that they had turned men out of their classes who had been of the very greatest use. A policeman saved life in the time of the election at Liverpool, through the knowledge which the society had imparted. in that case there was great ex- citement opposite the Conservative Club, and two gentle- men hau their heads cut in a very dangerous way. Many people, he said, had not sufficient centidence and assurance to enable them to be of use in any emergency, and he ' certainly found that a great deal of the backwardness on the part of an Englishman proceeded from the idea that his fellow-men were going to laugh at him. (Laughter.) When- ever a man was found stricken down ill the street people were always ready to administer brandy; he must have brandy. But if they followed the teachings inculcated at , tir SQ classes, they would be prevented from giving brandy. Nothing could be worse in such cases. The speaker appealed to Dr. McNicoll, who was near.—Dr. McNicoll said that in some cases the administration of brandy was pernicious.—Colonel Paris went on to say that he had been in a railway accident. 'rile terror of a person was increased by the screams of those who were not injured at all. The ignorance of those who handled the sufferers was painful ; and the terrible want of knowledge displayed by people who were educated in thoee matters was wonderful. It was of the utmoscitamortance that railway men should be members of the classes. Colonel Paris read some statistics of London mortality, from which it appe ired there were more people injured and killedoby horses and horse' accidmts then by rail- way accidents in that city. Dr. McNecoat, sail if they hid not known that Colonel Paris was connected with the mili.ary they ivould have set him down as a professor of medicine, or one of the doctors of one of the branches tint existed in Liverpool, because he bad shown an acquaintance with the medical science. But as to never giving a man brandy, if he saw a man on the ground who had a very ano-eletic look, and whose face looked as large and as rd as the moon in a fog he would not administer brandy : but if he saw a man on the ground who had suffered loss of blood, who had a pale and bloodless appearance, he thought he should give it him. They could not have a rule applying to all cases. It would be for the classes to discover the difference. One would have imagined that Colonel Paris would have been brandishing his sword at the head of an army, but he was rather of the good Samaritan pouring oil into sufferers wounds. Colonel Paris did Rot attempt so much to urge and to plead for that insti- tution, but seemed rather to take it for granted that every man and woman were prepared at once to give in their adhesion to a society like that. Very likely he thought he would not insult them by pressing !hem, no matter how proper a thing it was. Well, it belonged to no sect or party, and was for the geod of all rich or poor. It was for the craftsman who was liable to mechanical injuries which made him fall out of the rank and swoon, and require the good offices of his brother. Being a Society which had for its object the amelioration of the sufferings of a working brother, it commended itself to every one of them. He did not think that St. Helens would need much pressing of this subject upon them. No young man would refuse to join a society which had such an honourable object. T'ne savages, except in wartime, would respond on an appeal; those men with their poisoned arrows and scalp- ing knives would lend their hospitality and would render their aid for the relief of sufferers. It had been said on great authority that the age of chivalry had passed. He did not think anything of the' kind. He did not think a n_noat volunteers for tire e S ti Helens, service which their hic bad o u n tsuchry asocobnatdinogfenim contingent of Noln would be prepared for the sake of humanity to have a con-, tingent of another kind to be of better serv-ice than the old order of St. John, and give their aid in times of extremity. When first he heard of the movement, he thought it was the hobby of some dilletante philanthropist, but since then he had heard a great deal, and something that night. It was everything that was good, and he hoped it would meet with that success which it certainly deserved. Mr. J. C. GAMBLE moved "that a branch of St. John's Ambulance Association be formed in St. Helens; and that a committee consisting of His Worship the Mayor, Dr. McNicoll, Dr. Gaskell, Dr. Jamison, Dr. Garton, Dr.'Rickets, Dr. Hay, Colonel Gamble, Colonel Bothwell, Major Pilking- ton, Mr. Martin, Major Willcocks, Captain White, Messrs. J. C. Gamble, J. H. Craik, Sinclair, Jessie Boyden, R. W. H. Thomas, W. H. Relghsedge, Sharpies, be appointed, with power to add to their number, to carry out all the necessary arrangements." Throu m ih the operations of that society a considerable amount of good had been done. There were so many works and collieries in St. Helens, accidents were con- tinually happening, and if they could get the foremen of the works to attend the classes they could make themselves particularly useful. They knew that there were many cases of severe accidents in w !rich a little prompt help would pro- bably save life, at any rate suffering could be removed. It was of greater importance to have a branch In St. Helens i , than even in Liverpool, because in accidents ▪ n the street, the latter place, a doctor was more likely to be seen than in coal pits and such places. meDort.wGoaunir mweestecwointdhedentthierereeosooleueteiso.n, and hoped the move- The MAYOR regretted that Colonel Gamble was not present, but he bad a letter from him in which the Colonel said an engagement prevented him. The Mayor went on to say that si threo n gm eneltui sotgerwoafs minq i ties t ear sr eopf r erseeini gt ot inv,edoonoet 0, rags, at hoed ffi r eo wasc e ras of the two regiments of volunteers in St. Helens. He felt indebted to Colonel Paris for giving them anexplanation of the objects of the society, which seemed to hi▪ m (the Mayor) to be the carrying out of the lessons of the parable of the gHoeo dmoveda Samaritan.‘,ote of They thanks eou to Colonelallatlreaasrtisb.e half a doctor. Mr. H. L. RILEY seconded the motion. The age of chivalry was not passed, as Colonel Paris had invited them to a brotherhood of knights, and sisterhood of nurses. They had so many ladies with them that night who had known so long the necessity both of knowledge and nerve in emergencies, that they could count upon their help. There were also fore-

div.head: INJUNCTION AGAINST THE WIDNES LOCAL BOA RI),
div.p: INJUNCTION AGAINST THE WIDNES LOCAL BOA RI),

Vice-Chancellor Sir C. Hall had on Thursday before hint the case Tebay, v. the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincoln- shire Railway, and the Widnes Local Board.—Mr. Pearson, Q. C., moved for an injunction to restrain the defendants from infringing the rights of the plaintiff respecting certain nd.—Mr. Robinson, Q.C., said he appeared for the Widnes Local Board, and as be had not had time to answer certain affidavits that had been filed, he was willing that the interim order should be continued as against himself until next week. With respect to the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lin- colnshire Railway Company, for whom Mr. Speed appeared, he must say they had no more to do with the matter than the Great Western or any other railway, the proper defend- ants were the Cheshire Lines Committee.—Mr. Pearson was willing the motion should stand over, but he desired that the injunction should also be continued against the Man- chester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire Railway.—Mr. Speed, on behalf of the defendant Company, objected to the injunction being continued against him, and maintained that the plaintiff had made a mistake in making the Company for whom he appeared a party to the action. The real defend- ants were the Cheshire Lines Committee, and on that ground he protested against the interim injunction it was sought to continue as against him.—Mr. Pearson said the plaintiff sold certain land to the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincoln- shire Railway Company, under certain conditions, and the Company had dealt with the land. Some one was infringing the rights of the plaintiff, and the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire Railway Company now said it was not thern, but was some so-called Cheshire Linls Committee.— Mr. Robinson said his friend had no right to use the words "so called," because the Cheshire Lines Committee was well known, and had been in litigation over twenty years.—Mr. Pearson admitted that it was said the Cheshire Lines Com- mittee bad an interest in the land, but if his friend would say be would not do anything in the interim he would not ask for the injunction to be continued against him.—Mr., Speed replied that he would give the undertaking not to do anything, and Mr. Pearson then asked that the iaterim in- junction might be continued against the Widnes Local Board, and that he might have leave to amend his writ and notice of motion if, after looking into the Acts of Par- liament, they found it necessary.—Mr. Robinson sail that as he believed it would turn out upon the hearing that the plaintiff had no right of action at all, he must ask that he ive the ordinary undertaking in damages.—Mr. Pearson consented to the undertaking being given, and the motion „ was then ordered to stand fora week, the injunction to con- tinue only as against the Widnes Local Board.

div.head: MEETING OF WIDNES LIBERALS.
div.p: MEETING OF WIDNES LIBERALS.

On Monday evening, the members of the South Division of the Widnes Liberal Association held their annual' meet- ing at West Bank schools. Mr. Joseph Robinson presided, and amongst those present were Messrs. S. Owens, J. 13riggs, T. R. Warne, A. Truscott, W. Whitby (secretary), and H. B. Shores, secretary of the Association.—Mr. SHORES' said it would perhaps be of interest to the meeting to know what part the South Division had taken in the recent registration. As they were aware, the total net gain in the district was 50. The details of the South Division were as follows :—Struck off register, three Liberals; struck oft £l2 list, nine Liberals and 21 Conservatives; new property claims allowed, 3 Liberals and 2 Conservatives; new £l2 claims allowed, 6 Liberals and 1 Conservative, resulting in the South Division in a gain of 15 Liberals. (Cheers.)—The following gentle- men were then appointed, on the motion of Mr. Whiner, seconded by Mr. BRIGGS, to form the General Committee of the Division :—Messrs. T. Whitby, G. Chrimes, P. Ireland, H. S. Hall, F. H. Gossage, H. Gaskell, jun., R. Shaw, J. W. Coxon, T. Lewis, W. Scott, T. Hughes, J. Ankers, J. Griffith, J. Heath, J. Jackson, I'. Snape, J. Hartland, J. Alderson, T. Lewis, jun., John Shuttlewortb, T. Ankers, T. W. Scott, J. ' Evans, R. Woodier, T. Perrin, T. R. Warne, A. Truscott, W. Truscott, James Deakin, and E. Lock. The fellowing were also appointed the Executive Committee :—Messrs. E Knowles, J. W. Coxon, J. Briggs, W. Crabtree, T. Bold, Jas. Scott, S. Owens, Jos. Robinson, W. Whitby (secretary), and T. Sutton-Timmis (chairman).—ln proposing the re-election of Mr. NV. WHITBY as secretary for the ensuing year, Mr. S. OWENS paid him a high compliment for his p Ist services, and the very material assistance he had rendered the Liberal party at the Registration Court.—The motion was seconded by Mr. BRIGGS, heartily supported by Mr. SHORES, and car- ried.—The following gentlemen were elected the Registra- tion Committee :—Messrs. James Scott, J. W. Coxon, Jos. Robinson, S. Owens, J. Briggs, W. Crabtree, and W. Whitby. —Mr. S. OWENS had great pleasure in moving that the best ' thanks of the meeting be given to Mr. Timmis for his services as Chairman during the past year; and that he be re-elected. In Mr. Timmis they had a good and tried Liberal, who, while many others were slumbering, was active in the Liberal cause. They all regretted his recent illness, and were now pleased to know that he was recovering. He hoped they woul,l soon have him among them to feel the value of his services.—The motion was seconded by Mr. T. R. WARNE, and carried unanimously.—ln declaring the re- solution carried, the CHAIRMAN referred to the recent illness of Mr. Timmis. They all knew how thoroughly indefatig- able Mr. Timmis was, and how much in earnest he was in everything he took in hand. It was a pleasure to them that he was to be their chairman for another year. His absence that night, through a protracted illness, was much to be re- gretted; for he did not look upon that meeting as one of a purely formal character, it was one of considerable im- portance, forming part, as it did, of the great work of Liberal orgauisation. To some of them it might appear an insigni- ficant part, especially when they looked at the small num- ber present at the meeting, but on that account it was none the less important. The Liberal party of the country was made up of such associations as that, and from the history of the political parties they might learn a valuable lesson. During the administration of the late Government the Liberal party was like a fish out of water. At that time they also saw the political torpor that stole over the rank and file of the Tory party. The Liberals had now taken office, and their attention was too much engrossed with the ,cares and dirties of office for them to have leaiure to rally and organize the Liberals, es they did when they were not in office. It was important that every one should feel his re- sponsibility in the matter. It was at a time like the present, when their party was in the greatest danger of disintegra- tion, and decay. They could not look around them but they saw the same topor creeping over the Liberal party. Tney ought not to rest satisfied with the position they bad. They ought not to think, because they wielded a power that was capable of overriding opposition, that there was no work for them. (Hear, hear.) They might depend upon it that a Government was wanting in the first elements of permanence and strength when its supporters ceased to feel their own responsibility. He was glad they had a gentleman like Mr. Timmis at their head. He would keep them up to the mark, and it was a pleasure to him that he was to be their chair- man for another year. (Applause.)

MAYORAL BANQULT AT ST- HELENS

On Thursday night the Mayor of St. Helens (Mr. Coun- cillor Richard Pilkington) gave a grand banquet in the Assembly Room of the New Town Hall to the mentbf_rs of the Town Council and leading inhabitants of the town. Extensive and elaborate preparations had been made for the • occasion, and the Assembly Room presented a very gay and elegant appearance, the large orchestra being filled with a choice collection of plants and flowers, and in the centre the arms of the town. The tables were also plentifully adorned with beautiful and rare !lowers. His Worship bad issued invitations to about 170 gentlemen, the greater part of whom were present. The Council Chamber was utilised as a reception room, and here each guest was personally intro- duced to His Worship. The Mayor presided, and was sup- ported on his right by Lieutenant Colonel Gamble, J.P., and on his left by Mr. Thomas Brewis, Town Clerk. Atoon.4,:t the fa-nests present we noticed the Rev. Canon Carr, Lra.D. (vicar), %/hey. latner uttatuorne Catholic), Rev. R. J. Ward (Independent), Alderman Joseph Harrison (Ex-Mayor), Messrs. E. Johnson, J. Cook, J. Rad- ley, Leach, Twyford, W. W. FOOTBALL.

CREWE BRITANNIA. v. WIDNES.—This important fixture and roturn match was brought to a conclusion on the ground of the former on Saturday, in the presence of a large number of spectators. Each side was well represented, and after the kick-off the play was of an even character. Up to half- time, and on changing ends, the home team played hard, and for some time pressed their opponents, when Widnes in turn pressed them. When no time was called the game ended in a draw—Britannia, one touchdown; Widnes, one touchdown apd two dead balls. Amongst the visitors, behind the scrim- mage, Kendrick, Farrell, Harrison, Mason, and Norris, did good work; while Kershaw, Hardman, Malone, and Kilian were the pick of the forwards. For Britannia all the backs played well, especially Moore who made some magnificent runs; amongst the forwards I/ooler's play was a treat to see, who was far away the best, Greensmith, Carter, and Harding playing well up to him. Britannia—W. Talbot, back; three- quarter backs, J. Brooke and Simon; half-backs, ii Moore and W. Bailey; forwards, T. Greensmith (captain), Dooler, Harding, Carter, Heaps, Halfpenny, Sinker, Roberts, F. Tal- bot, and Bebbington. Widnes—Dorning, back; three- quarter back, Kendrick (captain), Farrell, and Harrison ; half-backs, Mason and Norris; forwards, Byrne, Hill, Grice, Brown, Kershaw, Hardman, Malone, Williams, and Kilian.

NEWTON-LE-WILLOWS V. RUNCORN.—The return match between the above clubs was played on the ground of the former on Saturday last, and after a rather noisy game, the visitors were returned the winners by 1 goal, 1 disputed goal, 1 disputed try, and 4 touchdowns, to 1 try and 1 dead ball. Bate started the leather for the visitors, and the for- wards following up smartly prevented a return, when a few good scrimmages ensiled in the home 25, for which they had to save. Hobson starting the ball again, scrimmages were the order of the day, only 1 touchdown and 1 dead ball being scored up to half time. On changing ends, Hobson started the ball for Newton, and after a bit of smart play, Wood was successful in scoring a try. The place was en- trusted to Massey, who made a miserakle attempt. Broady, charging the ball down, secured and worked his way to the centre, where Egan brought him down, after which the visitors seemed to have it their own way, forcingi their op- penents to save three times. Andrews ran n three times in quick succession; once they disputed. For Runcorn Andrews, Larkin, and Broady, backs, and Hottland, Cox, Mason, Wright, and Gatley, forwards, played very well; Hobson and Woods, backs, and Fairclough and Rimmer, for- wards, were the pick of the home team. Runcorn--J. Pownall, back; Broady, Larkin, and Hughes, three-quarter hacks; Andrews and Lightfoot, half backs; Bate (captain), Wright, Hoffland, Lewis, Cox, Mason, Joule, C. Pownall, and Gatley, forwards: Newton—Hobson, back; Hewitt, Wood, and Egan, three-quarter backs. Lane and Massey half backs; Liptrott, Fairclough, Boardman, Gough, Brom- , ley, McCormick, Holt, Rimmer, and Appleton, forwards. •

His Wonsnip, on rising to give the first toast, received quite an ovation. In giving the toast of "The queen," he spoke in terms of the highest praise of her exemplary con- duct, and referred to the fact that: her crown rested on the affection of her subjects. The MAYOR also spoke in eulogistic terms of the readi- ness which the other members of the Royal family mani- fested to do good when opportunity served, and gave the toast of "The Princess of Wiles and the other members of the Royal family." The MAYOR afterwards proposed "The Bishop and Clergy of the Diocese and other ministers of religion," and in doing so spoke in praiseworthy terms of the good work they were quietly but merely doing for the benefit of the human family. The Rev. Canon Carr, in responding, expressed an opinion that the Cowley schools standing idle for the want of £6OO, was a reproach to the town. The Rev. Father Ullathorne, ana the Rev. R. J. Ward, also responded. His WORSHIP gave as the next toast "The army, navy, and reserve forces," which was responded to by Lieutenant Colonel Gamble. _ _

Mr. Ernmeil—ga;(-3--""i:he magistrates," which was - sponded to by Mr. Hall. Alderman GAMBLE then proposed the toast of the evening "The mayor," and spoke in terms of the highest praise of the connection of his worship's family with the town. The toast was drunk with musical honours, and duly responded to. The other toasts were "The chairmen of committees," "The town and trade of St. Helens," and "The vice- presidents." The Excelsior Glee Party wlth Mr. Gee. Barton, senior, as soloist, Mr. Edward Grime as conductor, and Mr. Chas. Grime as pi Inist, were in :tttendarlce. and rendered in a very satisfactory manner the solos, glees, and part songs allotted - to them.
WARRINGTON CEMETERY.—Returns of interments in the Warrington Cemetery during the week ending yesterday : Adults, 4; children, 15; total, 19.

div.head: FROM WAhPdNGTON TO LONDON,
div.p: FROM WAhPdNGTON TO LONDON,

Having resolved to visit the great metropolis, we took the \ advice of a friend and obtained a ticket from Warrington by the Great Western Railway, and as we thoroughly enjoyed I the trip we have thought that a brief description of the ride I by this route might be interesting to others. Leaving Bank Quay station we crossed the Mersey and had a pleasant ride into the ancient city of Chester, where we met the Liverpool express, and on the way from Chester to Wrexham we caught a glimnse in the distance of Hawarden Park, the seat of the veteran statesman, the Right Hon. W. E. Gladstone. Wrex- ham is a busy well-built town, and it is stated that the tower of the church there is one of the " seven wonders," because it rochs in windy weather, but whether this be true or not we must admit that it is a fine specimen of the fifteenth century architecture. Before reaching Ruebon we passed the site of a small station now shut, which, whilst it was in existence, rejeiced in the euphonious name of Rhosllanerchrugog ! (We wonder whether the porters who bad to shout oat this name on the arrival of each train were Englishmen, and how many of the passengers understood what was said.) Leaving Ruabon we very quickly came in sight of one of the cele- brated Vales of Llangollen, of which we had a magnificent view from the railway which spans the valley by means of a splendid viaduct over 1,500 feet long. This is one of the most charming bits of scenery in Wales, where formerly was the fastness of Owain Glendower, and is one of the favourite resorts of tourists in the summer. Rapidly steering past Chirk with ite fine castle and beautiful church, we cross the river Ceiriog and find ourselves again en the English side of the Welsh border, and are carried over old battlefields, past remnants of decayed castles and beautiful mountains, val- leys, rivers, and stream?, through a fertile and well- cultivated agricultural district to Whittington, Baschurch, Lenten, and Shrewsbury. This is the chief town of the border county in which there is much of which the inhabi- tants—the "proud Salopians "—may justly feel proud, and some other things of which they may feel ashamed. For instance tradition says that at one time the market house was rented by the company of draper e who bought there the flannel l''.-aTia'ut to the town by the Welsh wPavz7;, and "the mode of purchase was both novel and profitable to the purchaser. A drum revolving on an axle was used for measuring the flannels. This drum, exactly one yard in circumference, was turned by a handle, and each revolution of the handle was counted a yard without any consideration for the gradual in- crease in the diameter of the drum by the successive folds of the article measured thereon." That was how the honest (?) Salopians traded with their Welsh neighbours! Leaving Shrewsbury, we crossed the Severn, and soon arrived at Wellington, a place of great antiquity, and which was once the residence of the Princes of Powys. Almost immediately after leaving Wellington, we had a striking view of that curious mountain called Wrexlain, rising 1,000 feet above the bed of the Severn, and from the summit of which can be obtained views of no less than seven English counties, and! upon a clear day a horizon of from 350 to 400 miles in cir- cumference, with Snowdon and its cloud-capped peak in the distance. We shortly afterwards pass the ancient town of Shiffnal and arrive at Wolverhampton, a well-built and thriving town on the borders of the "black country," of which it forms the capital. This is the seat of the lock trade, it being stated that nearly 30,000 dozens of locks are pro- duced yearly here and at the neighbouring village of Witten- hall. Our route from Wolverhampton lay through the centre of the "black country," with its heaps of slag, cinders, and soot, its large blast furnaces, which, when lit up at night, give a weird appearance to the district. Rapidly passing through Bilston, Wecine,hury, and West Bromwich we arrive at Birmingham, with its network of factories, fires' and millions of lights, and in the neighbourhood of which? Watt, the great improver of the steam engine, died. Some idea of the trade transacted in Birmingham may be gathered from the fact that the present manufactures embrace almost every kind of iron, brass, steel, and electro-plate; bronze, ormolu, and japanned wares; buttons, toys, jewellery, papier machie, pins, steel pens, tools, saddlery-, glass, cutlery, &c., Having rested for a brief space here, we resumed our journey and were taken through the rich agricultural districts of Warwickshire, and as we approached Warwick, we had a good view of the church and castle, the latter being supposed to date from the reign of Edward the Con- fessor.* After leaving Warwick we very shortly came in sight of the pretty inland watering place of Leamington where waters celebrated for their curative qualities, have flowed for centuries past. Passing the station of Southam- road, a fellow passenger reminded us that it was here that Charles I. showed his authority as the temporal head of the Church by causing all the church doors to be locked and sealed because the inhabitants had offended him by not causing the bells to be rung at hisapproach. Rapidly passing Fenny Crompton and Edgecott, where Charles I. remained the night before the battle of Edgehill, we soon got to Banbury, a place celebrated in nursery rhymes. On past Aynho with its fine church, and several interesting villages on either side of the line, one came in sight of Blenheim Park in which once stood the Royal palace of Woodstock, and shortly afterwards arrived at the beautiful city of Oxford, delightfully situated at the con- fluence of the rivers Isis and Cherwell. Every tourist, should, if possible, break his journey at this grand old city, and pay a flying visit to its numerous colleges and magni- ficent libraries. After we left Oxford, we had a series of magnificent landscape views on our way to Reading, where we should have liked to have had an opportunity of inspec- ting the solemn looking ruins of the Abbey, where the feet of kings and queens, abbots and monks have trod in the past ages. We subsequently passed the pretty village of Seiplake, with its ivy covered church, where the poet Tennyson was married. Having passed Troyford and Maidenhead, we next caught sight of the little church of Bray, whose vicar is well known to have manifested a keen relish for the good things of this life by being "first a Papist then a Protestant, then a Papist and then a Protestant again," according to the view of the reigning monarch, be being determined That whatsoever king should reign Re would be the Vicar of Bray. As we approached Slough we- had numerous excellent views of Windsor Castle, the chief residence of Her Majesty, and the royal standard flying at the summit of the highest tower proclaimed our good Queen's presence. On the left after p teeing Slough we had a fine view of Langley Park and the Rack Park, the latter being a great fir wood of 300 acres. Passing West Drayton, Hayes, Harlington we came to SJuthall where there was once a cattle market only inferior to, Smithfield, and then we came in view of Hanwell, with its

well known lunatic asylum, and were shortly afterwards landed at Paddington, the terminus of the Great Western iilway system, which covers an area of 312,000 square feet. The immense traffic that is here carried on is enough to bewilder those who come in from the provinces, for about 100 passenger trains arrive and depart from here daily, and about a third of that number on Sundays. It would be superflous for us to refer to the attractions which the great metropolispresents to visitors, for they are innumerable, but we would say that if an one wishes to enjoy a pleasant ride through plctur2sque scenery on the way from the north to London they will f,llow our example and travel by the Great Western line, for by so doing we muet say that we f:und the jourmy both pleasant and profitable. RAMBLER.

div.head: ASSAULTING THE POLICE AT PRESCOT.
div.p: ASSAULTING THE POLICE AT PRESCOT.

HEAVY PENALTY. On Tuesday, at the Prescot Petty Sessions, before Messrs. W. L. Evans and W. Blinkhorn, John Jones, a rough look- ing fellow, was charged with being drunk on the licensed premises of Robert Charles, Queen'. Arms Hotel, Market Place, Prescot, and refusing to quit; and also with having assaulted P.C. Cruickshanks whilst in the execution of his duty.—Prisoner said he did not remember anything about the affair.—Robert Charles said that about hair-past eight o'clock on the night of Saturday, the 21st inst., the prisoner came into the bar of his house and called for a glass of beer and a "small " wine. As prisoner was drunk, witness refused to serve him, anc/ requested him to. leave the

premises. He would not leave, and witness called in a con- stable, who also reques...d the prisoner to retire, but he re- fused, and the officer was obliged to forcibly eject him. He did not see what took place outside. This was not the first time the prisoner had been proceeded against for refusing to leave his house.—P C. Crnickshanks said he was called into the last witness's house, and found the prisoner there quite drunk. He requested him to leavg hut h aim wit- ness go: i—oa anti put him out. He then became very disorderly. Witness asked him to go home and be quiet, but be again tetustA, and behaved in a violent man- ner. Witness got hold of him by the arm, and prisoner then co nmenced to kick him. Prisoner threw him to the ground twlce, and he had to obtain the assistant of P.S. Pollitt to convey him to the station. —Mr. Evans: Did he hurt you ? —Witness : Not seriously, sir.—Mr. Evans: But he kicked you ?—Witness: Yes, sir; on the lags—P.S. Pollitt cor- roborated the last witness's statement as the assault.—Mr. Superintendent Barker read a long list of convict Ens against prisoner' for assaults on the police, breaches of the peace, drunk and disorderly conduct, tote.—For being drunk and refusing to quit prisoner was tined 10s. and costs, or 14 days; and X 5 and costs or two months for the aesauq, one term of imprisonment to f .Ilow the other.

The Board of Trade enquiry into the loss of the Bath City, en her outward voyage from Bristol, has resulted in .tiae Court finding that nobody was to blame in the matter. The Bath City was lost in December las,, when the master and ten men were drowned, or died subsequently from exposure in open boat. Messrs. Henderson's engineering works in Glasgow, were a'most entirely destroyrd by fire on Wednesday morning; and the oil works of Mr. John Parker, in the same city, were also burned ,own on Wednesday. In the first case the loss is estimated at £14,000 and in the latter, at £30,000. Amongst the many repo-ts which Ii tve been circulated in regard to the nature of the new parliamentary rules which. the Government purpose bringing forward in the ensuing session, the latest is to the effect that occasions for discus- sing the principle of a bill will be limited, the Speaker to close the debate by putting the question ; that certain bills are t) be referred to a Select Committee instead of a Com- mittee of the whole House ; that no member is to move adjournment during question time; that the Government are to have more complett.coturol of the business on Government nights; and that there is to be a modification of rule prc- , venting official business being taken after 12-3/
