div.head: WARRINGTON POLICE COURT.
div.p: WARRINGTON POLICE COURT.

MoNDAT.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Pickmere), Alder- man Chandley, and Major Cartwright. AN UNSAFE NEIGHBOURHOOD.—A rough looking young fellow named James Higham was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Chorley-street. On Sunday afternoon P.C. Ct!ckett saw a large crowd of men assembled in that neighbourhood, where the prisoner was grunk. The prisoner called upon the crowd to throw the officer in the pond, and threatened him with violence. Knowing the neighbourhood was a rough one, he fetched another officer, when they took. the prisoner into custody, several men in the crowd sending stones at tke officers.—Mr. Hunt said it was not safe for a policeman to enter that neighbourhood alone, and he should be obliged some Sunday to send down 20 policemen and charge the persons with riotously assembling.—An officer stated the men were pigeon flying.—The Mayor said this was a case where tbe police had no chance. People in the out- skirts of the town gathered for pigeon flying and other bad practices, especially on a Sunday, and defied the police and law and order in every way.—Prisoner was fined 203. in- cluding costs or a fortnight's imprisonment. OBSTRUCTING A. STREET.—EIIen Burrows was charged with obstructing the free passage of Sparling-street, off Old- road, Latchford, by suspending a clothes line across.—P.C. Chantler said that on the 17th inst., the defendant was dry- ing her clothes on a line suspended across the street, and people were obliged to lift it up in order to pass.—Defendant said it was a very common practice to dry clothes in that manner.—The Mayor remarked on the danger of the practice, and fined the defendant 33. 6d. CRUELTY TO A HoßsE.—Michael Molaghan was charged with cruelly illtreating a horse by working it whilst in an unfit state, and John Whitlow was charged with causing it to be worked.—P.C. Shaw said on Saturday morning about seven o'clock, he saw the defendant Molaghan driving in a milk cart a horse which was" hopping on three legs." Two days previous he had warned the man against working the horse.—P.S. Spinks confirmed this statement, and said the horse apeared to be in great pain. Molaghan stated to him that they could not afford to keep the horse idle.—Mr. Robinson, veterinary surgeon, who had examined lh& .norse, said it was suffering fromstrai =dons of the near fore- leg, anel lytt:', worked the animal would have acute pain. it was not in a fit state to work.—Mr. Hunt believed the horse had since been destroyeci.—Defendant Whitlow said he was not aware that the horse was in such a bad state on the morning in question.—Molaghan was fined 7s. 6,1. and costs, and a penalty of 103. and cost was imposed on Whitlow. FLOGGING A "BUCK JUMPER."—John Bosco, employed by Mr. Goodier, butcher, Bridge-street, was charged with hav- ing on the 18th inst., cruelly illtreated a horse by flogging it with a stick in Bold-street ; and also with furiously driv- ing the animal at the same time and place.—lnspector Singleton and P.C. Chantler gave evidence that whilst waiting at Arplev station for the 10-18 train, they saw the defendant drive past at a," fearful rate, flogging the horse in a most shameful manner," with a large stick on a whipstock. —Mr. G. T. Moore, who appeared for the defendant, cross- examined the witnesses to show that defendant was endeavouring to stop the horse from running away, and called three witnesses, who stated the horse was a " jibbet ," a " buckjumper," and altozetlster "eccentric."—The Mayor said Mr. Goodier ought not have such a horse in Warrington with its narrow streets. It had been proved that the horse was thrashed whilst at full gallop, and that was a wrong thing to do.—For the first offence defendant was fined in the costs, and in the second 103. and costs. DAMAGE TO PROPERTY.—MichaeI Connor, Bernard Man- nion, and Peter Laffie ( boys), were charged with having on the 15th inst., wilfully damaged property in Tanners- lane, in the occupation of Mr. Isherwood. Defen- dants pleaded guilty, and they were each fined 2s. 6d. and costs.

INDUCEMENTS TO STEAL.—SHOPKEEPERS AND THEIR GOODS.—A young fellow named Henry Davies was charged with stealing 12 neckerchiefs of the value of 65. 6d., the property of Thomas Wareing, of Buttermarket-street.— Prisoner pleaded guilty.—The Chief-Constable stated that on Saturday the prisoner was handling some jackets at the door of Mr. Poole's shop, but noticing that he was observed) he crossed the street, and took from a hook at the door the neckerchiefs produced. He was followed up Buttermarket- street, and arrested.—The Mayor : Do the shopkeepers pay toll for hanging their goods in the street.—Mr. Hunt : Oh, no, sir.—The Mayor said pedple were so tempted to steal things that be really had no feeling towards those shop- keepers who hang their goods outside. He had seen little children take boots and shoes off the hooks, and put them back again. He did not think it was right for the shop- keepers in the town to hang their goods in front of the shop. They ought to pay toll. It ought not to be allowed.—Mr. Hunt observed that the attention of the Watch Committee bad been called to the practice, and he had taken upon him- self the responsibilities of warning the shopkeepers against thus exposing their goods. The prosecutor was warned before the robbery, but he still placed his goods outside his shop. In same places where such inducements were given to thieves, the prosecutor was made to pay the expenses.— Major Cartwright : Have the Watch Committee power to stop the practice P—The Mayor : Notunless the goods are on the footpath.—Mr. Hunt, replying to Alderman Chandley, said this was the third robbery from the prosecutor's shop door.—The Mayor remarked that to poor needy people the temptation to steal goods placed outside a shop was very strong, and the drapers and shoemakers in Warrington were especially addicted to the practice.—Prisoner, who stated he was drunk when he committed the theft, was fined 205., or in default 14 days' impri.onment with hard labour. A DESPERATE CifeatAcrEra.—Thomas Miscall was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Rose and Crown-street, on Sunday morning, and with wilfully damaging the house of Ellen Burke to the extent of 103. The prisoner was further charged with assaulting Constables Clynes and Cokely whilst in the execution of their duty.—At two o'clock on the morning of the day named, P.C. Clynes re- ceived information that the prisoner was making a distur- bance in Rose and Crown-street, and proceeding there with P.C. Cokely, he discovered the prisoner drunk and shouting "like a madman." With his clogs, he savagely kicked both officers, then he lay himself on the ground and refused to move.—The officers were "obliged to drag him to the police station."—Mrs. Burke stated the prisoner had brOken her window frame, and almost all the panes of glass.—The pri- soner, Mr. Hunt stated, was a de'perate man in drink, and he was fined 103. and costs for being drunk, and 20s. and costs for the assault on the police, and 103. damage; or, in default, go to gaol for two months. SCHOOL ATTENDANCE CASES.—Mr. George Riley, the school attendance officer, summoned a number of parents for not sending their children regularly to school, and the cases were disposed of as follows :—Peter Baguley, 55.; John Bolton, ss. ; Wm. Roberts, 55.; Edward Thomas, 23. 63. in two cases; John Bailey, 5e.; Thos. Hagan, 23. 6d. in two cases ; Thos. Lightfoot, 2s. 6d. in three cases ; Sam Adcroft, 23. 6d. in two cases; Sam Jackson, 53. TUESDAY.—Before Major Cartwright, and Mr. Ziba Armitage. DESERTED HIS WIFE AND HIS QUEEN.—Jeseph Hardman, a young fellow' was charged under warrant, with having run away from the borough on the 24th December, 1879, leav- ing his wife anet child chargeable to the common fund of the Union.—Mr. Harbourne, releiviug officer, said the defen- dant's wife received 30s. in relief, but defendant owed to the Guardians, £4 7s. 63., his wife having been previously deserted by him—Defendant was committed to gaol for a month with hard labour: and he was then charged with being a deserter from the 47th Regiment of Foot stationed at Porto Bello Barracks, Dublin. He was remanded to Walton to await an escort. A SOBERING INSTITUTION: THE GAOL—Patrick McDermott, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Lilford- street, on the evening. He appeared to think the charge a joke, having a smile on his face during the inquiry.—Mr. Hunt said this was defendant's 21st appearance, and he had been in an asylum two or three times through drink.— Major Cartwright remarked that a month in gaol would sober him—Prisoner: It would kill me.—Councillor Monks: Then you would be no further trouble to any body. (Laughter.)—Prisoner was fined 40s. and costs, or a month's imprisonment. T HUTZSDAY.—Before Alderman Webster.

THE DRUNEARD AND HIS MONEY.—John Gerrard was brought up in custody charged with being drunk in Man- chester-road.—P.C. Corcoran said the prisoner was ejected from the Cemetery Hotel, at half-past six on the previous evening. When in the road four sovereigns fell from his pocket, and witness suspecting he had a large sum of money in his possession, took him to the police station. It was there found that he had £52 13s. id, and a watch and guard upon him.—Alderman Webster: I think you may consider yourself very fortunate that you fell into the hands of the nolice.—Prisoner said be did, and he was fined 10s. and costs.

WEDRESDAY.—Before Alderman Davies and Alderman Chandley. TITE HIGHWAY ROBBERY AT BEWSEY. Darby Rohan was charged with haying, in company with William Moran and others violently assaulted John Lee flat captain, pear Bewsey Old Lodge, at 1-30 a.m., on Sunday, January Ist, and stolen from his person 7s. in silver, a pocket knife' and a neckerchief. The particulars of the robbery have been fully given in The ExamineP.—The prisoner was remanded until Saturday. FRlDAY.—Before Captain Reynolds, Mr. John White, and Mr. Ziba Armitage. FRAUDULENT ENLISTMENT. James Heaton, of Wigan, was charged with fraudulently enlisting into the army, by making a false answer when attested on the 27th December. Prisoner had stated that he was a single man, whilst he had a wife living at Wigan.—He was sentenced to 14 days' im- prisonment. A BEDROOM SCENE.—Thomas Mooney was charged with having, on the 23rd January, assaulted his wife Mary.— Complainant stated that when she undressed herself to go to bed, her husband " pulled her all over the room, with not a stitch on her only her chemise." He maderaer a black eye, with knocking her to the floor.—Defendant said when he went home to his tea at six o'clock, he found a " houseful of women drinking." He said nothing to her, but went into the Bay Horse and bad a glass of beer. A short time after- wards, his wife followed with a young woman and a man, and called for four glasses of ale, and when that was con- sumed, she called for a quart of beer. Ile went home and asked her if the bed was made, and she said "No; wait for it." His mother then made it. When they were in the bedroom together, she threw the contents of the chamber utensil upon him; then sent it threw the window smashing four panes of glass.—Captain Reynolds asked complainant if she admitted this to be true.—Complainant said she was obliged to do something when he was abusing her. De- fendant said it was hard for a man not to have his tea ready when he went home after a hard day's work.—Com- plainant said there was some bacon and onions in the oven, "cooked by another young woman," but he would not have

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JANUARY 28, 1882.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JANUARY 28, 1882.

IL—Defendant admitted making his wife a black eye, and he was bound over to keep the peace for six months. Cap- tain Reynolds advised the wife to keep from drinking and refrain from giving her husband provocation. • UNiorr CLsns.—John Barrow was summoned to show cause whyan order should not be made upon him to contribute towards the maintenance of his wife, Alice, who was living apart from him, and chargeable to the common fund of the Union.—Mr. Shearer, relieving officer, asked for an order of 2s. 6d. per week, and the defendant being agreeable' the Bench made the order.—An order of 2s. per week was made upon Michael Allcock for the support of his mother, Esther, who was an inmate of the workhouse. At; AMAZON IN THE WITNESS Box.—Lena Warburton, a young girl, claimed 153. 9d. from James Cooper, fustian cutter, for work done prior to the 21st January.—Mr. Moore appeared for the defendant, and said he admitted only 4s. 11d, of the claim.—Comnlainantl said defendant stopped a is. from her wages on the 25th December; she was not paid 9s. 3d. for a piece cut the week following, and ss. 6d. was owing to her for a piece cut on the week ending the 14th January.—The mother stated she had asked for the money from the defendant, who did not deny to her that he owed it. He did not pay it, however' and she went to his house. She was told he was "not in," but she had been "tricked with him too often," and she "walled straight in, and hauled her mon out of the scullery." (Laughter.)—Mr. Moore: You frightened him ?—Witness: I would ha' dun if I bed met him in a field. (Laughter.) He goes boast- ing about drinking 17 pints of beer and four glasses o'th best whiskey—that's where money goes. (Laughter.)—Mr. Moore: I dare say you wouldn't object to it ?—Witness: I dare say not if you'd pay for it. (Laughter.)—Mr. Moore : You are a regular amazon. I would not like to meet you.— Defendant gave in a written statment showing the payments made to the compl ,inant, who, however, stated that a piece the number of which she gave, had not been paid for. Defend- ant said his wife had paid the money. She was called, and said she had not.—The Bench made an order for the mount claimed.

WARRINGTON BOARD OF GIJARDI ANS. At the fortnightly meeting held on Wednesday there were present: Mr. Jos. Harrison (chairman), the Rev. J. Yonge, Messrs. Darbyslaire, Appleton, Hall, Heaton, Garnett, Humphrivs, Cartwright, Woolfall, Swinton, Cooper, Houghton, Hunt, Owen, Greeciall, and J.C. Sutton (clerk). STATE OF TUE HorsE. The MASTER reported 532 inmates, against 513 in the cor- responding week of last year. There bad been 166 vagrants —135 men, 21 women, and 10 children—relieved during the week.

Mr. GARNETT said that he had listened to Mr. Heaton's explanation, and he felt compelled to say that the order given for furniture was a most extravagant and improper one. (Hear, hear.) He did not believe Mr. Heaton would have paid such prices for furniture for his own house. [Mr. Heaton : Yes, double.] He well remembered how this sort of thing had before been condemned by the Board, and he could not understand how such a proceeding as this could have taken place after what occurred as to carpets for the Master some time ago. The Master's room was a very small one, and here for six articles—for a couch, an arm chair, and four single chairs—was one item of £3B. He characterised such an expenditure as most unjustifiable, and said it was an expense very few people incurred for such articles. He very well remembered that in the days of Mr. Wm. Smith and Mr. Tunstall on the House Committee they would visit several shops to price goods, and if the article was a wash- stand and the price 165., they would discuss the thing for 20 minutes before spending even that sum for Workhouse fur- niture. His own view was that the purchase should be now aml at once peremptorily stopped, and means taken to pre- vent such attemptel extravagance in the future. (Hear, hear.) Mr. HALL thought the Board ought to consider the comfort and convenience of the master and matron—(hear, hear)— but he did not think in sanctioning such an expenditure for furniture for that house, the Board were doing their duty. The Rev. J. YONGE proposed that the matter be referred to the House Committee. Mr. DARBYSIIIRE was very glad Mr. Woolfall had hesitated before the furniture was delivered—(hear, hear)—because if it had been delivered the ratepayers would have been called upon to pay for it, and considerable discussion would have ensued, and Mr. Woolfall and the other members of the Board would have been blamed for permitting such expensive fur- niture to be obtained. (Mr. WooLYALL : Hear, hear.) Mr. Woolfall seemed to him to have been led astray by the word " purchase" instead of the word "select" being used. He did net know IIONY the letter W3S werdeA, hitt he thought the Committee might have acted with a little more discretion, and selected certain furniture for the approval of the Board, instead of purchasing it. He should like the master and matron's room to be well furnished, but he thought it could be furnished at less expense than that proposed. Mr. AppLrrort seconded the proposition that the matter be referred to the House Committee. The CHAIRMAN said it appeared there had been a little misapprehension iN the matter. They really seemed to have gone a little beyond what was laid down to be observed in , the purchase of furniture—innocently enough he had no doubt—and Mr. Woolfall seemed later on to have had the impression that they had acted a little in excess of their power. It appeared to him that the Board could not get beyond what had already been ordered, and made for their specific use (hear, hear) ; and he therefore thought they would have to confirm that whatever they did, but he believed the best way to deal with the matter was to refer it to the committee as proposed. In niture in the master's and matron's apartments was really of reference to the furniture, he had long noticed the fur- • a very shabby character—(hear, hear)—and when he bad paid a visit to Bolton and several other unions, he had found the furnished apartments, dec., for the domestic com- fort of the master and matron greatly in excess of theirs. The Board ought not to be niggardly in purchasing for the use of the master and matron furniture such as any res- pectable tradesman would like to see in his house. (Hear, hear.) The proposition was then carried. THE NEW SCHOOLS.

At a meeting of the Schools' Committee, the architects submitted correspondence between Mr. J. Daniel, of Man- chester, and themselves, having reference to arrangements for straightening the north-west boundary of land now used as building site for the industrial homes and schools, to- gether with plans of proposed straight line; also Mr. Daniel's offer to sell the required plot of front land for such straight line at the rate of id. per superficial square yard on lease, and 20 years' purchase if sold free.—lt was resolved that Mr. Pierpoint offer Mr. Daniel, at the rate of £2OO per statute acre as a final offer, subject to the approval of the Board of Guardians and the Local Government Board. The question of insuring the schools and homes from damage by fire was then considered, when the following resolution was agreed upon and forwarded to Mr. Napier :—" The commit- tee having considered the question of liabibity of the con- tractor to loss in the event of fire at the school buildings and homes at Padgate, and having also regard to the sums already paid by the Guardians to the contractor for work el ,ne and materials provided, is of opinion that the contractor should forthwith insure the buil4ings against fire in a com- pany to be approved of by the Guardians, and for a sum to be approved by the architects."

The minutes were confirmed. The CLERK said the schools had been insured. • Mr. DARBYSHIRE, replying to a member, said the contract expired on the 31st of March. The contractor told them he fully expected the buildings would be completed by that time. Neither the committee nor the architects considered they would be ready. Major CARTWRIGHT : The fact is we shall not get into that place before the end of October.. (Laughter.) The CHAIRMAN : I do not think we shall. VACANCIES FILLED.

Mr. COOPER propyois.e-d-, Mr. HALL seconded, and it was carried, that Mr. Gillespie, of Newton, be elected a member of the Assessment Committee in the place of the late Mr. Winstanley.—On the proposition of the CHAIRMAN, Major Cartwright was elected to fill a vacancy on the Schools Committee, also caused by the death of Mr. Winstonley.
RUNCORN POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—Before Messrs. R. M. Brooke (chairman), and Henry Reynolds.

A DRUNKEN PENSIONER.—Wm. Houghton, a pensioner, was convicted, on the evidence of P.C. Bossons, of having, been found drunk in the vaults at Wilson's Hotel, on the night of the l'ith inst., after having received his Govern- ment allowance.—He was fined 10s. and costs, or, in default of payrrent, ordered to be committed one month. IxpEcENcv.-.-John Seddon was charged with indecent conduct in High-street, on the 18th inst., whilst drunk.— P.C. Bossons proved the case, and defendant was fined 10s., and Os. 6d. costs, or 14 days' imprisonment. TRESPASSING IN SEARCH OF GAME AT CLIFTON.—TWO young men named Joseph Allman, and John Fishwick, were charged with having, on the Bth inst., trespassed on land in the occupation of Mr. Joseph Stokes, at Clifton, in search of game.—John Rowlands, labourer for Mr. Stokes, proved seeing a number of men on the land upon the Sunday in question, in search of game. He believed that both defen- dants were amongst them, but he would swear positively to Fislowick.—Mr. Stokes also gave evidence as to the great annoyance he had suffered from the conduct of a number of men of a similar kidney to the defendants, and he had been compelled to engage Rowlands to watch.—Allman called Thomas Gaiter, a Frodsham young man, whom Row- lands said was one of the poaching gang, to prove that at the time mentioned Allman was at his house.—The Chairman said that there being a doubt as to the identity of Allman, be would be discharged, but the other defendant would be fined 205., and 13s. 61. costs, or in default of payment, one month's imprisonment.
THE STRANGE PROCEEDINGS OF A LIVERPOOL
DOCK BOARD ENGINEER.

Mr. W. Talbot Code (or Codd), in the employ t.'ne Liver- pool Dock and Harbour Board, livinz was a few weeks ago bound at Fairfield, and who "Z)ver to keep the peace owing to hi s violent hel_n7lour in the house of Mr. Samuel Yarwood, auctioneer and livery stable proprietor, now appeared in the character of complainant, and charged several persons with assaulting him, including Mr. Yarwood ; Superinten- dent Williamson, and P.C's T. Kelly, W. H. Morris, and R. H. Noden Mr. Bartlett, of Liverpool, appeared on behalf of the complainant, wko, on this occasion did not conduct himself with the eccentricity which marked his previous ap- pearances; and Mr. Cartwright. of Chester, represented the police. Major Hamersley, chief constable of the county, occupied a seat on the bench during the hearing of the cases; and the court was crowded by an audience who were evi- dently a little disappointed that the proceedings were of a comparatively tame description. No doubt the ratepayers generally will be gratified at the result of the case, which must be very satisfactory to Mr. Yarwood, the Superinten- dmt of Police, and his subordinates. In order to condense the report of the proceedings, which occupied about three hours and a half, we shall give the complainant's statements in the various summonses in a connected form.

Mr. Bartlett briefly opened the case, and, in the course of his observations, said it appeared to him that Mr. Code had been most grossly illtreated in Runcorn, not only by Mr. Yarwood but by the police. Judging from the instructions given to him, the assault committed upon his client had been most unjust;fiable, and it was one which he _hoped the Bench would see fit to treat with due severity. Complainant was then called, and said that on Saturday, the 10th December, he came to Runcorn after two dogs, be- longing to him, which had got into the wrong train at Edge- hill, and which were intended for Mr. Turner, gamekeeper. On arriving at Runcorn he went to Mr. Peck, cab proprietor, who had driven him many times, and asked him if he could let him have a cab. He said he had no horses sharpened, and, moreover, he had a child dying. Peck said he would take him to Mr. Yarwood's house and leave him at the door, as he was not very friendly with him. This Peck did, and he (complainant) went into the shop and asked Mrs. Yar- wood to let him have a cab to take him to Weston Point. She said it was a very bad night, and she did not know whether any of their horses were sharpened. She, however, remarked that she would ask Mr. Yarwood, who was in bed. At his request a young woman who was in the house brought him a glass of milk and some bread and butter. This he ate, in the meanwhile pulling off his coat and placing it with his hat, gloves, and cane on the sofa. He then began to write a note to Mr. Turner, the gamekeeper, explaining why the dogs had not been sent, and as Mr. Yarwood was a long time in coming down, he shouted out, "Are you going to keep me here all night? Come downstairs." Yarwood came downstairs with his braces off, and, with an oath, enquired whether he was a - keeper on the spree. He (complainant) at the time was wearing a shooting jacket and gaiters. He replied that he was not a keeper, and wanted a cab to take him to Weston Point. He said he should have nothing of the kind there, and gripped him by the throat, pulled him off the chair, dragged him from the kitchen into the shop, and kicked him violently in the side. When he got upon his feet near the door, Yarwood tripped him backwards, and he fell heavily in the street. Then some young brute, who called himself Yarwood's son, boasted that he had also kicked him while he was on the ground. He lay stunned, and was then abused to such an extent that he was in a very bad state indeed afterwards. His kidneys were injured, and he was examined by one of the first physicians in Dublin, who gave him a certificate of his state of health. On his return to Runcorn he was also seen by Dr. McDougall. His arm was perfectly black, and was so at that moment; his side was blistered, and be yet wore bandages. He gave Yar- wood no provocation to treat him in such a manner. On recovering consciousness, after he was thrown into the street, he found that P.C. Kelly had his foot on his arm, which was extended on the ground. Kelly called him a scoundrel, and said if he opened his mouth he would knock his brains out. He was then allowed to get on his feet. and his hat, gloves, and stick were thrown into the street. He did not like to state the foul language used by P.C. Kelly, as there was a lady present in court. He followed that officer and P.C. Morris to the police station. On the way he told them that if they did not take him to the superintendent of police or a magistrate he would follow them about all night, and the officers turned upon him and said, "If you follow us we will knock your brains out." He told them he would shout "Murder," and claim the public protection. The men then said, "Walk before us." "No," he said, "I will walk behind you" At the police station he made a statement to Sergeant Morris. He was treated with the greatest kindness by Sergeant Walley, who offered him part of his tea at the station. He asked him for a glass of water, declining to have the tea, and for a basin of water to wash the blood off his face. He was told the water at the fountain was poisoned. He remained at the station until six o'clock the following morning. At four o'clock, as he was sitting in the chair, P.C. Noden tried to knock him over. At six he went to Widnes, where he made a report to Sergeant Robinson about the conduct of the Runcorn police. On the Sunday afternoon he again went to the Police Station at Runcorn, and asked for the sheet of paper on which he had written out his complaint. Superintendent Williamson came to him in a most over- bearing manner and said, "You have been drinking." He replied "Yes, I have been drinking." Superintendent Wil- liamson said, "What have you been drinking," and .he answered "Milk." This appeared to irritate the superin• tendent and he (witness) walked into the public office, as he declined to be alone with hi.n in his private office. Super- intendent Williamson then shouted to him in a most abusive manner, "Don't you come here again. You have been drinking." He (complainant) replied that Las had been drinking "tea, soda water, and soup." The- Superintendent said, "You have been drinking and are now labouring under the effects of drink." He said, "You may be, but I am not." Mr. Williamson then got into a great rage, and used very strong language to him. ' On the Monday evening he was at the police station with Mr. Bradley, solicitor, of Liverpool, and remained outside while that gentleman went into the office. In a short time the Superiptendent shouted out in an astonishing manner, " Codd, I want you; come in here." He declined to go into his private office, and Super- intendent Williamson came to him in a most excited manner in the public office, and, putting up his band, said, "Don't you come here until Monday next." He (complainant) re- plied that be was going to Ireland, and did not know whether he should be able to come then. He again shouted "Don't come here." Mr. Bradley was standing outside and said, "The Superintendent of police is drunk." He (complainant) said to Mr. Bradley "Yes, you can substantiate that." A subpcsna had been served on Mr. Bradley to attend there to support the statement. On the 3rd inst., he went to the police-station to get a copy of the statement he had made, so that he might take out a crown summons against Kelly and Morris for robbery with violence. Superintendent Wil- liamson said, "Have you come here to annoy me again 2" He stated that he was in quest of a magistrate on official business. The superintendent took him by the collar and marched him to the door. He (complainant) said "Very well, I shall summon you for that." The complainant then made a statement to the effect that he paid another visit to the police station, and was told by Sergeant McMichael that on the 10th December he saw him in the town drunk at six o'clock. Sergeant Walley was paying the men some money and told him he could not attend to him, and he said he would sit in the office and not annoy them. He was told by McMichael that if he did not go out he would chuck him out.. On hearing this threat he left the office.

• Cross-examined by Mr. Bartlett: In the coat that was thrown out of Yarwood's house there was a purse, a £5 note, a sovereign, a few shillings, some postage stamps, and a letter from Mrs. Christian, a solicitor's wife. There was also in one of the pockets a christening cloak that he was taking to Mr. and Mrs. Ormer, at Weston. There could be no other me-ns by which the police had ascertained that his name was Codd except by the papers.

In cross-examination by Mr. Cartwright, complainant ad- mitted that when at Mr. Yarwood's he had a flask of spirits wirh him, but said he did not open it during his stay at Runcorn, neither did he have it filled at Wilson's Hotel, which the police said be had. He maintained that a detec- tive who had been employed by him in Runcorn was pre- pared to prove that Mr. Yarwood had been convicted in that court of using gbusive language. On the night in question, he worse a snuff coloured velveteen coat the same as gentle- men on the bench often wore. He denied having taken off his coat and boots, and sat down in defendant's house with- out invitation. He maintained that defendant took hold of witness without any reason whatever.—What did you mean the other day by saying that your name was Code in Eng- land, and Codd in Ireland? I mean't the truth.—Why didn't you stick to your Irish name ? Because it happened that in 1844, When I was first bound apprentice, there was a mistake made in the spelling of my name in the Custom House, and this continued in in discharges and certificates, and when I passed the board in 1851. But, if you wish to see it, I can show you on my baptismal certificate that it is William Talbot Codd.—What are you, Mr. Code? lam a

div.head: REMOVAL OF LUNATICS.
div.p: THE REMOVAL OF LUNATICS.

The CLERK said he had written to Mr. Bleckly, on the aboye subject, as follows :—" January 17th. Dear Sir,— You will recollect accompanying me a few years back to the Broadmoor Asylum, our interviews with the Home Secretary and the Hon. Mr. Liddell at the Home Office, the difficulties we had to contend against, and the final removal of two criminal lunatics to Prestwich. The weekly cost for the two at Broadmoor was 285.; the cost at Prestwich is 14s. 4d., so that an annual saving of about £32 was effected, and this sum will in total be already about £150; and as years pass —both lunatics being young men—a very large saving will have resulted to this Union from the successful effort we then made. You will probably also remember that two were left at Broadmoor,—namely one Bolton, for whose main- tenance 7s. per week was only charged, and Margaret Daven- port, charged at 14s. per week. It was lodged best to leave the first by reason of the cost, and the second on the ground of her having then recently committed several murders. The subject of these charges has, however, again been con- sidered by the Guardians, and I shall be pleased if you will give me your view of the propriety of any movement being made now, either in the direction of Bolton's discharge, if fit, or of Davenport's removal to a county asylum, or both. We have several patients at Haydock at a cost of 14s. per week each. I fear they are epileptic or that some of them are so. The removal of the patients to Prestwich would result in a saving of over £l6 yearly each or of over £lOO per annum. Can you assist the Guardians herein ? If not to Prestwich, as you are a member of other asylum committees, can you assist us to their removal elsewhere." He had received the following reply : " Warrington, 23rd January 1882. Dear Sir,—You will re- member that the absolute cost of each prisonerat Broadmoor was over 20s. per week, and that as the cost of our two pri- soners together was ouly 10s. 6d. (7s. and 14s. separately), we thought it better to let well alone, as it the asylum were managed without red tape we might have had to pay 20s. for each prisoner. I have ascertained that at Prestwich they are quite full. On Friday morning we sent fully 20 patients to workhouses, so as to make room for more urgent cases. I recommend you to write to Lancaster, as I understand they are taking what may be called outside patients, that is patients who are not paupers. They have power to do this by Act of Parliament, but as it appears to me only in the event of the supply of paupers not being sufficient to fill the house. I should therefore advise you to write to them and state the circumstances, and ask for the admission of the patients you are at present maintaining at Haydock. Prest- wich new asylvm will not be ready for some months. Whittingham will be ready sooner, but after Prestwich, the cheapest asylum at present is, I think, Lancaster. Yours truly, H. BLECKLY."—He (the Clerk) had written to Lan- caster, but had received no reply. He had a reply from Whittingham stating they were not in a position to trans- fer patients from Haydock, but hoped to be able to do so in a few weeks. In reply to a communication fron the clerk, Dr. Orange, superintendent of Broadmoor Asylum, wrote that very little change had taken place in the condition of Samuel Bolton since he (the Clerk) had seen him last, and that Margaret Davenport's condition might be described as chronic mania, with numerous delusions. Her insanity had become more confirmed during the last few years, and her bodily health was only indifferent.

div.head: PURCHASING COSTLY FURNITURE.
div.p: PURCHASING COSTLY FURNITURE.

The CLERK reported to the Board a correspondence with Messrs. Johnson and Mr. R. W. Marsh, cabinet makers, and in explaining how it came about, said on Monday morning Mr. Woolfall consulted him at his office on what he ex- plained to be a matter that had occasioned him much un- easiness. He stated that on the preceding Thursday he received a letter from Mr. Mackey saying he and Mr. Heaton were appointed to purchase furniture for the Master's rooms, and requesting him to meet for the purpose; that he attended accordingly at Messrs. Johnson's and Mr. Marsh's shops, and that there was a desire expressed to buy very expensive furniture, and he offered opposition to it, but he had unwillingly consented to purchase what he had since considered altogether out of place for a workhouse. He (the Clerk) had the House Committee book open before him:at the time, and said that neither on the minutes of the Board nor on those of the committee did any snch motion appear, and he told Mr. Wool fall there was a distinct resolu- tion of the Board, passed 18 months ago upon an unpleasant discussion on the purchase of expensive carpets for Mr. Mackey's room and the staircase, directing that orders for furniture for the Master should always in future be preceded by an estimate setting forth the quality and price of the goods to be ordered. He intimated to Mr. Woolfall that he was most undesirous of interfering in any House matter, and he preferred not to interfere. Mr. Woolfall, however, felt the position he was in very strongly, and, as he cor- rectly might, insisted upon the clerk writing letters, which he did as follows :--t‘ January 23, 1882.—Dear Sirs,—Mr. Woolfall, a member of the Workhouse Committee, has con- sulted me upon a resolution by the Board relating to the purchase of furniture, and as Mr. Woolfall finds that no actual authority to make the purchase has been given to him, and is of opinion that the contemplated expenditure much exceeds what is reasonable and necessary, I am de- sired by him to say that he can be in no way responsible for the expenditure being incurred. lam desired also to say, as clerk to the Guardians, that an estimate of the prices should in the first instance be submitted to the Board for their approval prior to the execution of the order." The Clerk, continuing, said the only minute on the books was that some furniture be taken from the master's rooms to the fever hospital nurse's room, and new chairs supplied to the master's rooms in their stead. This minute was sub- ject to the resolution he had named. Mr. Woolfall intimated that he should stop the receiving of the furniture at the gates. The cabinet makers sent letters in reply say- ing that the two guardians, and Mrs. Mackey had ordered the goods and agreed to the prices. They further said that the furniture had been sent for on Saturday but was not ready, and that Mrs. Mackey had intimated she wanted the window pole and drapery, &c., removed and new substituted. He informed them the matter was for the Guardians to consider and approve, and they must await instructions. Mr. IV6OLFALL remarked, that he need only say in addi- tion to what the Clerk had said, that the letter from Mr. Mackey informing him he was appoipted to meet the parties to select the furniture, came to him on Thursday. He .met Mrs. Mackey and Mr. Heaton accordingly, and he soon found it necessary to object or much more expensive goods would have been selected had he not done so. He said it would not do; there would be a "row at the Board." (Hear, hear, and laughter.) He was, however, very unwillingly induced to consent to what was ordered, but after he left the parties and con- sidered the few things ordered would about £l2O, he felt very uncomfortable. (Laughter.) Unfortunately the next day he met with an accident by being thrown out of a trap, ad this prevented him from at once taking steps. On Monday he was determined to consult the clerk, and whilst the clerk was sending the letters, he went to give orders to the porter not to admit the furniture if It came. He consi- dered suitable furniture could have been got for much less money. (Hear, hear) Mr: HEATON said the ratepayers had sent him there to spend money as if it were his own, and he had done so in the present instance. He would have spent more on the fur- niture if he had been purchasing it for himself. The account from Mr. 8.. W. Marsh,eßridge-street, was as follows :—Ash bedroom suite £2O, half-tester brass and iron bedstead £7, straw mattrass 139. 61, feather bed, bolsters, and two pillows, £10; total, £37 13s. 6d. Messrs. Johnson's account was—lounge, gentleman's chair, and four i single chairs, upholstered all hair and covered n morocco, £3B; walnut sideboard, with a glass and shelves and cel- larette, £l3 10s.; dining table £l3 10s., brass fender £2 145., brass fiteirons £1 55.; black skin rug (£2 55.), 28 yards carpet (Brussels, at 48. 61., £6 65.), £8 us.; making etc., of carpets with rings and studs, 25 yards at 51,105. 5d.; making two loasgocks 3s. 6d., laying carpet, two hours at 4d., is. 7c1.; total, £7s 58. sd.

div.head: PAYMENT OF SCHOOL FEES.
div.p: THE PAYMENT OF SCHOOL FEES.

Mr. DannvssuriE, in moving that school fees be allowed in a number of cases, said the committee directed investiga- tion into the circumstances of the people who asked for school fees, and every exertion was made to obtain a return of their earnings. The Rev. J. YONGE seconded the motion, and said he thought it was a pity that Mr. Riley, the school attendance officer, made the remarks which he did the other day before the magistrates, in reference to the way in which the School Committee of the Union did its business ; but perhaps in justice to Mr. Riley he should state that he came to him to explain that somehoir or other an error had happened. What he wished to say was that he thought nobody had any right to say the payment of school fees was done in a slovenly way whatever. A year ago he sat on that com- mittee, and he knew they gave a most patient hearing to every case which came before them, and he did not think it was true the Guardians paid school fees for half-timers, and still less true was it that the Guardians paid school fees for non-attenders. He was only sorry to see that Major Cart- wright confirmed the Mayor in his error that the Guardians were imposed upon. Major CARTWRIGHT maintained that the relieving officers were often deceived. He asked supposing the committee granted fees for children, and those children did not go to school, where did the money go? The CHAIRMAN explained that the coarse now pursued was this: that the Guardians paid only in cases where the children go to school. Where a boy went to school one day and did not go again that week, they would have to pay the school fees for that week. He had looked over the list, and he found that there were exceedingly few children that they paid for who did not go to school. Major CARTWRIGHT : Suppose he goes three days in one week, three days in the next, and three days in the third week? The CHAIRMAN: YOH will have to pay for the three weeks. Major CARTWRIGHT : Precisely; that is what I say. Wherever children do not attend school who get school fees granted, I say a portion of that money is paid for the non- attendance of those children. Mr. DARBYSITIRES said when the committee had ("ranted fees they bad done all that was required of them. It was not their duty to see that the children go to school.

div.head: HUYTON-WITH-ROBY LOCAL BOARD.
div.p: HUYTON-WITH-ROBY LOCAL BOARD.

A special meeting of the Iluyton-with-Roby Local Board was held at the public efices, Huyton, on Friday, for the purpose of laying the rate for the ensuing year. Mr. E. C. Leventon presided, and there were also present Messrs. W. Burnyeat, R. Brown, and T. Watkin, with Mr. W. Swift (clerk) and Mr. Joseph Worrall (surveyor). The meeting was called for seven o'clock, and although there are 12 members on the board, it was nearly eight o'clock before there was a quorum ; anl it was very doubtful whether there would have been a quorum tiled had not the surveyor gone round in a cab and hunted some of the members up. Mr. W. Burnyeat was the only member who put in an appearance in good time.—Mr. BURNYEAT moved, and Mr. WATKIN seconded, that the seal of the Board be attached to the rate of 2s. 6d. in the pound agreed upon at the previous meeting. The amount expected to be realised from the rate on a rateable value of £28,990 19s. 11d. is £3,400, and the estimated expenditure for the year, as shown at the last meeting, is £3.402 16s. 3d.--The CHAIRMAN observed that the estimate had already been explained.—The CLERK said the Board had to decide when the rate should be made payable; and it was resolved that it be payable on the 27th Inst. as in the previous year.—Mr. BURNYEAT observed that there had been some changes in the valuation..—The Ctratames: Yes; it will bring the Board something like £4oa year more.—There being no other business the meeting separated.

sailor.—Are you following any business at the present time? Yes —Where? In Liverpool.—What kind of business? Surveyor to the Mersey Docks and Harbour Board.—You are fulfilling that engagement now? lam on leave of absence.—How long have you been on leave of absence? Since the 10th December, when this brutal outrage was corn- mitted.—Haven't you been indulging in drink ? No.—ln further cross-examination, Mr. Cartwright said :—Didn't you tell the defendant you were a barrister-at-law ? Yes, —Then you are a barrister-at-law? Yes, I am.—Perhaps you will tell us of what Inn ? (Laughter.) I shall not, but I could show you my wig and gown if I liked.—The magistrates will put what construction they like upon that statement.—Complainant : They are at liberty to do so. (Sotto voce) All this was caused by two dogs getting into the wrong train. (Laughter.) Sergeant Robinson, of the Widnes Police force, stated .that about 0-30 on Sunday morning, the 11th December, Captain Code came to the Widnes station, where he (wit- ness) was on duty, and made a complaint. He appeared to be sober, and there was nothingavrong with him. Mr. Cartwright then addressed the magistrates for the defence. He remarked that when they heard the evidence he had to call, the Bench would come to the conclusion that Mr. Code must have been either very drunk and had for- gotten what he was doing, or must have been afflicted with some peculiar mania, and for the time being lost his mind. He must have been temporarily bereft of his senses between the 101 ii December and the 3rd January. Taking the case all round, it was as peculiar a one as was ever brought before a court of justice. He thought the cab proprietor, Peck, was an uncommonly shrewd man, who, seeing there was going to be trouble with Mr. Code, barrister-at-jaw, same to the conclusion that he had better get rid bi him and so put him upon Yarwood, which was a 'Sery unkind cut on the part , of Peek, (r, TI.ISn this " Captain " Code in Eng- land, and Codd in Ireland, barrister at law—(laughter)-- went into the premises of Mr. Yarwood, rapped with his heavily-loaded stick on the table, and, he was going to say, somewhat after the manner of Richard tLe Third, who cried "My kingdom for a horse," demanded a cab. After acting, in the strangest manner possible' and insulting Mrs. Yar- wood, complainant was put out by the owner of the house. The street was slippery, and Code fall to the ground, and very possibly Mr. Yarwoed somewhat violently, as was natural under the circumstances, threw his things out into the street after him. While he was sitting on the ground tbe policemen came up, but far from assaulting him, they picked him up and put him together. They had not, how- ever, been long in his company when he charged them with assault, and stated that he would follow them all the night. Were the police to be harassed in the performance of their duties in this style, at such an hour of the night? It was a piece of consummate .effrontery for Captain Code or Codd, barrister-at-law—(lau4ater)—to stand up and deliberately tell the Bench what he had. It would have been quite right if the officers had entered a charge against him for interfer- ing with them in the performance of their duty, and com- plainant must be told that he could not interfere with police- men while on duty. Whilst at the station he had taunted the police, and asked them to lock him up. He considered Mr. Code had been treated in a most kind manner by the nolice. With regard to the alleged assault at the station by Noden, he was allowed by Sergeant Walley to remain at the station all night, and as Noden was passing his chair at some . part of the morning, he knocked down his stick. Immediately com- plainant jumped up and charged him with assault. Sergeant Walley threw away a considerable amount of trouble upon the ungr iteful m in, as he could plainly see that he was either suffering from ciderium tremens, or drunk. There could be no two opinions about it. The man was either diabolically wicked and wished to bespattes the character Of respectable men with mud, for which he had no justification whatever, or he must have been bereft of his senses. Mr. Cartwright went on to speak of the conduct of Superinten- dent Williamson to complainant, who, upon his first visiting the police office, seeing that he was decently attired, educated, and having the appearance of a man who had moved in a respectable position in life, treated him with every considera- tion, though he was under a strong suspicion that he was ' either suffering from delerium tremens, or drunk. Mr. Cartwright also dwelt upon the manner in which complain- ant had altogether disregarded the responsible position held by Mr. Williamson; and his overbearing, impudent, and ' loud-toned manner in conversation. Mr. Williamson re- quested Mr. Code to put his affairs in the hands of a respect- able solicitor. Complainant had visited the Superintendent's , private offices with a couple of dogs; had persisted in re- maining there though frequently asked to leave; and had been a great source of annoyance ever since his first appear- ance on the scene. There could not he the slightest doubt that Mr. Code did not know what he was doins, at the time. ' As to the marks upon complainant's body, the magistratos ' might take it for granted that he would be marked, and well marked, because a more unreasonable man never eaisted, and there were some people in this wicked world who would not tolerate the sort of nonsense of which he had been guilty. Of course if complainant had come in contact with a sharp, clever fellow, and indulged in such an outrageous course of proceeding, it was highly probable that he would "down him" in a moment, as his conduct was simply unbearable. It appeared that complainant had determined to try to dis- grace every one with whom he came in contact. Witness his animus and false statements about Mr. Yarwood, who was a most respectable man, entrusted with the work of carrying Her Majesty's mails in that district, and not likely to risk his position over such a rubbishy affair as this. Mr. Yarwood had never been convicted of any such offence as that with which Mr. Code charged him. It was a telling fact against Mr. Code that Mr. Bradley, who was a highly respectable solicitor in Liverpool, though asked to attend and give evidence in his behalf was not present. In con- clusion, he would call witnesses who would prove the entire want of foundation there was for the wild assertions made by camplainant.

. . During the course of the proceedings, Mr. Bartlett, ad- dressing the Bench, slid they would have gathered from the statement made by Mr. Code that he was not in a position to call any witnesses to give evidence on his behalf. But the manner in which he had given his evidence and replied to the cross-examination of Mr. Cartwright must have carried with it the conviction that he had told the simple truth, and had only tried to detail a course of procedure that was entirely unjustifiable and improper. Mr. Code, being in a good position, had no cause of quarrel with the police or Mr. Yarwood. He (Mr. Bartlett) could hardly find words to express sufficiently the disgraceful character of the con- duct of the police. When they looked at the animus of the police and, as the newspaper reports showed, the animus felt by Superintendent Williamson, who, even in the court, be- haved in a most improper manner-
Mr. Cartwright: Has that anything to do with the case? Mr. Bartlett: Yes. It is illustrative of the way in which Mr. Code was generally treated by the police while he was here.

Mr. Cartwright: I must object to it. I do not know what my friend is going to lead to. The simple question is what happened on the occasion of the assault. My friend should not speak of reports. Reports may not be right, or twenty things.

Mr. Bartlett: But reports are always right. Mr. Cartwri4ht : I.object to it. Mr. Bartlett. continuing, said the language used by Super- intendent Williamson was most unbecoming. The Superin- tendent when charged with assault thought proper to stand up from his easy chair, but when complainant was charged he was ordered to go into the dock where the other prisoners stood. There was a sort of overbearing feeling on the part of the police towards him, which was highly unbecoming and exceedingly improper. The conduct of the police had been indescribably disgrace- ful, most shameful, and most shocking. Ihey knew that although they had most difficult duties to perform, which he was happy to say could not be better performed by any other class of men in the country, sometimes they took up a feeling against someone and acted overbearingly, which he did not think would be sanctioned by any court in the country.

Mr. Frederick Yarwood, son of Mr. Yarwood, said he came home on the night of the 10th inst., from a journey, at about twelve o'clock, and found his father requesting Mr. Codeleave the house Complainant declined to do so, and said he should stay there all night. His father took complainant by the coat, lifted him from the seat, and then he (witness) seized him round the waist and put him out on to the cause- way. No more fotce was used than was absolutely neces- sary, and complainant would not have fallen had not the frost made the flags slippery. The two policemen assisted complainant to rise and he saw him hold a short conversation with the men, and then walk away with them. Mr. Yar- wood was in his stockings. Cross-exatnined by Mr. Bartlett: Then, according to your account, you were treating him almost like a little baby— you were so tender with him. (Laughter.) Did you notice that the policemen had sticks in their hands? fdid not.— It appoars to me that you did not notice anything in his favour, but everything that was against him.

Miss Susan °kelt, niece to Mr. Yarwood, said that com- plainant helped himself to the bread and butter without being asked. She provided him with some milk and soda- water at his rcquest, and observed him put a little spirits into the glass. She distinctly heard complainant say he would either sleep on the sofa or with Mrs. Yarwood. Mrs. Yarwood called for her husband, who came down and said "This is my hong() ; I kindly ask you to leave it." Mr. Yarwood next got hold of him by the coat, pushed him into the middle room, and then Mr. Yarwood's son helped him into the street. I was not true that Mr. Yarwood took com- plainant by the throat. No violence was used, with the ex- ception of pushing complainant to the door. Mr. Cbde was in the house about half an hour, and when calling Mr. Yarwood to come downstairs, said "Come down, you old villain."

- : When Mr. Yarwood came into the house to go to bed, he was perfectly sober. Mrs. Yates, of the Rifleman's Arms, Church-street, said she was asked into Mr. Yarwood's by his wife, who said she had got a man inside who was drunk. She entered, and saw Mr. Code there, drinking some milk. Complainant put something in the milk out of a flask in his possession. She heard complainant ask Mrs. Yarwood how long she had been in possession of false teeth, and utter other language of such a nature that she did not like to repeat it. Mrs. Yarwood told complainant to be kind enough to leave the house, but he declined and began to unfasten his gaiters. Mrs. Yarwood told him he could not stay there. She (wit- ness) asked Mrs. Yarivood why her husband did not come down, and added "As far as I am concerned, I would not ask for my husband to put him out. I would do so without a husband, if he had used the language to me which he has to you." She (witness) distinctly heard com- plainant say that if he could not have a cab, he should stay there and sleep upon the sofa.
