What had because whilst they had good men in the House of Commons followed upon the heels of the system to which he referred? -and he did not care how many good men they sent to Parlia- Not only excessive rack rent, but it was a fact that the laud- snent—they were but men, after all, and unless they were lord, had taken advantage of the tenants own improvements; .1, ported, and, in some instances, distinctly chastised by the 1 for at was not only in Ireland that the landlords had used

their beggrappling• hooks, "but they had done it in England." (Hear, hear, and a Voice: " 6hame.") One great reason why we had not had the same uprising in England as in Ireland was that when the labourers had been driven from the fields, they had had the large towns of the manufactur- ing centres to fly to. (Loud applause.) England did not owe her prosperity, her peace, and her security to any gracious acts which the landlords had done, but to the spirited manu- facturers and merchants she possessed, who had provided for the surplus labour. (Applause.) The question for them to consider was, Is this law to continue for ever ? No ; for they were prepared to go in and smash it up. Some said they ought to take the landlords' property from them. Now, that was a very grave question, and he believed in the golden rule of doing unto others as he should like them to do unto him, and he would rather dear with the matter from a political stand point. If the land owning class, when the mass of the people of this country were politically power- less, could put twenty millions a year upon the taxpaying population, which they themselves ought to have paid, then they could be dealt with by those who now possessed the franchise. In the days to which he referred, the land own- ing class, because they were pre-eminent and all powerful, passed laws which were like to a Roman wax nose, which, if they put it to the fire, could be made either into a Roman, an aquiline, a pug, or no nose at all. (Great laughter, and applause.) These men had passed laws which had enabled them to enclose thousands of acres. During the course of half a century no fewer than 3,741 acres, under the Enclosure Acts. They had managed to steal seven millions of acres of land which was once the rightful property of the hard-work- ing man, who could at that time keep his goose and his pig. What was this land to day.? Sporting ground for the privileged few, over which the once rightful owners were pro- hibited from passing! He was quite willing to admit that two wrongs did not make a right; but let him suppose a case. If some one present was to take the watch out of his (the speaker's) pocket that night, and he was to meet him to-morrow and say to him, "Look here, my friend, you have got my watch," and the thief was to say, "Well, you have got to give me five shillings for it," he would not pay the money; but he would tell them what he would do—he would let him have a double over until he took the time- keeper from him. These were questions which could not be played with; but most certainly the British purse had no right to be drained to compensate the men to whom he referred, who had compensated themselves out of the money they ought to have paid to the starving men and women whom they had created in the rural districts of England. Then some would say he would perhaps do away with the class referred to altcgether. Well, he would sooner lose half a dozen lords than half a dozen workingmen. (Laugh- ter.) He did not court anyone's smiles, or fear their frowns, and one day he told a celebrated duke that he owed hie position to the sweat and lalleur of men like him (the speaker). Let him take the case of a great landed pro- prietor, who lived upon one of the finest estates in England, under which were some of the richest minerals. Well, the proprietor of the estate might just as well be possessed of a large piece of wood in his pocket as belong to the estate, unless he was prepared to bring skill and thought—which be had not got himself—to bear upon it. (Hear, hear, loud laughter, and applause.) He had worked on railways, and in various departments of work, but he never yet saw a bishop wheeling a barrow—(much laughter)—but, never- theless, he believed that if there was anything noble in life, it was the pursuit of honest industry, whether it was in the production of a good book, the making of something to please the eye or charm the ear. As long as something was produced, so and good, but so long as a man was simply employed in consuming and produced', nothing he belonged to the residium. (Applause.) He must now draw his remarks to a close. (Cries of "Go on.") There was a system in con- nection with the entail and settlement question called the dowry system, which was one of the most inhuman of which he knew. There were landlords at present whose rent-roll was about £25,000 or £30,000 a year, and whose private in- come was about £B,OOO, the balance being paid out to aunts, uncles, and other relatives. How could a male who had to find this sum in evil times as well as in good do so without raising the rents of his tenants and perhaps reducing his own income. On such an estate as that they could not expect tenant farmers to thrive. They might as well expect a man to be healthy and comfortable with half-a-dozen leeches bleeding him. (Applause ) These things were cursing the land, and he would like to see estates divided fairly among the different members of families. One gentleman said to him the other day, "What would you do with the lady under such circumstances? Would you divide the estate fairly ? " He replied, "This is what I would do. Let Tom have his share and Lucy her share." Then his questioner proceeded, "But suppose the lady did not feel disposed to farm, what tben ? " "Then," said he in answer, "let her get a husband who would do so." (Laughter and applause.) He knew that absenteeism had been a curse to Ireland, owing to taking so much money out of the country that it was left very poor; but was it not a fact to-day that they had tens of thousands of pounds—and perhaps he should not be wrong if be said hundreds of thousands, or millions—which had been drained from the agricultural labourers, and where did all this money go to? To maintain men who for years were "sporting it" on the continent. (Loud applause, and a voice: "Shame.") Need they wonder at tenant farmers being bankrupt, when the poor agricultural labourers, a few years ago, were so cruel as to make them pay 38. a week more for their work! (Loud laughter and applause.) Well, the fact was that the cause of these evils was not in the farmers, or in the land, but it was in the system which was cursing the land, and must be broken down. (Applause, and a voice: "Shame.") Mr. Arch next spoke of land that land-laws were driving out of cultivation. He knew of 60,000 acres in Wiltshire that had thus ceased to be cultivated. He spoke of heirs to estates who had wasted their substance, and ruined their estates, but could not sell them. And why? Because someene in the past had bequeathed it to his heirs and assigns, and the dead hand of the past clung to it, and he supposed the hand of someone yet unborn would influence it too. It would be said that his views were very Radical; but he called them Conservative, because he wanted to conserve the benefit of the 'land for the people' and to obtain the greatest good for the greatest number. Mr. Arch referred to having passed through Warrington, and here he saw the people huddled together, whereas if the conditiona which ought to obtain were in existence many of the workingmen there would be on the soil, producing food 30 per cent, cheaper than it was now produced. The squires did not want the workingmen to have land •, they thought it, possession would make them too thrifty; but there was no doubt it would prove an in- culculable boon. They told them to "hush, and be quiet ; " No. He did not care who hated him; he hid not care who blessed him ; he did not care who cursed him; but while he knew that England's grandeur, England's glory, and England's stabilility had been built upon the horny hands and broad shoulders of her workingmen, and that 600,000 of his own class must fall victims to the picture of pauperism he had described, Joseph Arch would never let his voice rest. (Loud cheers). Political power was what they wanted. They were told by some that if the working classes were enfranchised that it was very easy to buy his vote for a pint of beer, but he said that the man who bribed a simple honest workipgman in that way was a much greater scamp than the man he had bribed. (Cheers). Those who would bribe began to feel the weakness of their position. Workingmen had got no stake in the country, but a landlord, if he chose, could go away and still be re- ceiving his lordly income. Why should not the labourer have an interest in the land he tilled? It might be that his views were too advanced, but he believed that the great question was imminent. It would be a struggle when it did come and he hoped when it did come they would find the people of the country true blue. (Cheers). They might be called all sorts of names at the present time, but generations yet unborn would read the history of the present century with delight. They might read of scientific frontiers, of stolen Cypruses and Afghanistan wars; but there was no chapter in which they would read with so much delight as that which the present Government bad begun to write. (A voice, "Not Coercion !") It might be that every line was not written in accordance with their wishes, but if the Government did not write as they wished when the people got political, let them send men to Parliament who would I make an amendment for every wrong word in that chapter of history. (Cheers). They did not want Whitleys or Hamiltons. (A voice' "par Randy Pandy's "). No, nor Randy Pandys. (Loud laughter and cheers). Generations yet unborn would feel the benefits of the work which they were doing to-day, and that which they would do when they got political power, and they would be charmed by its haloes of light and joy, and be charmed that their heirlooms were rot those relating to an aristocracy, but to the sacred cause of truth and justice. (Loud cheers.) At this moment there was great uproar in the body of the hall, caused by an excited Liberal opponent who wished to overpower the arguments of Mr. Arch and the Liberal party generally with his wild and heated harangue. It was with great difficulty he could be silenced. Mr. Arch concluded amid loud cheers. The resolution was put and carried with acclamation. • The following resolution was moved by Dr. O'KEEFFE "That this meeting desires to express its deep sympathy with the people of Ireland, and its earnest desire that the Government will at au early date abolish the Coercion Act." The motion was seconded by Mr. BROWN, and carried unanimously. On the motion of Mr. Siam, seconded by Mr. S. OWENS, cordial thanks were given to Mr. Arch, and a similar com- pliment having been paid to the Chairman, the meeting terminated.

div.head: MEETING OF PARLIAMENT.
div.p: THE MEETING OF PARLIAMENT.

The following letter has been issued by the Prime Minister to his supporters in the House of Commons:— " Hawarden Castle, January 20, 1882.—Sir,—The 7th Feb. has been appointed for the opening of the Parliamentary Session; and I venture to hope you may be in your place, as matters of pressing interest will at the earliest practi- cable date be submitted to the House of Commens.—l have the honour to be, sir, your very faithful and obedient servant, W. E. GLADSTONE. Earl Granville has issued the following circular to the supporters of the Ministry in the House of Lords :—" 18, Carlton House-terrace, January 20, 1882.—My Lord,— Parliament will assemble on February 7. Important business will be proceeded with, and I hope it may suit your convenience to be in your place at the date I have named.-1 have the honour to be, my lord, your obedient servant, GRAN VILLE."

div.head: WIDNES LIBERAL ASSOCIATION,
div.p: WIDNES LIBERAL ASSOCIATION,
PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

MONDAY. TWO MONTHS' IMPRISONMENT FOR THREATENING.— Henry Stowles was charged with threatening Mary Jane Jessop, on the 18th instant.—The evidence showed that complainant was a witness in a case against Catherine Matthews, who, some few days ago, was committed to gaol two months for using violent threats to a witness in a case which has yet to be heard at Liverpool Assizes. Stowles is the brother-in-law of Matthews, and he went to complain- ant's house on the day named, and told her she had sent one woman to prison two months, but he would take care that she did not cause anyone else to go there, tor he would kill her before seven o'clock that evening.—Mary Clarke was called to prove the truthfulness of this statement, and the prisoner was ordered to be bound over, himself in £2O and two sureties in £lO, or go to prison two months.—Prisoner could not find the sureties. A WIDNES ROUGH SENT 'TO GAOL.—Thomas Scally was charged with committing a violent assault on Mary Bartley. —Complainant lives in Wellington-street, and on Saturday night, whilst drunk, the prisoner went to her house, and asked for a woman who used to lodge there. He was told by Bartley's brother that she was not there, but he refused to leave, and knocked the man down and kicked him. Com- plainant tried to assist her brother, on which the prisoner hit and kicked her.—Scally, who had already, at the same court, been sentenced to a month's imprisonment for drunk- enness, was committed for a like period for the assault. WEDNESDAY.—Before Messrs. Holbrook Gaskell, senr. (chairman), and George Pilkington. DRUNK ON LICENSED PREMISES.—James Ploughman was convicted of having been drunk in the Ram's Head public- house, Sutton's-lane, on the 14th instant, and was fined 10s. and costs. ATTEMPTING TO RESCUE A PRISONER.—AntIe Smith was charged with obstructing P.C. Rogers in the execution of his duty, on the 14th instant.—On the night in question, a disturbance took place in Midwood-street, owing to a man named Newall quarrelling with his wife. The last named man afterwards assaulted the police, and was apprehended. As he was being taken away, a crowd interfered with the object of rescuing him.—Defendant was fined 10s. and Is. 6d. costs, or 14 days' imprisonment. NOISY PROCEEDINGS IN MIDWOOD-STREET. Patrick Newall was charged with causing a breach of the peace.— P.C. Rogers said that on the 14th instant he saw defendant striking his sister in Midwood-street during the attempt to rescue Newall.—Defendant denied the assault, and called his mother and several other witnesses to prove that he only pushed his sister, and was guilty of no breach of tie peace. —Superintendent Barker said he did not think the case a very bad one, and the magistrates decided to dismiss the case on payment of costs (7s. 6d.) A DIRTY CHIMNEY.—John Martin was, on the evidence of Sergeant Clarkson, ordered to pay 55., including costs, for having permitted the chimney of his dwelling-house to be on fire, on the morning of the 12th instant. A SUNDAY MORNING'S AMUSEMENT.—Thomas Doyle, a young man, was convicted, on tie evidence of P.C. Brown, of having, on Sunday morning, the 15th inst., in Charles- street, discharged two stones from a catapult, and ordered to pay 7s. 6d. costs. A QUEER PLACE OF REFUGE FOR A CONVICTED THIEF.— James Spencer, a man about 30 years of age, was charged with stealing three pairs of stockings, the property of Mr. Richard Baker, draper, Victoria-road. Mrs. Baker said that about a quarter-past seven on the evening of Saturday, the 14th inst., whilst she was serving a customer, she heard a string broken near the shop door. She discovered three pairs of stockings were missing, and ran to look if she could see anything of the thief, whom she was astonished to see in the arms of P.C. Murray, who had witnessed the theft.—The stockings were found under the man's coat.—Prisoner said he should not have committed the theft, but he was under the influence of drink at the time.—Superintendent Barker remarked that in April last year. Spencer was charged with stealing a ham, belonging to Mr. Gandy, of Warrington, and be had suffered various terms of imprisonment—The Chair- man said the prisoner would be sent to gaol four months, with hard labour. LIVELY PROCEEDINGS AT MOSS BANK.—Mary Daley was charged with committing a breach of the peace in Mary- street, Moss Bank—P.C. Pitt gave evidence to the effect that on the Bth inst., defendant made a great disturbanee, and challenged another woman to fight.—Daley denied the charge.—There were two other cases in which defendant was concerned, and the Bench decided to hear them together. In the first, defendant was charged with using defamatory language towards Mary Barke. There had been bad feeling between the women for some time, and on the 21st instant defendant went to the door of complainant's mother's house, and used very,. offensive language. She also visited com- plainant's house and acted in a similar manner, insinuating that complainant was an immoral woman. There was a cross-summons in which Elizabeth Lightfoot, mother of the complainant in the last case, was charged with using de- famatory language to Mary Daley. Mr. Husband defended. Evidence having been given in support of the case, Mr. Husband contended that complainant had not come into the court with clean hands, as she had been the first to use the offensive remarks.—The Chairman said that both in the 'police case, and the one brought against her by Burke, the 'defendant must be bound over to keep the peace for six , months, in one surety of £lO, or two of £5, with the alterna- tive of 14 days' imprisanment. The case against Lightfoot would be dismissed. THROWING STONES AT A RAILWAY TRAIN. Michael Crosby and Wm. Butler, two boys, were charged with having, on the 15th inst., thrown stones at a carriage on the Cheshire Lines of Railway, so as to endanger the safety of 1 the guard. The case was conducted by the police inspector to 1 the Company.—Mr. Samuel Foxley, of Exeter-street, Liver- pool, said he was goods guard in the employ of the Cheshire Lines Company, and on the 15th inst. he was working a goods train from Godley to Liverpool. As he was passing Farnworth station at ten minutes to three in the afternoon, and going from under the bridge, he felt a stone strike the brake van. He then looked in the directiun of the bridge, and saw _another stone thrown after the train had passed. He observed four or five boys on the bridge at the time, and be immediately reported what had happened to the station- master.—Two youths, named Weldon, Alfred-street, and Albert Edwards, Kent-street, were called, who said they were on the bridge at the time, and when the train was passing Weldon heard one of the defendants say "Let us throw at the brake van," and Edwards the others shout "Let us throw at Jack-in-the-box."—The Chairman said the offence was a very serious one, as, if one of the stones had hit the guard the consequences to him might have been very alarming. The magistrates felt they were bound to make an example of the defendants. If the lads had been under 14 years of, age, they would have, been enabled, under the statute, to order them to be whipped with a birch rod. Certainly the inclinati.n of the magistrates would have leaned to order- ing the youngsters such a severe whipping as they would never have forgotten. As defendants were above the age named, it was not in the power of the Bench to order this punishment, and they did not desire to send boys of such a tender age to prison. Under these circumstances, each of their parents would be ordered to pay a fine of 403., or, in default, the lads would be sent to prison one month. He' certainly hoped the parents would not forget to give each of the youths a severe flogging.—The magistrates afterwards held a consultation with the representative of the Company present, who expressed his willingness that the fine should be reduced. Under these circumstances, the magistrates decided to reduce it to . 205., and the imprisonment in de- fault of payment to 14 days. The costs would be paid by the county. as'provided by the statute. "WHEN LOVELY WOMAN STOOPS TO FOLLY." John Owen, a respectably attired labourer, was charged, under a warrant, with hssaultina• a good looking woman, named Elizabeth Pendlebury, about 35 years of age, who had for some short time been living with him in a state of concu- binage.—Complainant said she did net want to press the case as the prisoner was as good a man as ever lived when he was not in drink, which lad him into low company, and he expressed his sorrow for his conduct and promised amend- ment.—Mr. Gaskell remarked that as the complainant had gone so far as to issue a warrant against Owen, she must now tell what took place.—From her statement, it appeared that owing to the prisoner's drinking, she had separated from him some few days ago, and on the 23rd inst he went to the place where she was staying and beat and kicked her. He was, however, in drink at the time, and she would be very sorry to send him to gaol.—ln reply to Mr. Lewin, deputy magistrates' clerk, complainant admitted that the prisoner also pulled out his knife and said he would cut her throat. —The Chairman said Owen. had conducted himself in a very brutal manner, and he would be sent to gaol one month, with hard labour. A CAUTION TO NON-PAYERS OF LOCAL BOARD RATES. —A furnaceman, named Edward Bibby, of Anne-street, West, was summoned for non-payment of £2 15s. Bd. owing to the Widnes Local Board for district rate.—Evidence was given by the collector that for five weeks the earnings of defendant had been £8 193. 6d., and he also let off the front of his premises for 4s. a week.—Bibby was instructed to pay the amount in 14 days, or, in default, be committed to gaol one month. THE ScirooL BOARD AT Wonx.—The following people wete summoned by the Widnes School Board, for not send- ing their children to school :—Samuel Stanley, James Tom- linson, James Lewis, John Worthington, James Tallent, and John McCann. Mr. G. H. Danby, clerk to the Board prose- cuted, and each defendant had ss, to pay.

GOLBORNE. SUDDEN DEATH —On Friday, Mary Ann Twist (24), a native of Ciolborne, was invited to tea in aneighbour's house. She accepted the invitation, and she bad not been in more than a few minutes before she was seized with a violent fit of coughing, and died before assistance could be rendered. She had been unwell for some time. DEATH OF A WATERLOO VETERAN.—OR Saturday, Rd. Holt, a Waterloo veteran, aged 89 years, died at Golborne. He was in the Peninsula war, and also fought under Wel- lington at Waterloo. He had several medals, of which he was particularly proud. His funeral took place on Thursday afternoon at St. Thomas's Church, at which many friends and relations were present.

The usual fortnightly meeting of the Prescot Board of Guardians was held at the Board-room, Whiston Workhouse, on Thursday, Mr. S. Marsh presiding. There were also present the Revs. T. Chambers, and J. Barnacle, Messrs. W. Tyrer, J. Fidler, J. T. Hall, J. Leatherbarrow, W. A. Mea- dows, Fisher, Kenwright, Leigh, Birchall, Gerrard, Syder, Penketh, Ranson, Jackson, and Buckley, with Mr. S. H. Hartley (clerk).—The minutes of the last meeting were read and confirmed.

WORKHOUSE MASTER'S REPORT. The WORKHOUSE MASTER (Mr. W. H. Bicknell), ieported that there were 504 inmates in the workhouse at the end of this week, as compared with 499 in the preceding week, and 532 in the corresponding week of last year. There were 147 boys and girls at Kirkdale schools. THE VISITORS' BOOK. The CLERK read the following entry in the visitors' book: —" I have inspected the old and new vagrant wards, the sick wards, and the infectious ward to-day.—H. STEVENS, 17th, January, 1882."--In answer to a question, the Clerk said Mr. Stevens was the assistant inspector. INFORMATION REQUIRED BY THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT BOARD. The CLERK read a letter from the Local Government Board requesting to be furnished with a statement of the number of paupers in receipt of relief on January Ist, in the Prescot Union. The Clerk also read'another letter from the Board asking for returns relating to children whose births were registered during the year 1880, and the period from the Ist January, to the 30th June, 1881. THE BOARD AUTHORISED TO SIIIBSCRIBE TO CERTAIN PUBLIC

INSTITUTIONS. The CLERK read the following letter, dated January 16th, from the Local Government Board :—" I am directed by the Local Government Board to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 30th ult., in which you request their sanction to the Guardians of the Prescot Union subscribing to the funds of certain institutions mentioned therein. The Board in pursuance of the provision contained in the statute 14 and 15 Viet. cap. 105, section 4, sanction the proposed annual subscription of £5 ss. to the funds of the Royal Infirmary, Liverpool, and they direct me to enclose herewith copy of a letter, which they addressed to the Guardians on the 29th of June 1855, in which subscriptions of £5 55. and £3 3s. respectively to the funds of the school for the Blind, Hardman-street, Liverpool, and the Deaf and Dumb Institution, Oxford:street, Liverpool, were sanctioned by the Board. W. SENDALL, assistant secretary."—Mr. FIDLER moved that cheques be drawn for the sums named.—This was seconded and agreed to, and it was:understoad that the cheques would be forwarded to the governors of the respec- tive institutions.

AN APPOINTMENT CONFIRMED. The following letter, dated January 24th, from the Local Government Board was read :—" I am directed by the Local Government Board to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 16th instant, and to inform you that, under the circumstances therein mentioned, they will offer no objec- tion to the appointment of Mr. James Houghton to the office of assistant overseer for the Bold district of the Prescot Union. EDWARD SUTTON."—The CLERK said he had written to Mr. Houghton asking him to see 'Mr. Rigby at once, and he had also written to Mr. Rigby asking him to give up the books so that Mr. Houghton could get on with the collection of the rates of the Bold district. THE RE-VALUATION OF THE RAILWAYS IN THE UNION. The CLERK reported that Messrs. Marshall and M'Con- nell, who had been appointed to assist the Assessment Com- mittee in arriving at the proper value of the railways in the Union, hoped to be able to complete the re-valuation by the end of April next. AN INMATE IN WANT OF TOBACCO. The CLERK said he had received another letter from the inmate, John Owen. (Laughter, and cries of "Don't read it.")—The CHAIRMAN: He only wants a little tobacco. What age is he P—The CLERK: He is 60 years of age.—Mr. MEADOWS said there was no doubt the poor fellow was falling away fearfully.—The CHAIRMAN said if the doctor would put it on the books some tobacco would be given to him.—Mr. FIDLER said that when the doctor was on the premises let his attention be called to the matter, so that a s'op might be put to the fellow's clamour. He was like a living skeleton.—The CLERK observed that he would se e the doctor, and the subject dropped. THE REMOVAL OF PAUPER CHILDREN TO PANTASAPH. The CLERK said he had received the following letter from the Rev. Father Henry :—" Portico, January, 23rd, 1882.— Dear Mr. Hartley,—l send you enclosed a list of 20 girls whom I think fit to be sent to Pantasaph. I have acquainted Mr. Chambers, as chairman of the placing-out committee, and asked him to take the matter in hand. Will yon be so kind to give Mr. Chambers the list. The committee could examine it perhaps after the Board meeting, so that the children might go at an early date. I had a letter from Pantasaph telling me that there is room for 20, who might go at short notice. The examination at Kirkdale Schools will be over I think, or at least, near at hand."—The Rev. T. CHAMBERS said he had had a private letter from Father Henry, asking if he knew why such a request he had made had not been attended to before He (Mr. Chambers) there- fore hoped if there was no good reason why the request should not be attended to, the children should be sent at once.—The CLERK said that when Father Henry sent his former application, many of the statements in hie letter were not quite correct. He had been misinformed, and some of the children were not fit to be sent. We can only send a certain number of children.—After further discussion the matter eves referred to the placing-out committee. ALTERATIONS TO THE ST. HELENS RELIEF OFFICE. The Clerk submitted tenders for alterations to the relief office at St, Helens, so as to adapt it to the purposes of three relieving officers instead of two, as formerly.—On the motion of Mr. RANSON, it was resolved that the tender of Mr. Chas. Sutherland, of Croppet's Hill, St. Helene, to carry out the alterations for £6 18s. be accepted. A DIFFICULTY NOT EASILY SURMOUNTED. The CLERK stated that at the last meeting a woman named Green was ordered to be discharged from the house. As she was leaving the Workhouse his attention was drawn to her condition. She was pregnant, and near her confine- ment. She had a husband living in Trantnere, Birkenhead, and hi sent over Mr. Seddon to ask him if he would fetch his wife, but he refused to do so. In this "case the woman left her husband; the latter did not turn her out, and they could not bring him up for neglect of family. He was afraid he Could not obtain an order for her to be removed to the Birkenhead Union, because her chargeability was caused in the Prescot Union from sick- ness.—The CLERK read a lot of correspondence, from which it appeared that the woman bore a bad character, having been in gaol on various occasions for theft, &c.—lt was resolved that the Clerk visit Birkenhead and see what I arrangements could be made. THE RELIEF QUESTION AGAIN.—MR. HALL AND MR. MEADOWS. Mr. HALL said that some short time ago he made a state- ment to the Board showing that on account of the revisions an average saving would be effected of something like I £2,000 a year. The following meeting Mr. Meadows attended and asked for certain information to be supplied to him through the Clerk. Whether he disputed his (Mr. Hall's) statement he could not say. He had been waiting to see if Mr. Meadows had got the information or not, to see whether he (Mr. Hall) was right or wrong. Mr. Meadows observed that of course the revisions showed a great saving immediately after they were held, but in two or three months afterwards, instead of there being a saving as the statement made out, there was an actual loss. He (Mr. Meadows) had asked for a statement, but the statement he required had not yet been obtained. If he could get the statement he had asked for, he should be most happy to go into the matter, and show Mr. Hall this saving of £2,000 was very erroneons. He bad seen a statement showing that more than one half of the peop'e who left the house had re- turned to it. •He wanted to know the number of persons struck off the books for out-door relief together with the amounts they were receiving at the the time, and the num- ber of persons sent out of the house. He also wanted to know bow many of those struck off the books for out-door relief had been put on again and the amounts they were now receiving, and also how many of those sent out of the house had returned again. He also wanted the cost of the expenses for conveyances and for refreshments for the days on which the revisions were held. Mr. HALL said he had not intefered with the house at all—he had not touched the cost of the house. All he spoke.of was that an average saving was being effected in out-door relief since the revision, and that was shown in figures prodaced by Mr. Hartley since. He thought it very unkind of Mr. Meadows to say that his statement was erroneous. He would not allow it.—Mr. MEADOWS: You will grant that people struck off the books have been put on again ?—Mr. HALL: I shall grant nothing. —Mr. MEADOWS said that Mr. Hall's statement went out to the Board as a saving of £2,000. He maintained that it was misleading.—Mr. HALL observed that he had said it was an average saving.—ln the course of further conversa- tion the clerk remarked that so far as his office was con- cerned, Mr. Meadows had been supplied with all the infor- mation that was necessary to prove the accuracy or in- accuracy of Mr. Hall's figures.—Mr.HAraeasked for returns, and they were prepared with considerable trouble and loss of time by the relieving officers and others. These returns showed what amount of relief was given a month before the revision and for several months after. They showed that at the time Mr. Meadows asked for information—he thought in November—the relief then given was leas than in July, im- mediately after the revision took place, so that people cou3d not be put on the books again, or if they were put on others were struck off.—Mr. MEADOWS moved that returns be pre- pared of the number of persons receiving out-door relief struck off the books at the revision, and the amount they were receivin, the number reinstated and the amount they were receiving; also the number of persons discharged from the Workhouse and the number readmitted, with the Guardians' costs of conducting the revisions.—Mr. RANSON considered that, taking the year through, very little saving would be effected. He would second Mr. Meadow's motion, only he did not think it would do any good.—The subject was then allowed to drop. THE ADMISSION OF SICK PERSONS TO THE WORKHOUSE: IMPORTANT INFORMATION.

The Rev. T. CHAMBERS said be should be glad to know I for the information of the poor in the union, the relieving officers; and the medical officers, upon what certificate a- man or woman taken suddenly ill, would be admitted to the house. Was it necessary to get the relieving officer's note, or the medical officer's certificate or was it necessary to get both. The reason he asked was becauso he happened to know of a case where a medical officer's certificate was given the person was refuted admission becav-le the relieving oUicer had not

div.head: WENSFORD.,
div.p: WENSFORD.,

- - SAD ACCIDENT AT WINSFORD.-00 Saturday night, Wm. Grimshaw was killed on the London and North-Western Railway. It is supposed he had trespassed on the line, and was taking a short cut home, but was knocked down and run over. He was a member of the Over rifle corps, and leaves a wife and several children to mourn his loss.

The report of the Committee on the Revision Bill was discussed in the French Chamber of Deputies. The House Tejectei, by 298 votes against 173, a proposal by N. Barodet in favour of " unlimited revisiou,".

(given it.—Mr. FIDLER observed that he knew admission to the house had been refused on simply a medical order.—The CLERK, in answer to Mr. Chambers, said there were four modes by which a sick person could get admission to the house. One was by obtaining an order of the relieving officer, , another by an order of the Board of Guardians; and in ex- treme cases where the relieving officer could not be met with, by an order from the overseer; or failing all these a master might admit without an order at all, and then report the case or cases to the next meeting of the board. ' A medical officer had no right or power to give an order for admission to the workhouse. He could recommend. Mr. CHAMBERS asked if it I was necessary for a man to go from a medical man to the relieving officer before coming to the 1 house.—The CLERK replied in the affirmative, and observed 1 that every person admitted to the Workhouse on a medical i officer's recommendation, that recommendation must be ac- ' companied by the relieving officer's certificate.—Mr. FIDLER remarked that the inference to be drawn from Mr. Cham- bers' remarks was that some man had been refused admis- sion to the house. If a man had been refused, on what grounds. Let them have it out.—Mr. CHAMBERS said he asked for information and he had e'o•ot it. He would not go any further in the matter.—Rev. J. BARNACLE asked if Mr. Chambers would allow an officer to neglect his duty and not bring it before the Board.—Mr. CHAMBERS replied in the negative, and observed that if it came before his notice again he should bring it before the Board.—After further conversation the subject was allowed to drop, and the Board rose.

FIRST ANNUAL SUPPER OF THE L. AND N.-W. RAILWAY CO.'S LOCO. DEPARTMENT AT WIDNES. On Saturday evening the employs in the locomotive department of the London and North-Western Railway Co., at Widnes, held their first annual super at the Temperance Hotel, Victoria-road. Among the invited guests were Mr. E. Sansom, station master, and Mr. T. Carter, traffic inspector. At eight o'clock 56 sat down to a well-served and substantial repast. Mr. Turnbull, chief locomotive foreman, presided at the after proceedings, and the vice chair was occupied by Mr. Carter. The CHAIRMAN apologised for the absence of Mr. Newton, their respected master, who had written expressing regret at his inability to be present, and a hope that all would enjoy a pleasant evening. The usual loyal and patriotic toasts were drunk; and Mr. Gibson, in a neat speech, proposed that of the Queen. He said this toast was one which all true Englishmen would drink with pleasure. Her Majesty was a pure and a noble woman, whose example might well and profitably for the people be followed by all succeeding monarchs. Like her true subjects, she was a dear lover of peace; and he would therefore invite them to drink Her Majesty's health right heartily. The toast was drunk with much enthusiasm. Mr.. Hudson (traffic department) then sing "The lost child ;" and he was followed by Mr. Platt, who rendered "The anchor's weighed" with good effect. The CHAIRMAN called on Mr. Sansom to propose the health of the London and North-Western Railway Co. Mr. SANsom, who, on rising, was received with cheers, I sail the reception they had so kindly accorded him gave him much joy; but, he feared, those who on that or any other account expected from him a long speech were destined to disappointment. It would be ungracious in him long to engage their attention, the consideration being time and the hour. How- ever, having risen at their kind bidding they naturally expected to hear something and he proposed telling them of some feats they had themselves performed. (Applause.) He said some few nights ago at the supper which his own department sat down to, that during the last year they had carried no less than 50,000,000 passengers: 35,000,000 tons of merchandsse, over distances amounting in the aggre- gate to 35,500,000 miles !—(applause)—and that their receipts during the period named amounted to more than 10,000,000 sterling! He would now invite them to con- sider what a part they had played in the accomplishment of this the greatest success known to the company since its formation. Who in these enormous transits of men and women led the dangerous van? Some of them remembered the first journey they conducted, how exceedingly anxious they were lest they should lose time or overshoot the platforms—how they peered for the signals till their eyes dilated with the strain—for they knew if they hoped to main- tain their position they must prove themselves above all things else vigilent, precise and sure. (Loud applause.) Of the 50,000 workers employed by the company he knew of none who had more individual responsibility assigned to them. Many, and heart-felt, were the blessings bestowed on them by passengers as they passed their engines on their way out of the terminus after a long 40 miles an hour journey. They were the silently, but much admired and trusty servants of the public, and the flower of the railway service. (Loud applause.) He had not framed these expressions to please their ear that night, they were deep rooted, and had their birth long before he had contemplated making the service his profession. (Applause.) Might they live long and happy in the service, and have it at the finish to say no man was ever knocked down by the engine I drove for want of watch- fulness and warning on my part. (Loud applause.) The I toast was most enthusiastically drank with musical honours. Mr. PARR (driver) then gave "The dashing steam loom weaver," creating, as he went along, great mirth. The CHAIRMAN next proposed the "Donors." They, he said, had been most generous, and had most willingly furnished forth the feast which they had all so much enjoyed. (Applause). The toast was drunk with musical honours. This was followed by a violin solo by Mr. Gill, and a laughable song call "La-de-da," by Mr. Waldren. The CHAIRMAN now proposed The Town and Trade of Widnes." and called on Inspector Carter to respond. Mr. CARTER said when he came to Widnes 14 years ago, one shunting engine was sufficient with which to manage the trade of Widnes, but now they had no fewer than ten en- gines at work. Only a short time ago they were obliged to pull down their large engine shed and build ta more extensive one, and he hoped that before this year Was through, the increase of trade would render further accommodation necessary. They were all depending on the town and trade of Widnes, and he hoped they would ere long find it necessary to run double the number of trains from it. (Applause.) Next in order came several good songs; the toasts of "The Host," "The Health of the Chairman and Vice-Chair- man," and about 12 o'clock the large party broke up, having spent a most enjoyable evening.

WIDNES AND RITWORN CANARY SHOW. The first show of this recently formed society was held on Saturday afternoon, in the National schoolroom, Widnes. The President of the Society is Mr. E. Knowles, and the vice-president Mr. S. Davies. The members of the commit- tee are- Messrs. W. Pickthall, J. Lewis, J. Glenan, L. Knowles, W. Trudgen, W. Foyfoot, J. Pick thall, J. Stevenson, J. Ormroyde, J. Co mer, and D. Dale. The show was a highly successful one, and reflected the greatest credit upon those who had, under considerable difficulties, carried out the pre- liminary arrangements. About 200 birds, many of them of first class breed, were shown. Some of these were valued at £5O, and several were marked £2O. The judging was gone through by Mr. J. Brough, of Liverpool, a breeder of many years' experience. There was a capital attendance of the public. The amount of the prizes ranged from 103., 65., 45., and 35., to 25., and amounted in value to about £l5. We understand that a similar exhibition has been held at Prescot for several years. There are a large number of bird fanciers in this district, and the committee, who are much gratified at the manner in which their first effort has been received, feel assured that the Widnes and Runcorn show will in future years take a high rank. ADDRESS BY MR. JAMES TOMKINSON. A dinner to memorate Mr. Gladstone's seventy•second birthday was held at the Town Hall, Chester, on Wednesday' night, by the Liberal workingmen who were unable to part' cipate in the banquet held for the same purpose recentlY' Mr. James Tomkinson, the Liberal candidate for West Cheshire, presided, and the attendance numbered about 250. The The Chairman, in proposing the toast of the evening, " health of Mr. Gladstone," reviewed the right hon. gentle- man's career, and said that, following the principles ef Richard Cobden—(applause)—he had by Lis fiscal policy conferred upon this country material a.dvantays and a prosperity such as they had never seen in any country under the guidance of any statesman. (APPlanete') Alluding to the Conservative cry regarding Free Trader be said that taxes on imports by no means raised our revenue for we derived more pecuniary advantages from a - r ' All ty 4, when it was 61. in the pound than when it was 2s. 6d. •"' to the Liberal policy with regard to Ireland, he wculd sald that their motto was, never to despair of that country an... , never to give up hope with regard to it; whilst the Consus. vative motto was, to put Ireland under water for 10 toinuteb. , He had frequently said that if Ireland could onlY ,; ._ governed by coercion and held down by military forcer util ette ' Liberal party was not the party to deal with it. (I`e..st applause.) At the present time there were much b , signs with respect to the future than had been for a lon_g. time past. Outrages were diminishing, juries were fear' lessly doing their duty, and malefactors were at the 051: sent aced to such terms of punishment as must deter the '') accomplices from pursuing their wicked courses. (APPlneee:o Mr. Tomkinson then contrasted the state of the country 11 1874, when an ungrateful country turned Mr. Gladstone cu. , of office, with its condition in 18.80, when the Conservati:l7 , were turned out and the Liberals restored to povver. tv eue: Gladstone left in 1874 a surplus of six millions, the es. quer was overflowing, and trade and commerce flourishea When he resumed office in 1880 he found a debt of tweati; one millions. Two disastrous and dishonourable wars t hal; been concluded, whilst a third war was on the Peiiea-- ° breaking out. What had he done since thea ? He ut,,os not by playing one country against another, but by In`-s3 of the harmonious action of united Europe—settled th4r. questions which essentially disturbed the general peace', ail Gladstone was known, not only in our own country bui, . ir over the world, as a friend of liberty ; and he (Mr. 'l°s the the son) knew no more touching episode than that, when rof time the corporation of London voted that a marble bu.bi, the Premier should be put up in the Guildhall, the ightaDe tants of Greece sent a request that his features 'nig'''. 3 delineated in the marble of the quarries of Shares a' nf tribute to the man who had listened to the expressioas "re their national aspirations. (Applause.) As regarded fatcieto legislation, they knew that Mr. Gladstone had prouling Ireform our land laws, to give the county franchise, to h." 130, in a bankruptcy bill, and to simplify and cheapen electoral 1 (Applause.) He had also to undertake the reform ef 'uebot I Government in London, and a hundred other measures ; .64 it was impossible that even one of these could be cerri:ad through in due course until Parliamentary procedare was been thoroughly reformed. (Applause.) The toast.heral drunk with great enthusiasm. The toast of " The bi„-cied party "was proposed by Mr. E. P. Salisbury, and resP°' to by Mr. Stevenson. Other toasts followed.

CANA DA. The Marquis of Lorne arrived at Ottowa on Monday. 'RUSSIA. A correspondent at St. Petersburg, telegraphing on Tues- day, states that in the majority of the districts the inhabit- ants have informed the Provincial Commissions that they desire the complete expatriation of the Jews. An understanding has, the St. Petersburg Bourse Gazette says, been arrived at between the Russian Government and the Porte with regard to the payment of the war indemnity. EGYPT. The news from Egypt in a Cairo telegram of Monday's date is that the situation is more tranquil, in consequence of the firm attitude of the Control and the Ministers. Parlia- ment vacillates, and is inclined to moderate its demands, giving hopes of a possible compromise as regards the Bud- get, but the question of the responsibility of the Ministers remains open. According to a correspondent at Alexandria, the impres- sion continues to gain ground there that the differences between the Chamber of Deputies and the Ministry will be composed, and an amicable compromise efftcted. HERZEGOVINA. Austrian accounts of the rising in Herzegovina and Dal- matia state that the Prince of Montenegro informed a depu- tation of Iferzegovinians that they must not look for any help from him. The Prince, moreover, threatened to intern at Podgoritza all Herzegovinians who were found on his territory if they were engaged in hostilities against Austria. It is noteworthy that these assurances were given in the presence of the Austrian Minister to Montenegro. EARTHQUAKE IN CHINA.-250 PERSONS KILLED. Intelligence has reached England from Yokohama' of a , , destructive earthquake in China. The news which was despatched from Yokohama on December 25th, coming by way of San Francisco and New York, is exceedingly meagre. In simply announces the fact that a severe earthquake had occurred in the district of Kantcheon, and that more than 250 persons had been killed. THE AUSTRIAN WAR PREPARATIONS. Advices state that the rumour of Austria preparing for war with Italy created on Tuesday considerable excitement in Manchester and Liverpool, and on the London Stock Ex- change the situation was regarded as serious. TRIESTE, Tuesday.—A steamer leaving the port to-day for Cattaro will take a number of officers of general staff, several eurgeons of the reserve, and a detachment of the hospital corps. Landphr Battalions numbers 79 and 80 have been mobilised.
